Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: Back to Articles How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 23 +17 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget. To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points. Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain. An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated. A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running. That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%. What Changed in the Grader To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime. The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810. Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version. The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. items.content: What will our economic future look like? We don’t know yet how AI will reshape the economy. Will it lead to unprecedented growth? Widespread unemployment? Neither, or something else? How can we tell? Anthropic’s Economics team built a model of how AI might affect jobs, growth, and unemployment in the US in coming years. Read about possible economic futures and make your own predictions about AI capabilities to see the economy they imply. Read technical report Jump to explorer Read blog W e study how AI is reshaping the economy because we’re committed to ensuring that this transition is beneficial for society, including workers. By providing better visibility into our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure that everyone benefits from it. While our Economic Index measures how AI is being used across the economy right now, this scenario explorer is about looking ahead. Based on our technical report, Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI (Korinek et al., 2026), this explorer gives you a chance to find out what the economy might look like as AI continues to get more capable. In scenarios ranging from business as usual to an economy where AI increases growth to about twice the normal rate, unemployment stays within the historical range and wages remain flat or rise depending on the industry. But in scenarios where growth is faster than anything in economic history, there are adverse impacts on wages and job prospects for knowledge workers. In those scenarios, society is far wealthier, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are broadly shared. As you scroll down, you’ll see an overview of how AI affects the economy. Then, you can plug in your expectations for how capable AI will be, and how extensively it will be used across the economy in the future. The model will show you what the economy in 2030 might look like if your predictions come true—and how your predictions compare to others. A nurse ’s tasks Tasks unchanged by AI Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI The economy is made out of tasks This model represents all the jobs people do in the economy as bundles of tasks. AI can help people do a given task better or faster. It can automate the task. It might not affect the task at all. And it can lead to new tasks. Think of a day in the life of a nurse You can think of any job as a bundle of tasks that someone does. She does rounds to check on a sick patient. She draws blood. She triages incoming patients, charts patients’ vitals, and orders supplies for the ward. That’s just the start of the list. Each of the tasks listed are based on the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy, listing the tasks for each occupation. Jobs change over time Tasks leave the bundle ( hardly anyone hand-writes paper charts anymore ) and new tasks arrive ( 30 years ago, no one monitored patients remotely ). The bundle of tasks isn’t static, and the job changes as tasks change. Only humans can do some tasks For instance, AI can’t bathe a patient. Some tasks will get augmented AI helps a human do them better, or faster. AI helps the nurse draft discharge instructions, monitor patients remotely, and plan the shift’s care schedule. Some tasks may get fully automated For instance, AI may chart a patient’s vitals, or order the ward’s supplies. And new tasks will appear Historically, new technologies have also created new tasks for workers. For a nurse, that might be checking how well an AI triages patients, or reviewing an AI-proposed care plan. The result: the nurse ’s job changes As the nurse incorporates AI into her job, the nurse is able to oversee and accomplish more. She can spend more time talking with patients and helping them understand diagnoses. Productivity increases. Every task happens millions of times every day, across the country Nurses are doing their work on every ward and on every shift. As more nurses use AI, AI supports a higher percentage of these millions of instances of each task. From tasks to the economy Today, if you add up every single instance of tasks performed in the US, by people and by the machines and software they work with, you get the US economy: over $30 trillion of value created over the past year. So how will AI shape the economy of the future? The answer depends on how AI affects all the tasks that make up the economy, the new tasks it creates, and how fast AI takes on this work. Will AI lead to more task augmentation or automation? How much more productive will it make us? How quickly will it be adopted by workers and companies? The answers to these questions have direct effects on GDP, the labor market, and the share of the pie taken home by workers. There are many possible futures, but we’re highlighting three scenarios The future will depend on how AI’s capabilities advance, and how industries and workers adopt those capabilities. The three scenarios we share capture distinct kinds of impact. In the modest scenario , it’s hard to see the effect of AI in macroeconomic data: its economic impact is something like the internet’s. In the substantial scenario , AI makes a bigger impact than the internet, or the railroad. And in the extreme scenario , AI drives a completely transformed, unprecedented economy, likely driven by recursively self-improving AI systems and a faster rate of AI adoption. Small economic gains In the modest scenario , AI has roughly the same kind of impact as the internet did. It drives real economic gains, but they’re within the historical norm for new technologies, and they arrive gradually. A revolution in knowledge work In the substantial scenario , AI is capable of doing half of all knowledge work by 2030, the majority of it autonomously, but it’s not adopted for all of that work: most knowledge work tasks are still done without AI. The economy grows at twice its normal rate. Wages for knowledge workers don’t rise, but other workers see gains. A profound economic transformation In the extreme scenario , AI is more productive than humans at the vast majority of knowledge-work tasks. It does nearly all of them autonomously, and it creates essentially no new knowledge tasks for people. This scenario would likely require recursively self-improving AI, adopted quickly for knowledge work. As AI diffuses, annual GDP growth rates reach 15 % a year, leading the economy to double in size every 4.5 years. As a society, we’re far richer than we’ve ever been, but many fewer workers have jobs in knowledge work, and unemployment has risen beyond typical recessionary levels. How might powerful AI change the economy? How do you think AI development will go over the next few years? And what would that path mean for the economy? We invite you to consider these questions, and explore potential answers with our scenario explorer. Make your predictions Skip to the scenarios People’s expectations about future AI capabilities vary. In August, we surveyed more than 10,000 Americans about their views on present and future AI capabilities, adoption, and the ease of finding new work if they have to change occupations. The typical respondent’s answers imply outcomes close to the “substantial change” scenario: GDP is 10% higher by 2030 than it would be without AI, and the overall unemployment rate has risen to around 5%. Around 10% of respondents have views in line with the extreme scenario. How people answered the five questions (share of respondents at each answers) Capabilities What tasks can AI do? 0% 100% Adoption How much do people use AI? 0% 100% Autonomy How much does AI do by itself? Almost none Some of them About half Most of them Almost all of them Productivity How much more productive does AI make people? Same 1.5× 2× 4× 10×+ Adjustment How long does it take people to find a new job? 1–2 months ~3 months ~6 months ~9 months A year 2 years 3+ years or never General public n = 10,980 Site visitors n = 32,645 You predicted one possible future for the economy. Here’s what that future could look like. Finding 1: GDP growth AI grows the economy in every scenario, but some more than others AI drives GDP growth in all scenarios, although the scale varies enormously depending on the scenario. US GDP in 2030, by scenario (measured in trillions of dollars)* Modest scenario +1.6% $34.1T GDP Substantial scenario +8.3% $36.3T GDP Extreme scenario +32.4% $44.4T GDP Task types Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI Productivity *GDP is calculated at 2025 price levels But growth isn’t the only economic dynamic we care about. What would these potential futures mean for how much of this growth workers receive in their paychecks, or how many people have to find new jobs? This model isn’t a complete map of reality, but it shows us some interesting findings. The country’s GDP will grow, but a larger share of that prosperity might go to the resources and technology used to create more wealth (capital) compared to workers, even if society as a whole is much wealthier. And in most scenarios, job reallocation and unemployment both stay within ranges history has seen before, with one exception. In the extreme scenario, if we see recursive self-improvement and rapid adoption, unemployment could spike to historic levels. Finding 2: Job reallocation In more transformative scenarios, more workers have to change occupations. That may mean higher unemployment. There is always some churn in the job market—people losing jobs and finding new ones. In normal times, this process can be painful, but works relatively well from a macroeconomic perspective. Most job seekers find new jobs fairly quickly. In our substantial and extreme scenarios, knowledge workers may see a lot of automation and displacement. At the individual level, it means coders and call service center agents may have to switch to jobs like electrician and nurse, which are less exposed to AI. But changing occupations entirely is hard, and it takes many people a long time to land a new job. The more of this switching a scenario requires, the more people will be between jobs. Where workers are in 2030 (percent of all workers) Modest Substantial Extreme 2026 2030 62.2% Knowledge workers 37.8% All other workers 2.5% Displaced 1.8% Crossed over 59.7% Still there 39.6% All other workers 0.7% Still need to move Knowledge workers All other workers Displaced As we progress from 2026 to 2030, the number of jobs available in occupations AI affects (knowledge work) decreases, while the jobs available in occupations AI doesn’t affect increase. Switching to a new occupation is difficult for a few reasons: workers may not want to change occupations. They may need to learn new skills. And even when they do, it’s not easy to get a new job. In the extreme scenario, as large swathes of knowledge work are automated more quickly, affected workers may be unemployed for a prolonged period. Unemployment in knowledge work rises; in other occupations, it falls modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Total Finding 3: Wages Across the three scenarios, average wages rise, but this increase is concentrated in occupations outside of knowledge work. That’s because it takes time for workers to switch to occupations where demand is rising. If there’s less demand for human knowledge work, that puts downward pressure on wages. Meanwhile, as AI increases productivity within knowledge work, the demand for manual work that benefits from that productivity will increase. For example, more quickly producing designs and permitting for physical infrastructure could increase the number of construction projects, resulting in rising demand for construction workers, which pushes those wages higher. In the substantial scenario, wages for knowledge workers are essentially flat. In the extreme scenario, they fall by more than 10% by 2030. Pay by occupation group, percent above the same economy without AI modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Average Finding 4: Labor vs. capital share The pie will grow, but a larger share might go to capital Today, of each dollar the economy produces, about 60 ¢ goes to workers and 40 ¢ go to capital. If the economy grows, but AI automates more tasks, more of each dollar might go to capital. This can happen even when wages for all workers rise substantially. If capital becomes more useful for more things, it will be in higher demand, which raises its price. In that world, more of the gains from a growing economy flow to owners of capital. We find that the labor share falls noticeably in the substantial and extreme scenarios, and the capital share rises. Average wages rise—non-knowledge workers are paid much more—but wages for knowledge workers stagnate or decline alongside worsening unemployment. In the extreme scenario, the gains from a rapidly expanding economy are unevenly distributed. Most knowledge workers face either lower wages or unemployment, and workers overall get a smaller fraction of the larger pie. Total labor income is barely changed by 2030. In this scenario, the main challenge is not achieving economic growth, but making sure the benefits are broadly shared and the costs aren’t unequally dispersed. How GDP is shared between workers and capital Modest scenario $34.1T GDP 59.4 % to labor 40.6 % to capital (up 0.6 points) Substantial scenario $36.3T GDP 56.1 % to labor 43.9 % to capital (up 3.9 points) Extreme scenario $44.4T GDP 45.2 % to labor 54.8 % to capital (up 14.8 points) Task types Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI Productivity With each scenario, the total economy grows (measured in GDP). But more of the growth goes to capital, compared to the amount people receive in their wages. Some professions see their wages increase significantly, but overall, wages make up a smaller share of the country’s economic growth. The future is not predetermined. Ultimately, what the economy looks like in 2030 depends on many factors, like what AI can do, and how companies and workers choose to adopt it. It also depends on how the financial benefit of this technology is shared. Like any economic model, this one has limits. For example, we did not include scenarios where humanity develops hyper-capable robots. The model draws on our research and external review, and we’ll keep adding to it as the evidence develops. This model, alongside our full research portfolio, will inform the research Anthropic funds to identify effective interventions for labor market disruptions. It’ll also inform the policy ideas we propose , with the goal of ensuring that the economic benefits of AI are broadly shared across society, both in the US and around the world. Disclaimer and thanks to reviewers v1.0 of the Econ Scenario Explorer, September 2026 The economic scenario explorer is currently Version 1.0. Like every model, it is a stark simplification of a complex reality: it isolates a few key forces and omits many others that may become relevant and important in the coming years. For example, it leaves out policy responses, business cycles, potential aggregate demand or financial market disruptions, and possible catastrophic risks. The scenario explorer is a work in progress, and we expect it to evolve both as we invest more time and as economic research itself develops. We are grateful to the economists who read an early draft of the technical report that lays out the framework behind the explorer, Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI , and gave us detailed comments: Daron Acemoglu, Lukas Althoff, David Autor, Tom Cunningham, Lukas Freund, Joe Hazell, Ben Jones, Pete Klenow, Danial Lashkari, Kurt Mitman, Ben Moll, Emi Nakamura, Pascual Restrepo, David Romer, Jón Steinsson, Chris Tonetti, Ludo Visschers, and David Wiczer. Their feedback was generous and candid, and it has already improved our model. Two examples: several reviewers noted that advances in AI may raise the returns to capital, so that more of the gains flow to the owners of capital; and several noted that the wages of workers in the occupations AI affects most may diverge from those in occupations it barely affects. Both channels are now part of the scenarios. External reviewers were not asked to endorse our conclusions, and any remaining errors are ours. Other criticisms are still open, and we plan to address many of them in future versions. Reviewers pointed out that the model does not follow individual workers, so it can only paint a very coarse picture of the costs of job displacement. Some questioned whether occupations exposed to AI will shrink at all rather than grow. Some felt the most extreme scenario is better read as a thought experiment than a scenario, while others felt the most modest one understates what is already visible in the data. Several asked us to be clearer that the model does not include the aggregate demand effects driven by the data center buildout. And more than one reviewer argued that we may be underestimating how much AI could accelerate technological progress itself. We agree that many of these are limitations of the current model. The scenario explorer should be viewed as a tool for thinking about what different technological developments would imply for the economy—actual outcomes may differ materially. Anton Korinek, Chad Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, and Peter McCrory developed the economic model and co-authored the companion technical report. Santi Ruiz wrote this piece with them, with editorial support from Sarah Pollack and Adam Farina. Kelsey Nanan designed and built the interactive experience, with visual design and art direction by Nikki Makagiansar and Monika Tuchowska; Kyle Turman and Szymon Sacher built the scenario explorer and led the translation of the model into interactive form; Fayaz Ashraf and Ryan Heller contributed engineering, and Kim Withee and Maria Gonzalez supported production. Szymon Sacher and Tess Cotter designed and fielded the accompanying surveys with Morning Consult, with support from Ben Fowler. Peter McCrory, Anton Korinek, and Charles Yang coordinated the project, and Jack Clark provided direction throughout. Miriam Chaum, Jack Clark, Saffron Huang, Maxim Massenkoff, and Peter McCrory helped originate this effort. Jim Baker, Shan Carter, Johannes Hermle, Zoë Hitzig, and Eva Lyubich provided feedback.

What would these potential futures mean for how much of this growth workers receive in their paychecks, or how many people have to find new jobs? This model isn’t a complete map of reality, but it shows us some interesting findings. The country’s GDP will grow, but a larger share of that prosperity might go to the resources and technology used to create more wealth (capital) compared to workers, even if society as a whole is much wealthier. And in most scenarios, job reallocation and unemployment both stay within ranges history has seen before, with one exception. In the extreme scenario, if we see recursive self-improvement and rapid adoption, unemployment could spike to historic levels. Finding 2: Job reallocation In more transformative scenarios, more workers have to change occupations. That may mean higher unemployment. There is always some churn in the job market—people losing jobs and finding new ones. In normal times, this process can be painful, but works relatively well from a macroeconomic perspective. Most job seekers find new jobs fairly quickly. In our substantial and extreme scenarios, knowledge workers may see a lot of automation and displacement. At the individual level, it means coders and call service center agents may have to switch to jobs like electrician and nurse, which are less exposed to AI. But changing occupations entirely is hard, and it takes many people a long time to land a new job. The more of this switching a scenario requires, the more people will be between jobs. Where workers are in 2030 (percent of all workers) Modest Substantial Extreme 2026 2030 62.2% Knowledge workers 37.8% All other workers 2.5% Displaced 1.8% Crossed over 59.7% Still there 39.6% All other workers 0.7% Still need to move Knowledge workers All other workers Displaced As we progress from 2026 to 2030, the number of jobs available in occupations AI affects (knowledge work) decreases, while the jobs available in occupations AI doesn’t affect increase. Switching to a new occupation is difficult for a few reasons: workers may not want to change occupations. They may need to learn new skills. And even when they do, it’s not easy to get a new job. In the extreme scenario, as large swathes of knowledge work are automated more quickly, affected workers may be unemployed for a prolonged period. Unemployment in knowledge work rises; in other occupations, it falls modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Total Finding 3: Wages Across the three scenarios, average wages rise, but this increase is concentrated in occupations outside of knowledge work. That’s because it takes time for workers to switch to occupations where demand is rising. If there’s less demand for human knowledge work, that puts downward pressure on wages. Meanwhile, as AI increases productivity within knowledge work, the demand for manual work that benefits from that productivity will increase. For example, more quickly producing designs and permitting for physical infrastructure could increase the number of construction projects, resulting in rising demand for construction workers, which pushes those wages higher. In the substantial scenario, wages for knowledge workers are essentially flat. In the extreme scenario, they fall by more than 10% by 2030. Pay by occupation group, percent above the same economy without AI modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Average Finding 4: Labor vs. capital share The pie will grow, but a larger share might go to capital Today, of each dollar the economy produces, about 60 ¢ goes to workers and 40 ¢ go to capital. If the economy grows, but AI automates more tasks, more of each dollar might go to capital. This can happen even when wages for all workers rise substantially. If capital becomes more useful for more things, it will be in higher demand, which raises its price. In that world, more of the gains from a growing economy flow to owners of capital. We find that the labor share falls noticeably in the substantial and extreme scenarios, and the capital share rises. Average wages rise—non-knowledge workers are paid much more—but wages for knowledge workers stagnate or decline alongside worsening unemployment. In the extreme scenario, the gains from a rapidly expanding economy are unevenly distributed. Most knowledge workers face either lower wages or unemployment, and workers overall get a smaller fraction of the larger pie. Total labor income is barely changed by 2030. In this scenario, the main challenge is not achieving economic growth, but making sure the benefits are broadly shared and the costs aren’t unequally dispersed. How GDP is shared between workers and capital Modest scenario $34.1T GDP 59.4 % to labor 40.6 % to capital (up 0.6 points) Substantial scenario $36.3T GDP 56.1 % to labor 43.9 % to capital (up 3.9 points) Extreme scenario $44.4T GDP 45.2 % to labor 54.8 % to capital (up 14.8 points) Task types Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI Productivity With each scenario, the total economy grows (measured in GDP). But more of the growth goes to capital, compared to the amount people receive in their wages. Some professions see their wages increase significantly, but overall, wages make up a smaller share of the country’s economic growth. The future is not predetermined. Ultimately, what the economy looks like in 2030 depends on many factors, like what AI can do, and how companies and workers choose to adopt it. It also depends on how the financial benefit of this technology is shared. Like any economic model, this one has limits. For example, we did not include scenarios where humanity develops hyper-capable robots. The model draws on our research and external review, and we’ll keep adding to it as the evidence develops. This model, alongside our full research portfolio, will inform the research Anthropic funds to identify effective interventions for labor market disruptions. It’ll also inform the policy ideas we propose , with the goal of ensuring that the economic benefits of AI are broadly shared across society, both in the US and around the world. Disclaimer and thanks to reviewers v1.0 of the Econ Scenario Explorer, September 2026 The economic scenario explorer is currently Version 1.0. Like every model, it is a stark simplification of a complex reality: it isolates a few key forces and omits many others that may become relevant and important in the coming years. For example, it leaves out policy responses, business cycles, potential aggregate demand or financial market disruptions, and possible catastrophic risks. The scenario explorer is a work in progress, and we expect it to evolve both as we invest more time and as economic research itself develops. We are grateful to the economists who read an early draft of the technical report that lays out the framework behind the explorer, Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI , and gave us detailed comments: Daron Acemoglu, Lukas Althoff, David Autor, Tom Cunningham, Lukas Freund, Joe Hazell, Ben Jones, Pete Klenow, Danial Lashkari, Kurt Mitman, Ben Moll, Emi Nakamura, Pascual Restrepo, David Romer, Jón Steinsson, Chris Tonetti, Ludo Visschers, and David Wiczer. Their feedback was generous and candid, and it has already improved our model. Two examples: several reviewers noted that advances in AI may raise the returns to capital, so that more of the gains flow to the owners of capital; and several noted that the wages of workers in the occupations AI affects most may diverge from those in occupations it barely affects. Both channels are now part of the scenarios. External reviewers were not asked to endorse our conclusions, and any remaining errors are ours. Other criticisms are still open, and we plan to address many of them in future versions. Reviewers pointed out that the model does not follow individual workers, so it can only paint a very coarse picture of the costs of job displacement. Some questioned whether occupations exposed to AI will shrink at all rather than grow. Some felt the most extreme scenario is better read as a thought experiment than a scenario, while others felt the most modest one understates what is already visible in the data. Several asked us to be clearer that the model does not include the aggregate demand effects driven by the data center buildout. And more than one reviewer argued that we may be underestimating how much AI could accelerate technological progress itself. We agree that many of these are limitations of the current model. The scenario explorer should be viewed as a tool for thinking about what different technological developments would imply for the economy—actual outcomes may differ materially. Anton Korinek, Chad Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, and Peter McCrory developed the economic model and co-authored the companion technical report. Santi Ruiz wrote this piece with them, with editorial support from Sarah Pollack and Adam Farina. Kelsey Nanan designed and built the interactive experience, with visual design and art direction by Nikki Makagiansar and Monika Tuchowska; Kyle Turman and Szymon Sacher built the scenario explorer and led the translation of the model into interactive form; Fayaz Ashraf and Ryan Heller contributed engineering, and Kim Withee and Maria Gonzalez supported production. Szymon Sacher and Tess Cotter designed and fielded the accompanying surveys with Morning Consult, with support from Ben Fowler. Peter McCrory, Anton Korinek, and Charles Yang coordinated the project, and Jack Clark provided direction throughout. Miriam Chaum, Jack Clark, Saffron Huang, Maxim Massenkoff, and Peter McCrory helped originate this effort. Jim Baker, Shan Carter, Johannes Hermle, Zoë Hitzig, and Eva Lyubich provided feedback.

items.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
items.summary: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale Formal verification can prove that code is free of certain bugs, but historically it has only been feasible for small codebases. With AI models, however, this is beginning to change. Here, we used Claude to prove security properties in over one hundred real-world open-source libraries over the span of a few weeks.

items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: Featured projects TorchTitan is a PyTorch-native platform for rapid experimentation and large-scale pre- and post-training of generative AI models. It is designed as a minimal, clean-room implementation of PyTorch-native techniques, with flexible extension points for users’ needs. This has enabled TorchTitan to find widespread adoption across research and production in academia and industry. The TorchTitan team landed massive improvements in the past year, without losing its minimal, extensible ethos. Enhancements include support for SOTA models, dramatic improvements of out-the-box performance at scale, RL support and new communication features. TorchTitan is for everyone – easy to use, providing SOTA performance and allowing users to start small and scale up seamlessly. We will present all these new improvements in the following sections, and we look forward to your feedback! New model support SOTA model support is critical for the success of training frameworks, and TorchTitan aims to always provide the latest advancements when it comes to open-weights architecture. TorchTitan added PyTorch-native support for Muse Spark Open , Muse Glimmer , Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 , Kimi K2.7 , Kimi K3 , and DeepSeek-V4 . These were full training-stack integrations with support across TorchTitan’s 5D parallelism stack . This work also introduced a composable configuration system built around typed Python recipes, model-config transforms, and targeted component overrides. Users can change parallelization strategies, model components, or hardware-specific kernels without maintaining separate model forks. The same interfaces integrate optimized kernels from Attention Gym, including Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, and sparse-attention kernels, as well as opt-in Helion kernels such as fused RoPE, while remaining compatible with torch.compile. Each frontier model expands TorchTitan’s reusable toolkit, from multimodal data pipelines, sample packing, shared vision components, and Hugging Face checkpoint interoperability to composable 5D parallelism, declarative sharding, optimized Attention Gym and Helion kernels, and rigorous numerical validation. However, newer features such as distributed Muon optimizer and blockwise quantization of parameters warrant or benefit from more esoteric sharding policies that are not possible with FSDP2. To address this, TorchTitan now integrates with FlexShard – a new data parallelism library for sharding model and optimizer state. FlexShard offers a bucket-centric API where each bucket of parameters can be sharded according to a customized Placement policy and has an optimized runtime that overlaps bucketed communication with computation. FlexShard offers similar placements as FSDP1 and FSDP2, but additionally offers new placements such as Owned where one rank owns an entire parameter, and BlockShard that allows 2D tile-aligned sharding. On DeepSeekV3 at 256 H100s, this improves the Optimizer time duration by up to 79% compared to an equivalent FSDP-only implementation. FlexShard also enabled TorchTitan to support blockwise-quantized parameter AllGathers: where FP8-quantized parameters are gathered by the collective, reducing communication volume by ~50%. With FSDP2, since the sharding boundaries may not necessarily be aligned with the blockwise quantization boundaries – we were forced to either gather the parameters in BF16 – increasing communication volume, or perform the FP8 all-gathers but with additional collectives for the quantization scaling factors. FlexShard’s BlockShard placement enables TorchTitan to get the best of both worlds – gather the quantized parameters without any additional communication for scaling factors, as the sharding strategy is by-definition aligned with the quantization scheme: on LLama3 405B at 256 H100s, this improves end-to-end training step time by up to 20%. TorchTitan supports both graph-based and eager-based training paths with bitwise-matching numerical results. The graph-based trainer enables advanced graph-level optimizations that are complicated to express in eager execution, including cross-module fusions, explicit graph-level debugging, and tailored support for heterogeneous AI hardware accelerators. Distributed infrastructure TorchTitan serves as an important validation stage for new communications features as they ship in PyTorch. Large-scale training stresses every part of the communication stack (initialization, collectives, failure handling and memory registration), which makes TorchTitan a demanding testing ground. A new NCCL backend, validated on TorchTitan : In PyTorch 2.14 , the NCCL implementation from torchcomms was ported into c10d as a new, opt-in NCCL backend. This allows us to enable new features much faster. It is designed as a drop-in replacement for the existing one and registers under the standard "nccl" backend name. Compared with the existing backend, it adds: One-sided RMA windows In-place process-group reconfiguration for fault tolerance Eager communicator initialization (in PyTorch 2.15) Raw access to NCCL shrink/grow and suspend/resume APIs Symmetric memory: Symmetric memory continues to be an important performance lever for TorchTitan. TorchTitan’s MoE layers can now run on Dist-MoE, a newly open-sourced distributed Mixture-of-Experts library, with ready-to-use DeepSeek V3 recipes for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Dist-MoE moves tokens between experts over symmetric memory and fuses that communication with expert compute. FSDP in TorchTitan can also allocate its communication buffers from a symmetric memory pool. This lets NCCL use its symmetric-memory kernel implementations, including copy-engine all-gather when NCCL’s zero-CTA policy is enabled. Checkpointing TorchTitan has integrated support for a new distributed checkpoint library, torch_checkpointing . This new library removes per-save synchronization in the default torch.distributed.checkpointing (DCPv1) saves. We do one collective (on the default process group) before the first save to share metadata; after the first save, we do no collectives. As pretraining grows past 16k ranks, the previous approach of using GLOO collectives to achieve synchronizations scales poorly with the number of nodes. torch_checkpointing’s approach of only running a lightweight barrier per save wins out at these scales. We also improved upon other things within DCPv1, such as saving the whole checkpoint item (e.g. model, optimizer, etc.) in torch.save at once rather than calling torch.save on each individual tensor, and making custom components pluggable (e.g. writing a custom storage backend optimized for your infra). At a scale of 512 H100 GPUs running DSv3 671B with checkpoint interval 50, we measured the following improvements: Trainer blocking times Average P99 DCPv1 841.2 ms 941.46 ms torch_checkpointing 34.1 ms 36.6 ms Checkpoint write times Average P99 DCPv1 384.4 s 403.1 s torch_checkpointing 13.1 s 13.2 s Non-resharding load times Average P99 DCPv1 194.7 s 198.2 s torch_checkpointing 79 s 82.3 s These improvements reduce blocking times and checkpoint write times and unlock more frequent checkpoints without risking TFLOP drops for users who adopt torch_checkpointing in their Titan recipes. To get started Clone github.com/pytorch/torchtitan , and follow the instructions listed here . If you have any kind of feedback, we would love to hear about it!

items.content: PyTorch Conference North America 2026 brought 3,500+ attendees to San Jose on October 20–21 for two days focused on accelerating open intelligence and exploring the impact of PyTorch Foundation projects like PyTorch, vLLM, DeepSpeed, Ray, Helion, and Safetensors. PyTorch Foundation Executive Director, Mark Collier, set the stage for the entire event to demonstrate how the PyTorch Foundation is building the open source software to train and serve models on any chip, in any cloud, for any agent. Accelerating Open Intelligence Together Mark Collier’s opening keynotes connected work across research, models, frameworks, infrastructure, hardware, and production. Day 1 examined how shared advances across those layers help the community move faster together. Day 2 looked ahead to broader hardware participation, workloads moving across more environments, and training and customizing frontier models at greater scale. Recent milestones across the PyTorch ecosystem highlight how AI itself is joining the learning loop to improve code, kernels, and research workflows. Announcements and updates published during the conference and in the preceding days covered the following work. Native PyTorch on Google TPUs TorchTPU is an open source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It supports eager execution and torch.compile , with validated integrations covering TorchTitan for training, vLLM and SGLang for inference, and Ray for orchestration. Workload migration can require only a device change, while peak performance can require additional changes to shapes, sharding, and operations. Read Introducing TorchTPU. TorchNeuron for AWS Trainium TorchNeuron is an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (and corresponding Amazon EC2 instances: Trn2 and Trn3), enabling AI researchers and practitioners to experiment and run PyTorch workloads with a single configuration change. With eager execution, torch.compile, and native support for PyTorch APIs (DTensor, torch.distributed) and libraries like TorchTitan, TorchNeuron enables workflows from research experimentation to production deployment. The public beta launch under Apache 2.0 was on October 20th at PyTorch Conference. Read Introducing TorchNeuron. Compiler Development for IBM Spyre and AMD GPUs IBM’s “From KTIR to SpyreCode” explains how torch-spyre translates Inductor’s decisions about work division and tensor placement into executable programs. An open source Dataflow Scheduler builds pipelines for data movement and computation before device-specific stages produce SpyreCode. The October 21 FlyDSL update also described an optional backend for AMD MI350-series GPUs, connecting eligible operations to optimized kernels through existing PyTorch APIs while retaining existing implementations for unsupported workloads. Read From KTIR to SpyreCode. TorchTitan and TitanRL TorchTitan expanded model support across its 5D parallelism stack and introduced reinforcement learning through TitanRL. TitanRL keeps the same model implementation across pretraining, post-training, and execution inside vLLM, with asynchronous rollouts and multiple forms of parallelism for training and generation. The update also covers performance improvements, FlexShard, graph-based training, distributed communication, and checkpointing. Read the TorchTitan update. Helion and NVIDIA CompileIQ Helion’s integration with NVIDIA CompileIQ adds compiler controls to the kernel autotuning search. Developers can evaluate Advanced Control Files alongside kernel configurations such as tile sizes and warp counts, tune offline, and pin the selected configuration. Compiler defaults remain a candidate in the search. Read about Helion and NVIDIA CompileIQ. ExecuTorch on Arm Cortex-M CPUs ExecuTorch now provides a direct path from PyTorch training to on-device inference. The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow. Read Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs. Nine New Members Join PyTorch Foundation New Platinum members include Nebius, Nscale and Shopify, deepening the PyTorch Foundation’s role as the intelligence layer for open source AI development. The Foundation welcomes the following new members: Platinum: Nebius, Nscale, and Shopify Inc. Silver: LightSeek Foundation and Lablup Inc. Associate: SKOPOS INDIA FOUNDATION, Siksha ‘O’ Anusandhan, Messiah University, and Valencia College. AI innovation now happens across all stack layers simultaneously, with research, models, infrastructure, hardware, and production continuously driving each other forward. The PyTorch Foundation serves as the central hub of this interconnected ecosystem, uniting researchers, developers, and companies building open AI. “Open systems learn faster when more people, projects, and organizations are working together, creating compounding gains,” said Mark Collier, Executive Director of PyTorch Foundation. “Open source ecosystems let breakthroughs travel between organizations instead of staying locked inside one company.” Nebius has also long supported vLLM with compute for development, testing, and benchmarking, including multi-node work on large models such as DeepSeek R1. Nscale first came to the PyTorch Foundation’s project ecosystem through Ray, the open-source framework for distributed computing and scaling AI workloads. Following Nscale’s planned acquisition of Anyscale, the company behind Ray, Nscale has committed to continuing investment in Ray’s development and its contributor community, building on Ray’s governance under the Foundation since the project joined in October 2025. “Most infrastructure providers treat the framework and the data center as two separate problems. We treat them as one. PyTorch has remained the base layer of AI because it kept the Pythonic style researchers know, while getting serious about performance. Ray, also part of the PyTorch Foundation, does something different: getting that work to run across thousands of GPUs. With Anyscale, the creators of Ray, set to join Nscale, we’re not just using that ecosystem, we’re building the infrastructure underneath it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation as a Platinum member is us backing that directly, not just benefiting from it,” said Nick Jones, VP of Cloud Native Platform Engineering, Nscale Shopify’s work featured in Cody Mazza-Anthony’s keynote and an accompanying case study. Using a continual learning loop with PyTorch and vLLM, Shopify compresses production failures into model weights every day, beating frontier-model quality, and cutting serving costs by 96%. Read the full membership press release. Read more about Nebius joining PyTorch Foundation. Read more about Nscale joining PyTorch Foundation. Read Shopify’s continual learning case study. Day 0: Training, Workshops, and Co-Located Events Day 0 programming on October 19 included: PyTorch, Powering the Enterprise with Red Hat, NVIDIA, and IBM LF AI & Data Summit 2026 PyTorch Associate Training Jupyter Day From Academia to Adoption Workshop Arm Create with Google, Google DeepMind, Nota, and Renesas Fine-Tune LLMs on Amazon SageMaker and Run Them On-Device with GenieX The PyTorch Associate Training offered an in-person, instructor-led program focused on the foundational and practical skills covered by the PyTorch Certified Associate (PTCA) exam . Through lectures, demonstrations, guided labs, and assessments, the training was designed to help participants build and optimize real-world models from scratch. Course completion included a voucher for the certification exam. Thank you to lead trainer Faradawn Yang, content creator Sahdev Zala, and assistant trainers Allison Ding, Krishna Kalyan, Santosh Bahir, Lakshay Garg, and Ian Wang. Hosted by the PyTorch Foundation OSPO & Academic Outreach Working Group, the From Academia to Adoption Workshop focused on taking promising PyTorch projects beyond a single paper, experiment, or lab. The community event explored how research software can become reliable, reusable tools that others can adopt, contribute to, and build upon. items.raw_text: PyTorch Conference North America 2026 brought 3,500+ attendees to San Jose on October 20–21 for two days focused on accelerating open intelligence and exploring the impact of PyTorch Foundation projects like PyTorch, vLLM, DeepSpeed, Ray, Helion, and Safetensors. PyTorch Foundation Executive Director, Mark Collier, set the stage for the entire event to demonstrate how the PyTorch Foundation is building the open source software to train and serve models on any chip, in any cloud, for any agent. Accelerating Open Intelligence Together Mark Collier’s opening keynotes connected work across research, models, frameworks, infrastructure, hardware, and production. Day 1 examined how shared advances across those layers help the community move faster together. Day 2 looked ahead to broader hardware participation, workloads moving across more environments, and training and customizing frontier models at greater scale. Recent milestones across the PyTorch ecosystem highlight how AI itself is joining the learning loop to improve code, kernels, and research workflows. Announcements and updates published during the conference and in the preceding days covered the following work. Native PyTorch on Google TPUs TorchTPU is an open source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It supports eager execution and torch.compile , with validated integrations covering TorchTitan for training, vLLM and SGLang for inference, and Ray for orchestration. Workload migration can require only a device change, while peak performance can require additional changes to shapes, sharding, and operations. Read Introducing TorchTPU. TorchNeuron for AWS Trainium TorchNeuron is an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (and corresponding Amazon EC2 instances: Trn2 and Trn3), enabling AI researchers and practitioners to experiment and run PyTorch workloads with a single configuration change. With eager execution, torch.compile, and native support for PyTorch APIs (DTensor, torch.distributed) and libraries like TorchTitan, TorchNeuron enables workflows from research experimentation to production deployment. The public beta launch under Apache 2.0 was on October 20th at PyTorch Conference. Read Introducing TorchNeuron. Compiler Development for IBM Spyre and AMD GPUs IBM’s “From KTIR to SpyreCode” explains how torch-spyre translates Inductor’s decisions about work division and tensor placement into executable programs. An open source Dataflow Scheduler builds pipelines for data movement and computation before device-specific stages produce SpyreCode. The October 21 FlyDSL update also described an optional backend for AMD MI350-series GPUs, connecting eligible operations to optimized kernels through existing PyTorch APIs while retaining existing implementations for unsupported workloads. Read From KTIR to SpyreCode. TorchTitan and TitanRL TorchTitan expanded model support across its 5D parallelism stack and introduced reinforcement learning through TitanRL. TitanRL keeps the same model implementation across pretraining, post-training, and execution inside vLLM, with asynchronous rollouts and multiple forms of parallelism for training and generation. The update also covers performance improvements, FlexShard, graph-based training, distributed communication, and checkpointing. Read the TorchTitan update. Helion and NVIDIA CompileIQ Helion’s integration with NVIDIA CompileIQ adds compiler controls to the kernel autotuning search. Developers can evaluate Advanced Control Files alongside kernel configurations such as tile sizes and warp counts, tune offline, and pin the selected configuration. Compiler defaults remain a candidate in the search. Read about Helion and NVIDIA CompileIQ. ExecuTorch on Arm Cortex-M CPUs ExecuTorch now provides a direct path from PyTorch training to on-device inference. The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow. Read Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs. Nine New Members Join PyTorch Foundation New Platinum members include Nebius, Nscale and Shopify, deepening the PyTorch Foundation’s role as the intelligence layer for open source AI development. The Foundation welcomes the following new members: Platinum: Nebius, Nscale, and Shopify Inc. Silver: LightSeek Foundation and Lablup Inc. Associate: SKOPOS INDIA FOUNDATION, Siksha ‘O’ Anusandhan, Messiah University, and Valencia College. AI innovation now happens across all stack layers simultaneously, with research, models, infrastructure, hardware, and production continuously driving each other forward. The PyTorch Foundation serves as the central hub of this interconnected ecosystem, uniting researchers, developers, and companies building open AI. “Open systems learn faster when more people, projects, and organizations are working together, creating compounding gains,” said Mark Collier, Executive Director of PyTorch Foundation. “Open source ecosystems let breakthroughs travel between organizations instead of staying locked inside one company.” Nebius has also long supported vLLM with compute for development, testing, and benchmarking, including multi-node work on large models such as DeepSeek R1. Nscale first came to the PyTorch Foundation’s project ecosystem through Ray, the open-source framework for distributed computing and scaling AI workloads. Following Nscale’s planned acquisition of Anyscale, the company behind Ray, Nscale has committed to continuing investment in Ray’s development and its contributor community, building on Ray’s governance under the Foundation since the project joined in October 2025. “Most infrastructure providers treat the framework and the data center as two separate problems. We treat them as one. PyTorch has remained the base layer of AI because it kept the Pythonic style researchers know, while getting serious about performance. Ray, also part of the PyTorch Foundation, does something different: getting that work to run across thousands of GPUs. With Anyscale, the creators of Ray, set to join Nscale, we’re not just using that ecosystem, we’re building the infrastructure underneath it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation as a Platinum member is us backing that directly, not just benefiting from it,” said Nick Jones, VP of Cloud Native Platform Engineering, Nscale Shopify’s work featured in Cody Mazza-Anthony’s keynote and an accompanying case study. Using a continual learning loop with PyTorch and vLLM, Shopify compresses production failures into model weights every day, beating frontier-model quality, and cutting serving costs by 96%. items.title: Meet the 2026 PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors
items.summary: Open source AI thrives when people come together to learn, build, share knowledge, and contribute. Behind every project is a community of developers, researchers, educators, and contributors helping make these technologies more accessible to others. The PyTorch Foundation Ambassador Program brings together community leaders from around the world who share that commitment. Through education, mentorship, technical content, community events, and open source contributions, ambassadors help expand awareness, adoption, and participation across the Foundation’s growing ecosystem of open source projects. The 2026 cohort welcomes 24 ambassadors across five program regions, representing communities from Nigeria and Burkina Faso to Singapore, India, Romania, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Each ambassador brings a unique perspective, technical background, and connection to their local community. Together, they are creating more opportunities for people to discover open source AI
items.content: Open source AI thrives when people come together to learn, build, share knowledge, and contribute. Behind every project is a community of developers, researchers, educators, and contributors helping make these technologies more accessible to others. The PyTorch Foundation Ambassador Program brings together community leaders from around the world who share that commitment. Through education, mentorship, technical content, community events, and open source contributions, ambassadors help expand awareness, adoption, and participation across the Foundation’s growing ecosystem of open source projects. The 2026 cohort welcomes 24 ambassadors across five program regions, representing communities from Nigeria and Burkina Faso to Singapore, India, Romania, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Each ambassador brings a unique perspective, technical background, and connection to their local community. Together, they are creating more opportunities for people to discover open source AI, develop practical skills, and contribute to the technologies shaping its future. A community shaped by many kinds of work The 2026 ambassadors bring experience across AI research, software and infrastructure engineering, technical education, open source maintenance, and community organizing. Some work on AI systems, model training, and infrastructure; others focus on documentation, workshops, mentoring, or applications that address challenges in their communities. For someone new to PyTorch, that might mean attending a first hands-on workshop. For an experienced developer, it could mean discovering a new project, connecting with maintainers, or making a first open source contribution. Ambassadors help create these opportunities by bringing people together and connecting local communities with the wider ecosystem. Advancing the PyTorch Foundation’s open source ecosystem The PyTorch Foundation supports a growing ecosystem of open source projects that help developers and researchers build, train, optimize, and deploy AI systems. Beyond the core PyTorch framework, this ecosystem includes projects such as vLLM, DeepSpeed, Ray, Helion, and Safetensors, spanning model training, inference, distributed computing, performance optimization, and model sharing. The Ambassador Program helps connect these technologies with communities around the world. Through technical workshops, meetups, educational resources, mentorship, and community-led initiatives, ambassadors help developers discover Foundation projects, understand their practical applications, and find opportunities to contribute. An ambassador might organize an introductory PyTorch workshop for students, help developers explore scalable inference with vLLM, introduce engineers to distributed AI technologies, or create technical content that makes complex concepts easier to understand. By supporting learning, adoption, and contributions, ambassadors strengthen the communities that sustain open source AI. Meet the 2026 ambassadors The 2026 cohort brings together 24 community leaders across five program regions. AFRICA Adesina Lekan Samuel · Nigeria Soumana Dama · Burkina Faso Ronnie Atuhaire · Uganda Farah Abdou · Egypt Abraham Imani · Democratic Republic of Congo Simanga Comfort Mchunu · South Africa Mark Gatere · Kenya ASIA Alpha Romer Cooma · Philippines Tsai Li Ming · Singapore Mu Xiaohui · Singapore and Malaysia Wang Zhipeng · Singapore Sumantro Mukherjee · India Parichay Das · India Sudhir Dharanendraiah · India EUROPE Costin-Alexandru Deonise · Romania Ricardo Noriega · Spain Matthew Cossins · United Kingdom MIDDLE EAST Johnny Kozman · Egypt Ali Tavallaie · Armenia Amr Osama Abdellatif · Egypt Özge Çinko · Turkey NORTH AMERICA Aditya Mehra · United States Ali Gowani · United States Samaresh Kumar Singh · United States What being a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador means to our community For the 2026 cohort, being an ambassador is an opportunity to share knowledge, give back to the communities that shaped their journeys, and create pathways for others to learn and contribute. In their own words, ambassadors share what excites them most about joining the program. “Contributing to PyTorch documentation showed me how even a small contribution can become part of something much bigger. As a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador, I’m so excited to help more people experience that sense of belonging through practical learning, welcoming communities, and opportunities to contribute.” Özge Çinko · Turkey “Most of what I know about building AI I learned from open-source communities, so I’m excited to give back by teaching, mentoring and bringing more engineers from Egypt and Africa into the PyTorch ecosystem.” Farah Abdou · Egypt “As a PyTorch Foundation Ambassador, I’m excited to help more developers become open-source contributors through hands-on education and mentorship, while bringing the PyTorch and vLLM communities closer together in Singapore and across Asia-Pacific.” Mu Xiaohui · Singapore and Malaysia Together, these reflections capture what makes the Ambassador Program meaningful: a shared commitment to learning, collaboration, and helping more people participate in open source AI. Building the future of open source AI together Over the coming year, ambassadors will help create opportunities for developers, researchers, students, and open source enthusiasts to learn, connect, and contribute across the Foundation’s ecosystem. From introducing new audiences to PyTorch Foundation communities and related projects to supporting technical education and community collaboration, their efforts will help strengthen the global open source AI community. We’re grateful to this year’s ambassadors for bringing their time, expertise, enthusiasm, and generosity to the program. The strongest communities grow when people share what they’ve learned, welcome new contributors, and make room for others to build alongside them. We look forward to seeing what the 2026 PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors will teach, organize, create, and contribute in the year ahead. Learn more about the PyTorch Foundation Ambassador program at: https://pytorch.org/programs/ambassadors/
