items.content: Agentic AI / Generative AI English 한국어 中文 NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Powers Specialized Agents with Multimodal Reasoning Oct 15, 2026 By Chris Alexiuk and Chintan Patel Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model with a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture that activates 12B parameters per token for agentic workflows. The model combines reasoning, instruction following, tool use, and text, image, document, and video understanding in a single model, eliminating the need for separate vision-language models. On a single GPU, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category. Organizations including Scale AI, Ramp, and AI21 have post-trained the model for specialized workflows, achieving improvements such as 40x lower inference cost, 10x lower latency, and 40% higher accuracy. Developers can customize the model using NVIDIA NeMo with supervised fine-tuning, low-rank adaptation, and reinforcement learning on open datasets released on Hugging Face. The model uses LiLiCorr speculative decoding, NVFP4 quantization with quantization-aware distillation, multi-token prediction, and context reuse to optimize inference efficiency on platforms including NVIDIA DGX Spark . Next Steps Read the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details. Explore the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub for customization resources. Get started with NVIDIA NIM for optimized deployment. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Always-on agents are taking on longer, more complex enterprise workflows. A single request can involve reading a document, checking information across sources, following company policy, and calling several tools. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model for these specialized workflows. Its 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture activates 12B parameters per token, balancing model capacity with inference efficiency. On a single GPU, this model delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category. Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers over 600 TPS on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index agentic tasks on the Baseten endpoint The model combines reasoning, instruction following, and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding. By combining these capabilities into one model, teams can handle text and visual tasks without deploying separate text and vision-language models or passing task context between them. Developers can post-train Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with NVIDIA NeMo using their own data, tools, policies, and workflows. This post explains how to use that foundation to build specialized enterprise agents and describes the training and inference techniques that power it. Why Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specialized agents? Agents need to understand both their tasks and operating environments. A customer-service agent must follow company return policies. Research agents connect evidence across sources, while document agents interpret tables, charts, and page layouts. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines reasoning and visual understanding across a range of agent workflows, including: Coding: Test and validate code, analyze errors, and recommend fixes. Web research: Search across websites, connect information, and verify answers. Document intelligence: Extract information from tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries and reports. Cybersecurity: Identify security vulnerabilities and triage threats to prioritize remediation. Video understanding: Extract information for search, content review, and incident analysis. Within a system of models, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL handles specialized, multistep work that needs reasoning, tool use, and text and visual understanding together. Smaller models, such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , handle high-volume text tasks, while frontier models such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra tackle complex planning and orchestration. Customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain data, tools, and policies Specialized agents must learn how an organization works. Domain terminology, tool interfaces, operating procedures, and policy requirements shape how agents complete tasks successfully. Organizations in industries ranging from cybersecurity and finance to healthcare are post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to outperform frontier models in accuracy and efficiency across their production workflows. For example: Scale AI, an AI data and technology provider, post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for automated vendor credit processing at Skydance Corporation, a media and entertainment company. Inference cost for this workload will decrease by 40x and latency by 5x. Ramp, a financial operations platform provider, is converting receipt images into structured JSON containing merchant information, dates, and payment data. Ramp expects up to 50% higher throughput and 10x lower latency. AI21 and Alice post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for threat intelligence and vulnerability analysis, improving accuracy by 41%. Figure 2. Post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL achieves leading performance for specialized tasks across industries Teams can use NVIDIA NeMo open libraries to post-train models to meet these requirements. Developers can use NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to teach domain-specific behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance in agentic environments that reflect organizational workflows. Alongside Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, NVIDIA is releasing open datasets on Hugging Face. These include agentic tool-use and conversational data, finance reasoning and tool-calling datasets, instruction-following and chat data, long-context transduction and translation data, fairness data, and 40 vision-language datasets. These datasets can supplement proprietary data for SFT and RL. For multimodal data, start with NeMo Data Designer resources for chart question answering and long-document understanding . Explore NVIDIA NeMo RL and NVIDIA NeMo Gym for RL and environment-based evaluation. Organizations can adapt and deploy the model’s open weights in supported local, data center, or cloud environments to meet their infrastructure and data requirements. For customization resources, see the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub. Combine text and visual understanding in one workflow Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines text, image, document, and video understanding with reasoning and instruction following to answer questions across these inputs. Its visual training covers charts, tables, optical character recognition (OCR), multipage documents, and video understanding. A two-stage SFT pipeline trains the language and vision components, combining visual evidence with reasoning, chat, safety, long-context data, and agent trajectories. For document intelligence, the same model can interpret a chart, connect it with a table elsewhere in a document, and summarize both. Developers can tailor the workflow to their own documents and evaluation criteria. Diverse training data generated with NeMo Data Designer helped the model better understand complex charts. On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, the model scored 80.8%, compared with 63% for Nemotron 3 Nano Omni . With Python code interpretation, it reached 84%. For the approach and lessons learned, read the chart-understanding deep dive and the open-source chart question-answering pipeline . This model was built with support and expertise from Nemotron Coalition organizations. For instance, high-quality datasets from Perplexity helped improve and streamline the model’s mid-training. Environments from Prime Intellect enabled building better teacher models. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is also one of the top open models on the OCRBench v2 leaderboard . Accuracy and efficiency across agent tasks Evaluations of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL span Hermes, LangChain, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Claude. In addition to coding tasks, agent harness providers use their own evaluations to test a wide range of agent tasks. On Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra. Model Hermes Bench LangChain Evals Nemotron 3 Ultra 56.33% 84.3% Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 63.44% 87.05% Table 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain evaluations For always-on agents, efficiency determines how much work a deployment can complete. Throughput, token usage, tool calls, and the steps needed to reach a correct result all affect task completion time. Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses higher throughput and token efficiency to deliver 4x faster task completion This model was also optimized to run locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark . An independent evaluation by EXO Labs placed Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the Pareto frontier for accuracy and task completion time. Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL balances accuracy and speed for agent tasks on DGX Spark Nemotron 3.5 Super VL under the hood The model builds on a strong foundation and uses a hybrid architecture, speculative decoding, context reuse, and mixed precision to reduce inference work across repeated agent calls. Building a strong base model Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. Ultra’s coding capabilities, combined with the SkewReverse loss used during distillation, helped improve coding accuracy. During post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) combines guidance from specialized teachers across text and vision. The model generates responses, and the teachers score them for video reasoning and tracking, vision tool use, and alignment. Additional training on examples of agent actions, code repositories, and software engineering tasks improved the model’s performance on agent tasks. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL outperforms Nemotron 3 Super on SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench across multiple evaluation setups. Continued pretraining with high-quality natural and synthetic data improved Indic-language capabilities and contributed to higher overall scores after post-training. This stage added 10B Indic tokens, drawn from a 12-language subset of Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 and natural Indic text. NVIDIA is releasing the full dataset, which contains about 2.8T tokens across 22 Indian languages and was developed with IIT Madras and its AI4Bharat lab. The following results are based on the post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Figure 5. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers leading accuracy on Indic benchmarks, thanks to specialized Indic data Developers can use NeMo to build on this foundation and customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for their applications, adapting its reasoning and agentic capabilities to their data, tools, and workflows. LiLiCorr: An open speculative decoding technique LiLiCorr improves parallel speculative decoding by jointly evaluating token candidates across an entire draft, capturing dependencies that independent token predictions miss. A lightweight network computes compatibility scores in a single pass to produce more coherent drafts, leaving only a low-cost, sequential final selection step. On DGX Spark, LiLiCorr is the recommended drafter for low-latency inference with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. It delivers up to 2.3x faster token generation than decoding without speculation. NVFP4 and mixed precision The model uses NVIDIA Model Optimizer for post-training quantization and quantization-aware distillation (QAD). The NVFP4 recipe uses 4-bit weights and activations on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture . The same checkpoint runs on non-Blackwell platforms with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations. Precision is selected separately for sensitive components. NVFP4 makes the model smaller, and QAD helps it retain its accuracy at lower precision. During QAD, the quantized model learns to match the outputs of the original BF16 model, which closes the accuracy gap that quantization introduces. QAD also supports storing the key-value (KV) cache in NVFP4 instead of FP8 while still meeting accuracy targets. Because QAD happens during training, it adds no inference overhead. Multi-token prediction Multi-token prediction (MTP) gives Nemotron 3.5 Super VL an internal drafter that proposes several tokens for the main model to verify in one forward pass. Accepting multiple tokens at once reduces the number of compute-intensive verification steps needed to generate a response. A dedicated MTP-boosting training phase further aligned the drafter with the final model. Context reuse across agent turns Agents repeatedly pass system instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history back to the model. Prefix caching reuses computation from those shared inputs. The model’s serving optimizations preserve both attention caches and Mamba recurrent states. Additional Mamba checkpoints reduce the replay needed to recover inputs for speculative decoding, while internal checkpointing avoids extra model passes during prompt processing. Simplify production deployment with NVIDIA NIM and NVIDIA Dynamo NVIDIA NIM packages models with optimized inference engines, validated configurations, and standard APIs for cloud and data center deployment. NIM receives ongoing security, feature, and performance updates. Enterprise support is available through NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Get started with NIM . NVIDIA Dynamo supports distributed inference optimizations to increase throughput and reduce latency, including KV-cache-aware routing, KV cache management, and disaggregated serving. On 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, KV-aware routing with session affinity and KV cache offload serves up to 8x as many users while reducing first-token latency by 85%. Get started with the Dynamo deployment recipes . Figure 6. NVIDIA Dynamo serves 8x as many users and reduces first-token latency by 85% at the same per-user token rate Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Build specialized agents with multimodal reasoning and tool use. Customize the model for specialized workflows, then deploy it in a supported environment. The release includes base, post-trained, and NVFP4-quantized checkpoints with training recipes, data, and reinforcement-learning environments. See the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details and Hugging Face or ModelScope for deployment instructions. For hosted model access, see OpenRouter . Partner ecosystem Partners support customization and deployment of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain-specific workflows. Chris comes from a machine learning and data science background, and he is obsessed with everything and anything about large language models. View all posts by Chris Alexiuk About Chintan Patel Chintan Patel is a senior product manager at NVIDIA focused on bringing GPU-accelerated solutions to the HPC community. Prior to NVIDIA, he held product management, marketing and engineering positions at Micrel, Inc. Developers can tailor the workflow to their own documents and evaluation criteria. Diverse training data generated with NeMo Data Designer helped the model better understand complex charts. On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, the model scored 80.8%, compared with 63% for Nemotron 3 Nano Omni . With Python code interpretation, it reached 84%. For the approach and lessons learned, read the chart-understanding deep dive and the open-source chart question-answering pipeline . This model was built with support and expertise from Nemotron Coalition organizations. For instance, high-quality datasets from Perplexity helped improve and streamline the model’s mid-training. Environments from Prime Intellect enabled building better teacher models. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is also one of the top open models on the OCRBench v2 leaderboard . Accuracy and efficiency across agent tasks Evaluations of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL span Hermes, LangChain, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Claude. In addition to coding tasks, agent harness providers use their own evaluations to test a wide range of agent tasks. On Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra. Model Hermes Bench LangChain Evals Nemotron 3 Ultra 56.33% 84.3% Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 63.44% 87.05% Table 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain evaluations For always-on agents, efficiency determines how much work a deployment can complete. Throughput, token usage, tool calls, and the steps needed to reach a correct result all affect task completion time. Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses higher throughput and token efficiency to deliver 4x faster task completion This model was also optimized to run locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark . An independent evaluation by EXO Labs placed Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the Pareto frontier for accuracy and task completion time. Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL balances accuracy and speed for agent tasks on DGX Spark Nemotron 3.5 Super VL under the hood The model builds on a strong foundation and uses a hybrid architecture, speculative decoding, context reuse, and mixed precision to reduce inference work across repeated agent calls. Building a strong base model Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. Ultra’s coding capabilities, combined with the SkewReverse loss used during distillation, helped improve coding accuracy. During post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) combines guidance from specialized teachers across text and vision. The model generates responses, and the teachers score them for video reasoning and tracking, vision tool use, and alignment. Additional training on examples of agent actions, code repositories, and software engineering tasks improved the model’s performance on agent tasks. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL outperforms Nemotron 3 Super on SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench across multiple evaluation setups. Continued pretraining with high-quality natural and synthetic data improved Indic-language capabilities and contributed to higher overall scores after post-training. This stage added 10B Indic tokens, drawn from a 12-language subset of Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 and natural Indic text. NVIDIA is releasing the full dataset, which contains about 2.8T tokens across 22 Indian languages and was developed with IIT Madras and its AI4Bharat lab. The following results are based on the post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Figure 5. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers leading accuracy on Indic benchmarks, thanks to specialized Indic data Developers can use NeMo to build on this foundation and customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for their applications, adapting its reasoning and agentic capabilities to their data, tools, and workflows. LiLiCorr: An open speculative decoding technique LiLiCorr improves parallel speculative decoding by jointly evaluating token candidates across an entire draft, capturing dependencies that independent token predictions miss. A lightweight network computes compatibility scores in a single pass to produce more coherent drafts, leaving only a low-cost, sequential final selection step. On DGX Spark, LiLiCorr is the recommended drafter for low-latency inference with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. It delivers up to 2.3x faster token generation than decoding without speculation. NVFP4 and mixed precision The model uses NVIDIA Model Optimizer for post-training quantization and quantization-aware distillation (QAD). The NVFP4 recipe uses 4-bit weights and activations on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture . The same checkpoint runs on non-Blackwell platforms with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations. Precision is selected separately for sensitive components. NVFP4 makes the model smaller, and QAD helps it retain its accuracy at lower precision. During QAD, the quantized model learns to match the outputs of the original BF16 model, which closes the accuracy gap that quantization introduces. QAD also supports storing the key-value (KV) cache in NVFP4 instead of FP8 while still meeting accuracy targets. Because QAD happens during training, it adds no inference overhead. Multi-token prediction Multi-token prediction (MTP) gives Nemotron 3.5 Super VL an internal drafter that proposes several tokens for the main model to verify in one forward pass. Accepting multiple tokens at once reduces the number of compute-intensive verification steps needed to generate a response. A dedicated MTP-boosting training phase further aligned the drafter with the final model. Context reuse across agent turns Agents repeatedly pass system instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history back to the model. Prefix caching reuses computation from those shared inputs. The model’s serving optimizations preserve both attention caches and Mamba recurrent states. Additional Mamba checkpoints reduce the replay needed to recover inputs for speculative decoding, while internal checkpointing avoids extra model passes during prompt processing. Simplify production deployment with NVIDIA NIM and NVIDIA Dynamo NVIDIA NIM packages models with optimized inference engines, validated configurations, and standard APIs for cloud and data center deployment. NIM receives ongoing security, feature, and performance updates. Enterprise support is available through NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Get started with NIM . NVIDIA Dynamo supports distributed inference optimizations to increase throughput and reduce latency, including KV-cache-aware routing, KV cache management, and disaggregated serving. On 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, KV-aware routing with session affinity and KV cache offload serves up to 8x as many users while reducing first-token latency by 85%. Get started with the Dynamo deployment recipes . Figure 6. NVIDIA Dynamo serves 8x as many users and reduces first-token latency by 85% at the same per-user token rate Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Build specialized agents with multimodal reasoning and tool use. Customize the model for specialized workflows, then deploy it in a supported environment. The release includes base, post-trained, and NVFP4-quantized checkpoints with training recipes, data, and reinforcement-learning environments. See the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details and Hugging Face or ModelScope for deployment instructions. For hosted model access, see OpenRouter . items.content: Trustworthy AI / Cybersecurity English 中文 Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime NVIDIA Sentry governs agent access requests, monitors runtime activity, and contains threats from an isolated hardware security layer in milliseconds. Oct 21, 2026 By Ofir Arkin , Ariel Kit and Itay Ozery Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Sentry monitors AI agents and enforces access policies from a hardware-isolated trust domain on BlueField-4 DPUs, independent of host software. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy that terminates TLS and evaluates agent requests against Open Policy Agent rules, while DOCA Argus provides real-time memory introspection of the agent's execution environment. The framework correlates network traffic with runtime context to enforce policies based on container hashes, process integrity, and approved software bills of materials. Specialized AI models classify agent communications inline or out of band to detect behavioral drift, and in-silicon enforcement can contain agents within milliseconds. Attested telemetry and tamper-evident records preserved on BlueField-4 support forensic investigation and integration with enterprise security platforms. Next Steps Explore NVIDIA DOCA libraries and microservices to experiment with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them. NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA , runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs , and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries. Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity. This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software. An independent security layer for agent runtime protection An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host. NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent. Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge. In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs , while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior. Governing agent communications DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy , the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment. Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world. An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications. NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration. DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure. Figure 1. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to inspect access requests and a policy engine to evaluate authorization, with runtime context from DOCA Argus Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy. DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests. It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state. DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised. DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it. Using runtime context to evaluate agent access NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation. Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment. Extending controls to agent interactions Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can: Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications. Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation. Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic. Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords. Identify and block content prohibited by policy. NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services. Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift. The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior. Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations. Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior. Figure 2. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to submit inspected communications to a specialized model for classification, where potentially harmful content is blocked inline NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software. These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain. Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review. Figure 3. NVIDIA Sentry combines interaction telemetry, runtime detections, and policy context with enterprise security integrations to drive response actions through DOCA Tower Using agent identity in access decisions Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems. Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request. This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies. Preserving a trusted record of agent activity Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs. NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals. An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4. Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits. NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows. Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices. DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path. NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces. Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response. Building layered protection for AI agents Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4. Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries. Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA . Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year. He's passionate about creating innovative products that address customer needs, and has introduced several industry-first technologies. Ofir has authored numerous influential research papers and articles, and is a recognized speaker in the information security community. View all posts by Ofir Arkin About Ariel Kit Ariel Kit leads product strategy and delivery for NVIDIA DOCA, the software platform for NVIDIA BlueField DPUs and ConnectX SuperNICs that accelerates and secures AI workloads through infrastructure microservices. Ariel has led DOCA since its inception, growing it from initial concept into a complete SDK and runtime with global adoption and millions of downloads. He brings two decades of experience spanning cybersecurity, embedded systems, and R&D management, including leading customer program management for a semiconductor solutions group and previously serving as networking cybersecurity product lead at NVIDIA. He holds a B.Sc. in communication systems engineering and an MBA. View all posts by Ariel Kit About Itay Ozery Itay Ozery is director of product marketing for networking at NVIDIA. He drives strategic product marketing initiatives for NVIDIA networking platforms and solutions. Itay has a solid track record in building and launching impactful products and solutions to market, and previously served in various enterprise IT positions. View all posts by Itay Ozery Comments

NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment. Extending controls to agent interactions Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can: Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications. Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation. Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic. Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords. Identify and block content prohibited by policy. NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services. Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift. The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior. Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations. Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior. Figure 2. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to submit inspected communications to a specialized model for classification, where potentially harmful content is blocked inline NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software. These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain. Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review. Figure 3. NVIDIA Sentry combines interaction telemetry, runtime detections, and policy context with enterprise security integrations to drive response actions through DOCA Tower Using agent identity in access decisions Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems. Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request. This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies. Preserving a trusted record of agent activity Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs. NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals. An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4. Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits. NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows. Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices. DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path. NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response. Building layered protection for AI agents Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries. Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA . Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year. items.content: Agentic AI / Generative AI English 中文 How NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture Secures and Governs AI Agent Workloads at Scale Oct 21, 2026 By Hannah Coutand , Itay Ozery , Alex Sandu and Kirit Thadaka Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA OpenShell provides an open-source runtime that enforces security and governance for agentic systems by treating agent workloads as untrusted and granting access only when needed. The framework uses four components — Gateway, Supervisor, Sandbox, and Policy Prover — to manage sandbox lifecycles, mediate credential access, isolate workloads, and formally verify policy permissions. NVIDIA Vera CPUs accelerate agent workloads with 88 Olympus cores, second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric, and LPDDR5X memory, delivering up to 2x performance on critical agentic tasks versus x86. CoreWeave measured more than 3x faster sandbox startup and 1.8x faster agentic loop completion on Vera compared to a leading x86 CPU, with a single rack supporting over 11,000 concurrent agent environments. NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs and NVIDIA Sentry add hardware-isolated monitoring and in-silicon enforcement that can quarantine agents within milliseconds when policy violations are detected. Next Steps Explore the OpenShell GitHub repository to begin implementing secure agent governance. Review the Secure Agent Workspace Reference Design documentation for deployment guidance. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Autonomous agents can work for hours on complex tasks, accessing files, tools, the internet, and spawning other agents to collaborate with. Executing complex tasks over long time horizons leads to compounding risk: the agents may download code, build new tools, request additional privileges, and touch more of the underlying infrastructure. The agents’ action paths are determined as they work and reason through the steps needed to complete their goals. As they interact with the tools and systems around them, they adapt their reasoning and behavior to achieve their task. The adaptability of agents is what makes them so powerful, but they are goal-oriented and may not prioritize safety in pursuit of their objectives. In order for agents to work both autonomously and safely, we need to build environments that provide control and visibility in what the agent is doing. An agent cannot govern itself. Security and governance belong in the infrastructure the agent operates in. OpenShell provides deterministic governance outside of the agent’s reach NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source runtime to build the security and governance needed for agentic systems into the computing infrastructure. OpenShell defines and enforces which systems and data an agent can access, from files and internet services to systems that interact with physical devices. It is the foundation of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for building safe AI agents. OpenShell treats agent workloads as untrusted throughout execution. An agent is given access to what it needs, when it needs it. OpenShell has four key components: Gateway: The control plane that manages sandbox lifecycles and policies Supervisor: Checks outbound requests against policy and mediates access to credentials. This runs completely separate to the sandbox Sandbox: Isolates the agent workload and restricts filesystem and process access Policy prover: Adds formal verification, checking whether a policy’s permissions stay within an organization-defined ceiling. As the agents evolve, these components provide the infrastructure controls that allow them to work safely. Extending and integrating OpenShell Extensibility is a core principle of OpenShell’s design. Supervisor middleware lets you inspect, block, or change the content that an agent sends and receives over the network as an additional enforcement layer. Gateway interceptors let operators add deployment-specific governance to OpenShell control-plane operations without modifying the gateway. Organizations also need to establish who an agent acts for, what authority it holds, and whether an action fits the task. Identity, authorization, data protection, and auditing each address part of that problem. OpenShell provides enforcement points where those systems can be integrated. In the reference architecture, OpenShell runs on NVIDIA Vera CPUs. NVIDIA Vera, the compute layer beneath the controls OpenShell defines what agents can do. Vera determines how fast they can do it. Agents operate through loops of dependent steps where each step must complete before the next begins: reasoning, calling tools, executing code, querying data. AI factories run thousands of these loops concurrently, placing new demands on CPU architecture across five dimensions: They need massive core counts to run many concurrent workflows, and fast individual cores to shorten each sequential step. They need high-bandwidth fabric and memory to keep those cores fed with the live data agents depend on. They need massive I/O to move data at speed between CPUs, GPUs, storage, and network. They need hardware-enforced security, because agents increasingly operate on sensitive enterprise data and must be isolated from each other and the host. They need to deliver all of this within the power envelope of a modern data center (more agent work per watt, not just more raw performance). NVIDIA calls this combination the max single-threaded CPU at scale , and NVIDIA Vera is built for it: massive Olympus cores, a second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric, LPDDR5X memory, Gen 6 I/O, confidential computing, and an energy-efficient design purpose-built for power-limited data centers. Three architectural properties make Vera fast for agent workloads First, 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores with a 10-wide front end, neural branch predictor, and deep out-of-order execution deliver up to 2x performance on critical agentic workloads versus x86, shortening each tool call, code execution, and evaluation. Second, Vera’s second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric provides up to 3x core-to-core bandwidth and up to 50% lower core-to-core latency than x86 alternatives, keeping data moving predictably under load. Vera also integrates 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6, delivering the I/O bandwidth to connect GPUs, high-speed storage, and network at the throughput agentic infrastructure demands. Third, up to 1.2 TB/s of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth, with up to 40% lower loaded memory latency than chiplet-based designs, keeps agents supplied with the live context they need without stalling on memory access. LPDDR5X also makes Vera dramatically more efficient: Vera delivers 2x more performance per watt than x86 CPUs, while the LPDDR5X memory subsystem itself draws an order of magnitude less power than competing DDR5-based memory configurations, enabling more agent work within the same power envelope. Agent workloads depend on sandboxes: isolated execution environments where agents run code, invoke tools, and complete tasks without interfering with each other or the host system. The denser and faster those sandboxes spin up, the more agent work a given infrastructure footprint can sustain. CoreWeave , the AI cloud platform purpose-built for training and serving models at scale, found sandbox startup to be more than 3x faster on Vera than on x86, with a single rack supporting more than 11,000 concurrent agent environments. Running Terminal Bench, which measures CPU performance across real agentic loop tasks, CoreWeave found Vera delivered 1.8x faster performance versus x86, across agentic tasks ranging from scripting to database recovery. That density and performance under load is what agent infrastructure actually requires. Figure 1. CoreWeave demonstrates NVIDIA Vera delivers >3x faster sandbox startup and 1.8x faster agentic loop completion versus a leading x86 CPU across 20 real-world agent tasks NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Sentry for hardware-enforced protection OpenShell places authority outside the agent. For deployments that require additional protection, that separation can also extend into purpose-built silicon. NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs provide a hardware-isolated trust domain outside the agent’s reach. In the OpenShell reference architecture, BlueField-4 sits in the I/O path between agents running on Vera and the models they access. NVIDIA Sentry , a security software framework built on NVIDIA DOCA , runs in this independent domain to continuously monitor agent behavior and enforce runtime policy. NVIDIA Sentry observes requests and responses, networking and file activities, verifies identity and delegated authority, and analyzes selected host memory to detect deviations from authorized behavior without relying on agent self-reporting. When it detects a threat or policy violation, BlueField-4 enforces policy in silicon, allowing NVIDIA Sentry to quarantine the agent within milliseconds. Together, they add an optional hardware safeguard alongside OpenShell’s software boundaries. Learn more about NVIDIA Sentry in this technical deep-dive . Bringing secure agent runtimes to scale Running agents in production requires infrastructure that can keep thousands of workflows moving while governing every action they take. Vera provides the compute, memory bandwidth, and I/O to sustain those workflows. OpenShell supplies the runtime boundaries that determine which actions execute and which resources agents can reach. Together, Vera and OpenShell make secure agent execution a foundation for scale. Agents can run longer, use tools, and work with enterprise data within policies enforced outside their control. For deployments that require additional protection, NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 adds independent monitoring and in-silicon enforcement. The NVIDIA Vera Rubi n platform , where LLMs run, together with OpenShell and NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4, are the pillars of the OpenShell reference architecture. They form the complete stack for safe AI agents: a complete, hardware-rooted foundation that gives organizations the performance to make agents productive and the controls to keep their work within authorized boundaries. Get started To implement secure agent governance in your organization, begin with NVIDIA OpenShell, follow the documentation, and explore how NVIDIA Vera CPUs accelerate agent workloads . An agent-assisted workflow combines DSX reference designs, architectural references, site plans, requirements documents, and geographic data into an editable OpenUSD campus model that teams can inspect and revise. Frontier AI agents use USD Content Agents to generate geometry such as solar canopies, then refine designs using architectural references while keeping changes separate from source assets through additive USD layers. The campus model supports capacity planning studies that evaluate compute configurations within a fixed power budget, using illustrative comparisons such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference

Frontier AI agents use USD Content Agents to generate geometry such as solar canopies, then refine designs using architectural references while keeping changes separate from source assets through additive USD layers. The campus model supports capacity planning studies that evaluate compute configurations within a fixed power budget, using illustrative comparisons such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference under MaxP versus DSX MaxLPS. SimReady Foundation specifications and the SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face help teams assess asset data readiness and reuse simulation-ready OpenUSD assets for power and cooling analysis. Application providers including Dassault Systèmes, PTC, Cadence, and Siemens connect requirements management, CAD data, computational fluid dynamics, and thermal simulation to the digital twin workflow. Next Steps Build with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint to start developing an AI factory digital twin. Prepare and validate assets with DSX asset guidance and SimReady Foundation for simulation readiness. Prepare content for your workflow with AI factory pipeline samples covering CAD conversion, optimization, metadata, and validation. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Building an AI factory digital twin requires developers to bring site plans, equipment assets, and engineering requirements into a consistent model that teams can inspect, revise, and prepare for simulation. Connecting these inputs into an editable workflow helps teams explore design alternatives and incorporate engineering feedback as the design evolves. The NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint , part of NVIDIA DSX Sim , provides reference digital twin assets, sample scripts, and workflows for developing AI factory digital twins. Built on OpenUSD and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, the blueprint gives developers a foundation for assembling facility and equipment models with SimReady assets, and connecting them with engineering simulation tools. Frontier AI models can help developers work with this foundation through agents and connected applications and tools, as explained in Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations with Frontier AI Agents . Developers guide agents to bring together design inputs, assemble and revise OpenUSD scenes, and inspect the results. The blueprint supplies reusable assets and workflows, and the agents help developers apply and adapt them to specific design requirements (Figure 1). This post demonstrates an agent-assisted workflow for turning reference assets, site data, and design requirements into an editable OpenUSD campus model. Developers can use this approach to explore layouts, revise equipment placement, and prepare designs for engineering review and downstream simulation. Developers connect tools and guide changes, while engineers review results to inform the next iteration. Figure 1. Reference workflow from requirements through an OpenUSD digital twin to an engineering simulation, with results informing the next design revision Providing agents with a design foundation for AI factory modeling Consider a practical question: How should an AI factory hall be configured when the available power is fixed? Changing the compute configuration can impact equipment quantity, placement, electrical distribution, and cooling. Evaluating the alternatives requires those disciplines to work from consistent requirements and design data. An agent needs context before it can make a useful design proposal. Given only photos or renderings, it can produce a model that looks plausible but may have incorrect dimensions and proportions. Reference assets and project documents help ground the proposal, but the resulting model still requires dimensional checks and engineering review. A grounded workflow starts with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint and reference design, then incorporates the project’s requirements, drawings, equipment information, and site constraints. Each source has a different role: existing geometry supplies reusable buildings and equipment while architectural references inform appearance; aerial imagery and elevation data provide geographic context; project drawings and equipment information establish dimensions and placement; requirements define the conditions the design must satisfy. For example, the team used the NVIDIA Santa Clara Headquarters building, Voyager, as design inspiration for an AI factory campus site based on the DSX reference design. The inputs included: DSX 3D models: Data hall, central utility buildings, substations, generators, cooling equipment, vehicles, and vegetation. Architectural references: Images of Voyager from various aerial and on-the-ground views to inform the roof, facade, solar canopies, and landscaping. Site plans (DSX Reference Design): PDFs describing the campus arrangement and a more detailed first phase, including buildings, roads, utility areas, and access areas. Requirements documents: An indexed collection of architectural drawings, form-factor studies, Basis of Design documents, room layouts, and other records. Geographic data: USGS aerial imagery and elevation data of the selected site used to place the campus in the surrounding terrain. Figure 2. The supplied inputs resulted in an editable campus site model combining the DSX Blueprint reference design with an architectural facade inspired by Voyager Together, these sources provide a starting point for an agent-assisted workflow and basis for reviewing its output. They help teams trace design choices to their sources—for example, building placement to a site plan and facade styling to an architectural reference. That traceability supports review; dimensional accuracy still depends on checking the model against the applicable drawings, specifications, and site constraints. Building an OpenUSD campus site model using an AI agent To implement this workflow, a frontier AI model runs in an agent harness: software that manages context, instructions, and tool calls. Skills encode repeatable tasks and AI factory domain knowledge. Developers connect modeling and analysis operations through tool interfaces, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where supported, and define which changes the agent may propose or apply. In the campus model example, existing DSX reference designed buildings from the DSX Blueprint and equipment supplied the starting geometry, while the site plans guided placement and first-phase details. The team supplied photographs and the architectural references from the NVIDIA Voyager campus to guide the architectural additions. For the solar canopy, the frontier AI agent used USD Content Agents to help generate its geometry and materials, then refined the design using the Voyager references. This gave the team an editable architectural element to review alongside the existing buildings and equipment. The canopy remained a conceptual design where an engineering team could check for dimensions, structural properties, and suitability for simulation. The team then combined the reused assets and new architectural geometry in additive USD layers, keeping changes separate from the source assets. In the Omniverse RTX viewport, the team could inspect the canopy in the context of the campus, review its appearance and placement, and revise the model as design decisions change. USGS aerial data was used for the landscape and elevation plan. Figure 3. The campus model is fully realized in an Omniverse RTX viewport, taking design layout and existing assets from DSX Blueprint and elements from real images of Voyager for the site design Extending the campus model to evaluate a fixed power budget The campus model could support a subsequent capacity planning study: How should an AI factory hall be configured within a fixed power budget? The proposed extension would connect the modeled layout with compute, electrical, and cooling requirements to evaluate alternative configurations. One starting point is an illustrative NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference comparison. It contrasts a baseline using MaxP —the highest static GPU-level power setting—with DSX MaxLPS , an AI factory design and operating framework that coordinates facility design, dynamic power allocation, and performance-per-watt optimization. Applying this comparison to a hall would require evaluating the support power, cooling, and networking infrastructure. Normalized to a 1 MW power basis, assuming a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.1, the illustrative scenario shows a DSX MaxLPS capacity of 400 GPUs and aggregate token throughput of 1.35x the MaxP baseline (Figure 4). These figures are reference assumptions for the proposed study, not results generated by the campus model. Figure 4. Illustrative NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference comparison, normalized to a 1 MW power basis with PUE 1.1. The comparison provides context for the proposed capacity-planning workflow; it does not represent results from the campus model or specify a deployable rack layout. Vera Rubin testing remains in progress In the proposed workflow, developers would connect the agent to project data and engineering tools so it could help identify equipment and design assumptions requiring review. The reference comparison would inform capacity targets. Engineers would evaluate feasible configurations using complete racks, including their placement, electrical distribution, cooling connections, and network resources. Using Systems Modeling Language (SysML) , teams can represent requirements and link them to system elements. A project team could use these relationships to organize requirements drawn from source documents. If the modeling tool exposes those relationships through an API, MCP, or other supported interface, the agent could query them to flag potentially affected dependencies affected by the proposed change. Drawings and CAD would provide dimensions and placement references, while equipment catalogs would supply the parameters for engineering analysis. The handoff would be a proposed design revision, accompanied by the requirements, equipment, and follow-up engineering studies. After engineering reviews, the agent could help update the OpenUSD scene to reflect the selected rack configuration and layout. Preparing the scene for a specific simulation would require additional checks and configuration, including geometry, equipment properties, system connections, and boundary conditions. Assembling the digital twin with OpenUSD and SimReady After the team reviews a proposed configuration and its affected requirements, the next step is to prepare the design for analysis. This requires more than geometry: engineers need equipment properties and connection data to evaluate power and cooling. OpenUSD brings building geometry, equipment assets, and associated data into a shared scene. USD attributes and custom schemas can preserve links to engineering records and requirements, keeping changes traceable across applications. The DSX system architecture connects asset preparation, data storage, simulation services, and the digital twin application. For the fixed-power scenario, this provides a framework for bringing the revised layout together with the equipment information needed to evaluate its power and cooling implications. Figure 5. DSX system architecture showing the SimReady asset pipeline, simulation services, surrogate model, and the AIF-DT runtime for digital twin applications SimReady Foundation describes the asset data needed for particular simulation uses. While OpenUSD provides the shared scene, SimReady specifications help teams assess whether its assets contain the required data needed for the intended analysis, select the requirements and supported validators appropriate to the equipment and analysis, then check the geometry, properties, and connection data they cover. The agent can help surface missing information and associate it with the affected equipment for the team to review. Developers can also source equipment assets from the SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face, a free, ungated library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready OpenUSD assets . For AI factory digital twins, teams can discover and reuse OEM-provided racks, power and cooling equipment, reducing asset preparation. The AI factory pipeline samples provide examples for CAD conversion, optimization, metadata, and validation. Through connected tools, an agent can help invoke these preparation steps and collect their reports. The resulting handoff is an assembled scene tied to the proposed design revision, with its supporting data, completed checks, and remaining gaps visible. This gives the simulation team the context needed to prepare the study and evaluate how the configuration behaves within the fixed power budget. Evaluating power and cooling simulations to guide design revisions With the revised scene assembled and the data gaps identified, prepare the studies needed to evaluate the configuration. In the fixed-power scenario, electrical loading and cooling analysis help determine how the proposed equipment arrangement behaves under the specified operating conditions. The application uses the geometry, equipment properties, and system connections, with additional solver preparation where required. Where developers have implemented supported solver connections, an agent can submit studies, retrieve results, and associate findings with the affected equipment and requirements. Engineers review the assumptions and results to determine whether the design supports the proposed configurations or needs further revision. Each finding should identify the tested design revision and distinguish calculated results from stored results or AI approximations. The capacity question now becomes a basis for making design decisions: which equipment configuration to pursue, what supporting infrastructure it requires, and where further analysis is needed. Those decisions feed back into the editable design, enabling the team to refine the proposal and repeat the affected studies. Selecting compute for agent development, visualization, and simulation For a workflow like the campus example, select hardware around the task: developing the agent tool connections, editing the scene, or running the engineering studies. NVIDIA DGX Spark for personal agent development: Prototype agents, test compatible local AI models, and connect engineering tools. Pair with an RTX system for DSX visualization and simulation. NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU for interactive design and simulation: Prepare OpenUSD assets, review digital twins, and run supported engineering simulations. NVIDIA DGX Station for larger local AI workloads: Develop and run larger AI models and agents locally. Add an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU for visualization and supported simulation applications. NVIDIA RTX PRO Server for shared development and simulation: Follow the NVIDIA RTX PRO AI Factory reference architecture , which specifies eight RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs per server and groups four servers into a scalable unit. Size the deployment for inference, visualization, and supported simulation workloads based on scene complexity, solver requirements, and concurrent users. Connecting applications to the engineering decision Extending the campus model into an engineering study requires applications that manage requirements, supply equipment data, and calculate physical behavior. Application providers are addressing these scenarios across the workflow: Dassault Systèmes addresses the challenge of keeping system requirements and design decisions consistent with CATIA Magic . Its SysML tools let engineers model system elements and interfaces, check model consistency, and evaluate designs against the architecture. Within an agent-assisted workflow, simulation findings can inform proposed updates to the SysML model configuration, subject to engineering review, keeping requirements and the systems model connected throughout design iterations. Dassault Systèmes also supports the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for agent-to-agent integration. PTC is working to keep digital twin studies connected to the product data they represent through Windchill and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Windchill manages version-controlled Creo and other CAD data; the announced integration is intended to bring that data into a shared 3D environment for engineering review and simulation. This addresses the handoff from the managed equipment design to the AI factory digital twin. Cadence Reality Digital Twin Platform answers the fixed-power question: how many GPUs can run, and can they be cooled? It couples equipment and power models with computational fluid dynamics to simulate MaxP, MaxQ, and DSX MaxLPS. Stakeholders see the impact on power, cooling, and token throughput before a single rack is installed and continues through the life of the AI factory. Built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, SimReady assets, and OpenUSD, the Cadence Reality Digital Twin allows collaborative and agentic optimization of AI factory performance. Siemens supports detailed evaluation of fluid flow and heat transfer with Simcenter STAR-CCM+ , where engineers calculate how a proposed design behaves under specified conditions. For AI factory infrastructure, Siemens has also developed DSX-aligned reference architectures that combine power distribution, automation, and simulation-ready assets. These address the need to represent supporting infrastructure alongside compute equipment in the factory design. Get started with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint Choose one engineering question, connect the required data and tools, assemble the digital twin with OpenUSD, and use SimReady requirements to prepare assets for the intended analysis. Review the result before expanding. Ready to get started? Build with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint Assemble your digital twin with OpenUSD Prepare and validate your assets with DSX asset guidance and SimReady Foundation Prepare content for your workflow with AI factory pipeline samples Explore related simulation examples in Putting Astra to Work in Simulation With NVIDIA Omniverse Libraries Stay up to date by subscribing to NVIDIA news and following NVIDIA Omniverse on Discord and YouTube . With a colorful background in areas such as academia, fine art, and 3D workflows, Ashley reaches far across the community in M&E, AECO, and education.
