Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications. The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons: Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational. Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization. Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions. Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational ( paper , documentation ), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required. How Kumo Relational Works Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation ( e.g. , "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort. Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning , reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target ( e.g. , "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units"). Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference. To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works: Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables. Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL) , a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage. Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates. Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs. How Kumo Relational Was Built Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures. The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases. Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task. Performance In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box: ![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.] Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy. The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added. Limitations Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed. Demo Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular . The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model: # pip install structured-data-models import sdm model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device= "cuda" ) pred = model( # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets): x_context=..., y_context=..., # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps): x_query=..., # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities: related_context_tables=..., related_query_tables=..., ) See the library's relational examples for complete RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines, including how to sample each entity's related tables. To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request: # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]' import sdm_client client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url= "http://localhost:8001" ) # NIM URL query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery( # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL): "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id" , # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred): { "users" : ..., "orders" : ...}, ) pred = client.predict( # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict: query.materialize(indices=[ 1 , 2 , 3 ]), model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(), ) See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here . items.content: Back to Articles Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote - Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub . We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps. Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not. Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post , we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row. Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function. + So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing. Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it. We call this offline policy-relative difficulty . We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run. What happened after training We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt. Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool. Metric Base RL fine-tuned Change Observed 20/20 38 (7.50%) → 107 (21.10%) +69 tasks pass@1 (successful attempts) 5,242 (51.70%) → 6,163 (60.78%) +9.08 pt pass@20 (tasks solved at least once) 453 (89.35%) → 446 (87.97%) −7 tasks Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff. What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20. Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset. These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most. The training loop Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench. Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run. Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat). Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py . For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps. Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures. That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool. Offline policy-relative difficulty Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer: No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation. ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim. Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] . If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] . In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another. ++ A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user. The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool? We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy. So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records: Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look

The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub . We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not. For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps. Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures. That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool. Offline policy-relative difficulty Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer: No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation. ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim. Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] . If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] . In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another. ++ A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user. The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool? We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy. So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records: Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look

items.content: Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 14 +8 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. References ECMWF: Ensemble weather forecasting NOAA: North American Multi-Model Ensemble FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast Pre-trained Models for Enhanced Zero/Few-Shot Forecasting of Multivariate Time Series Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review Smith and Wallis (2009), A Simple Explanation of the Forecast Combination Puzzle Models mentioned in this article 5 Spaces mentioned in this article 1 More from this author ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model 25 October 20, 2026 Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again? 122 September 15, 2026 Community Edit Preview Upload images, audio, and videos by dragging in the text input, pasting, or clicking here . Tap or paste here to upload images Comment · Sign up or log in to comment Upvote 14 +2 Models mentioned in this article 5 Spaces mentioned in this article 1

Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.31657 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification Authors: Sachin Gupta View a PDF of the paper titled Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification, by Sachin Gupta View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.
