items.content: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification Sachin Gupta Affiliation: Independent Researcher United States sachinkg12@gmail.com Abstract Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: a routing policy is selected on calibration data under asymmetric costs and evaluated once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. With illustrative per-ticket costs of zero for a correct route, one for human triage, and five for a wrong route, term-frequency–inverse-document-frequency logistic regression selects a threshold of 0.60 and reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1 % relative reduction (95 % bootstrap confidence interval, 35.7 %–40.4 %), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3 % to 3.5 %. In a post-hoc 16-setting analysis, calibration-selected policies beat both always-route and always-defer in 14 settings. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic recalibration reduces expected calibration error but does not reliably improve ranking discrimination; one GPT-4o-mini setting emits a single confidence value and has correctness area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.500. At the break-even probability of 0.80, seven prompted conditions defer every ticket, and Haiku few-shot routes 19 of 1,000. A language-model-only agreement control and margin- and entropy-based rejection scores for the logistic-regression baseline provide nontrivial comparators. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification. Index Terms: trustworthy machine learning, calibration, cost-aware abstention, selective prediction, large language models, text classification, IT service management I Introduction Enterprise IT service desks process tens of thousands of internal tickets per month, where the “customer” is an employee asking internal IT for help with hardware, access, or software (not an external consumer). HDI/MetricNet reports the North American average cost per voice IT service-desk ticket at US$17.19, with walk-up tickets averaging US$37.52 [ 1 ] . Routing happens under an asymmetric cost structure. Sending a ticket to the correct queue is nearly free. Sending it to a human triager is moderately costly. Sending it to the wrong queue is much more expensive once you account for handoff latency, double work, and missed service levels. Accuracy or macro-F1 alone cannot represent this asymmetry or indicate when to trust an automated decision [ 2 , 3 ] . Two trends make this gap more pressing. First, large language models (LLMs) can be prompted as zero- or few-shot text classifiers [ 4 , 5 ] , potentially reducing the need for task-specific training. Second, modern neural classifiers, including LLMs, are known to be poorly calibrated. They often produce high confidence values regardless of actual accuracy [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Together these trends raise a concrete operational question: should a prompted LLM be allowed to auto-route IT tickets, and if so, under what abstention policy? We study this question on the public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset (47,837 tickets, eight categories). We treat cost-aware abstention not as a way to improve a classifier but as an empirical readiness test under stated assumptions. Predictors, confidence estimators, rejection scores, and policies remain separate. Our contributions are: 1. A comparison of four trained non-LLM classifiers and eight prompted LLM conditions on the same public corpus, including a common 1,000-ticket test subset. 2. A calibration analysis that reports expected calibration error (ECE), correctness area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and tie-aware area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC), plus separate mixed ( M = 9 M{=}9 ) and LLM-only ( M = 8 M{=}8 ) agreement pools. 3. A calibration-selected, paired-bootstrap cost analysis with top-probability, probability-margin, and entropy rejection scores; a post-hoc 16-setting cost-parameter analysis; and LLM policies that use a cost-derived threshold rather than test tuning. 4. A reproducible evaluation framework and per-ticket artifacts that expose prediction, confidence, rejection, and cost as separately auditable stages. The main observation is simple: abstention does not repair a weak classifier. It exposes when auto-routing is cost-preferred under a particular dataset, confidence signal, and cost model. Positioning. The components we combine are individually established: Chow-style error-reject [ 3 ] , Elkan-style cost-sensitive decision-making [ 10 ] , ECE-based calibration diagnostics [ 6 , 11 ] , isotonic recalibration, and self-consistency-inspired agreement signals [ 12 ] . We introduce no new abstention algorithm. This paper’s contribution is an empirical evaluation of deployment-relevant assumptions and its reproducible implementation, not a universal readiness certificate. II Related Work Selective prediction and abstention. The classical framework for rejecting uncertain inputs traces back to Chow’s error-reject trade-off [ 3 ] . It has been formalized for modern classifiers under the names selective prediction [ 2 , 13 ] and learning with abstention [ 14 ] ; a recent survey organizes LLM abstention methods, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics [ 15 ] . The closest line is learning to defer , where a classifier is trained jointly with the option to pass an instance to a human expert [ 16 , 17 ] . Our training-free confidence-threshold policy addresses the same route-or-defer action space without joint training. We evaluate its decisions under an explicit cost model following Elkan’s cost-sensitive formulation [ 10 ] . Calibration and overconfidence. Guo et al. [ 6 ] documented systematic overconfidence in deep neural classifiers and popularized Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [ 11 ] as a diagnostic. A growing literature studies whether LLMs are well-calibrated [ 7 , 9 , 8 , 18 ] . The broad finding is that verbalized confidence runs too high. We contribute a public-dataset measurement of LLM ECE in an asymmetric-cost classification setting, and report agreement-across-predictors as a confidence signal inspired by self-consistency [ 12 ] . LLMs for text classification. Off-the-shelf prompting of LLMs as classifiers [ 4 , 5 , 19 ] is operationally attractive, but on short, lexical-signal-heavy tasks strong classical text classifiers such as linear SVMs [ 20 ] remain highly competitive, as our IT-ticket results confirm (§ V-A ). Cost-driven LLM cascades and routing lower inference cost by escalating only hard inputs to a stronger model [ 21 ] ; we instead hold the model fixed and use abstention to decide when not to auto-route at all. Our evaluation lands in the same mixed picture for the IT-ticket domain. IT ticket classification. Automated routing of support tickets has a long applications-track history [ 22 , 23 ] but is rarely evaluated under explicit cost models or with abstention. Our framework is structured as a deferral layer that could be integrated into an IT service management pipeline rather than as a new classifier. III Method III-A Problem setup Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} be the space of ticket texts and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} a set of K K disjoint downstream queues. A base classifier h : 𝒳 → 𝒴 h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} emits a label. The policy-wrapped decision d : 𝒳 → 𝒴 ∪ { ⊥ } d:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\cup\{\bot\} either routes h ⁡ ( x ) h(x) or abstains ( ⊥ \bot ); abstained tickets go to a human triager. Each decision incurs one of three costs: c ok c_{\mathrm{ok}} (correct auto-route), c triage c_{\mathrm{triage}} (human triage), and c wrong c_{\mathrm{wrong}} (incorrect auto-route). The expected per-ticket cost is 𝔼 ⁡ [ c ] = \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c]={} ℙ ( ⊥ ) c triage + ℙ ( correct , ¬ ⊥ ) c ok \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\bot)c_{\mathrm{triage}}+\mathbb{P}(\text{correct},\neg\bot)c_{\mathrm{ok}} (1) + ℙ ( wrong , ¬ ⊥ ) c wrong . \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}(\text{wrong},\neg\bot)c_{\mathrm{wrong}}. Our primary analysis uses ( c ok , c triage , c wrong ) = ( 0 , 1 , 5 ) (c_{\mathrm{ok}},c_{\mathrm{triage}},c_{\mathrm{wrong}})=(0,1,5) . These values are illustrative rather than calibrated to any single organization, but they encode the qualitative ordering that motivates abstention: a misroute is costlier than a human triage because it still incurs the triage after a delayed hand-off plus rework, whereas a correct auto-route is effectively free. Because the ratio is an assumption rather than a measured quantity, every deployment conclusion is conditional on it. Equation ( 2 ) shows how local costs determine the routing threshold; an organization must estimate its own triage and misroute costs before use. As a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, we also cross c triage ∈ { 0.5 , 1 , 1.5 , 2 } c_{\mathrm{triage}}\in\{0.5,1,1.5,2\} with c wrong ∈ { 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 } c_{\mathrm{wrong}}\in\{2,5,10,20\} while fixing c ok = 0 c_{\mathrm{ok}}=0 . The ( 2 , 2 ) (2,2) pair is an equal-cost boundary; the other 15 pairs retain c wrong > c triage c_{\mathrm{wrong}}>c_{\mathrm{triage}} . III-B Predictors We evaluate four non-LLM baselines and four prompted LLMs. Non-LLM baselines. TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) uni- and bi-gram features feed three classifiers. Logistic regression and linear support vector machine (SVM) cap the vocabulary at 100,000 features; random forest caps it at 50,000. The headline baseline is multiclass logistic regression (LR; L2 regularization, C = 1.0 C{=}1.0 ). The linear SVM head is a one-vs-rest linear support vector classifier (SVC) wrapped in sigmoid-calibrated probability outputs. The random forest head uses 300 trees with default depth. Separately, the fourth baseline fine-tunes DistilBERT ( distilbert-base-uncased ) on tokenized ticket text from the full training split for two epochs with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. All four are fit on the same train split. LLM predictors. Each LLM is queried per ticket with a structured prompt (template v1 ; the strict v2 is used only in § V-D ) that lists the allowed labels, the ticket text, and an instruction to return JSON {"label": ..., "confidence": ...} . Few-shot variants prepend k = 3 k{=}3 exemplars per class (24 in total, class-balanced across the eight categories), drawn only from the training split. The main prompts contain label names and examples but no natural-language category definitions; the comparison therefore characterizes these prompting conditions, not each LLM’s intrinsic capability. We use temperature 0 and max_tokens =64 for all main runs. Out-of-set labels are tagged as invalid; malformed JSON is tagged as a parse error. Both invalid labels and parse errors are scored as incorrect predictions and assigned confidence 0; the threshold policies defer such rows rather than auto-route them, while always_route , by definition, routes them and incurs c wrong c_{\mathrm{wrong}} . The four models are GPT-4o-mini [ 24 ] , Claude Haiku 4.5 [ 25 ] , Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 26 ] , and Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite [ 27 ] . GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku are queried through their vendor APIs. 1 1 1 For reproducibility, the proprietary endpoints and query date were: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 , both queried on 2026-05-22. The Anthropic model is a dated snapshot; the OpenAI alias resolves to the provider’s then-current gpt-4o-mini snapshot, so those results reflect the endpoint state on that date. The open-weights models use Together AI endpoints Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite , provider-documented at query time as 8-bit floating point (FP8) and 4-bit integer (INT4), respectively; precision is absent from our saved responses and is not independently verified. We re-run the model families through DeepInfra (provider-documented bfloat16, or BF16) as a cross-provider check that does not isolate quantization; our conclusions are unchanged (§ V-E ). III-C Confidence and rejection scores We evaluate probability estimates and ranking signals separately. Model-reported. For a non-LLM baseline this is the maximum class-probability estimate returned by that model: multinomial probabilities for logistic regression, sigmoid-calibrated outputs for the SVM, tree-vote fractions for the random forest, and softmax for DistilBERT. For LLMs it is the confidence field parsed from the JSON output. Cross-predictor agreement. Given M M predictors evaluated on the same ticket, the agreement-confidence for the primary predictor is the fraction of the M M predictors that emit the same label. No held-out labels are used to compute this score at application time. In our mixed configuration M = 9 M{=}9 : the four LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings (eight prompted variants) plus the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline. Because this pool mixes the eight LLM variants with the stronger classical baseline, an LLM’s agreement partly reflects concordance with a more accurate supervised predictor, not peer consensus alone. We therefore also report an LLM-only M = 8 M{=}8 control. Operational trade-off: agreement requires running all M M predictors at inference. Because the pool is heterogeneous, its dollar cost and latency depend on the endpoints and are not necessarily M × M{\times} those of the primary alone. Isotonic incurs one calibration-time pass per prompted predictor and a constant-time lookup at inference. Isotonic regression on a held-out calibration split. LLM-emitted confidence fields are bounded in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] but are not logits, so parametric Platt or temperature scaling do not apply cleanly. We instead fit one isotonic regression per prompted LLM condition on the calibration split: pairs { ( c i , 𝟏 [ y ^ i = y i ] ) } \{(c_{i},\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}])\} of raw confidence and ground-truth correctness, mapped via sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression [ 28 ] (monotone non-decreasing, output clipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ) into a recalibration c ↦ Pr ^ ​ ( correct ) c\mapsto\hat{\Pr}(\text{correct}) . For each LLM predictor we fit on a stratified 500-ticket subsample of the calibration split (4,000 calibration queries across the 8 prompted variants). Calibration and test splits are disjoint : the isotonic mapping is learned only from calibration pairs and applied unchanged to test confidences. ECE is computed with 10 equal-width bins on test predictions. Discrimination metrics. ECE measures probability-level calibration but not whether confidence ranks correct predictions above errors. We therefore report correctness AUROC (ties receive half credit) and area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC; lower is better). Since LLM scores contain many ties, our AURC adds each equal-score group as a block and integrates the right-continuous risk step, avoiding arbitrary ordering within ties. Nontrivial rejection comparators. For TF-IDF + LR we also use the top-two probability margin p ( 1 ) − p ( 2 ) p_{(1)}-p_{(2)} and normalized inverse entropy 1 − H ⁡ ( p ) / log ⁡ K 1-H(p)/\log K . Each score’s threshold is selected on calibration over a 0.01-spaced grid in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and then evaluated once on test. III-D Abstention policies For the primary non-LLM analysis we compare always_route (route every ticket) with threshold@ τ \tau for τ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 , 0.8 , 0.9 } \tau\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} (route if conf ≥ τ \text{conf}\geq\tau , defer otherwise). Where stated, we also use the trivial always_defer reference policy, which defers every ticket at cost c triage c_{\mathrm{triage}} by construction. It appears in the LLM break-even comparison and the post-hoc cost grid; the primary non-LLM analysis uses always_route as its baseline. Cross-predictor agreement enters our experiments only as a confidence estimator (above), not as a deferral policy. Threshold selection. Non-LLM operating points are selected on the calibration split under the configured cost model. The best threshold over the stated grid, τ ∗ = arg ⁡ min τ ​ 𝔼 calib ​ [ c ∣ τ ] \tau^{*}=\arg\min_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{\text{calib}}[c\mid\tau] , is then evaluated once on the held-out test split. For the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline this procedure selects τ ∗ = 0.60 \tau^{*}=0.60 (calibration costs at τ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 , 0.8 , 0.9 } \tau\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} are { 0.493 , 0.461 , 0.477 , 0.537 , 0.654 } \{0.493,0.461,0.477,0.537,0.654\} ). Calibration and test splits are disjoint by construction. For each post-hoc cost-sensitivity setting, we select on calibration among always_route , always_defer , and thresholds from 0.01 to 0.99 in steps of 0.01, then evaluate the frozen choice once on test. For exact calibration-cost ties, the deterministic order is always_route , then always_defer , then the smallest threshold among tied threshold policies. For LLMs we do not select a threshold on test. If an isotonic score is interpreted as p = Pr ⁡ ( correct ) p=\Pr(\mathrm{correct}) , auto-routing is cost-preferred when p ​ c ok + ( 1 − p ) ​ c wrong ≤ c triage , pc_{\mathrm{ok}}+(1-p)c_{\mathrm{wrong}}\leq c_{\mathrm{triage}}, (2) which gives the fixed break-even threshold p ≥ 0.80 p\geq 0.80 under ( 0 , 1 , 5 ) (0,1,5) . Raw verbalized scores are not treated as probabilities for policy optimization. III-E Modular evaluation pipeline Predictors, confidence estimators, abstention policies, and the cost model are separated by interfaces. Registry-based predictor addition does not require changing the evaluator; other extension types require explicit builder or policy-set wiring in the current code. Fig. 1 shows the flow. Ticket text Classifier Confidence estimator Abstention policy Auto-route Human triage high conf. low conf. Fig. 1: Evaluation pipeline from ticket text to auto-routing or human triage, with prediction, confidence estimation, and abstention separated. IV Experimental Setup IV-A Dataset and splits We use the public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset [ 29 ] : 47,837 tickets, 8 categories ( Access , Administrative rights , HR Support , Hardware , Internal Project , Miscellaneous , Purchase , Storage ), median ticket length 175 characters, maximum/minimum class size 13,617 / 1,760 ( 7.74 × 7.74\times imbalance; Fig. 2 ). We use a stratified 70/10/20 train/calibration/test split (Table I ). Few-shot exemplars are drawn only from the training split. The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle under its posted terms. We use that preprocessed public release. The complete dataset and per-ticket text arrays are not redistributed in the camera-ready artifacts; only three brief illustrative excerpts from the public dataset are quoted in Section V-F . Each dataset row pairs a short internal IT request with a category label. TABLE I: Dataset summary (public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset). Property Value # tickets 47,837 # classes 8 Train / Calib. / Test 33,486 / 4,784 / 9,567 Median ticket length (chars) 175 Class imbalance (max/min) 7.74 × 7.74\times IV-B Test subsample for LLM predictors Per-call API budget makes evaluating all four LLMs on the full 9,567-ticket test set impractical. The 8 LLM configurations alone issue 8,000 8{,}000 test queries on the subsample described below, and scaling to the full test set would multiply that by an order of magnitude. LLMs are therefore evaluated on a stratified 1,000-ticket subsample (seed 42). To assess whether that subset preserves the non-LLM baseline ordering, we re-evaluate every non-LLM baseline on the same 1,000-ticket subsample (Table II ). Subsample and full-test numbers differ by at most 1.6 percentage points for every baseline. The strongest non-LLM baseline (DistilBERT) reaches 0.879 accuracy on the subsample, versus 0.477 for the best LLM on the same tickets, confirming the same ordering on identical examples. TABLE II: Non-LLM baselines on the LLM test subset ( n = 1,000 n=1{,}000 ). Baseline (on 1,000-ticket subsample) Acc. Macro-F1 ECE-raw TF-IDF + LR 0.847 0.842 0.111 TF-IDF + Linear SVM 0.867 0.869 0.056 TF-IDF + Random Forest 0.804 0.791 0.172 DistilBERT (fine-tuned) 0.879 0.883 0.043 IV-C Reproducibility Runs save configuration, seeds, dataset and split hashes, package versions, and per-ticket outputs. Intervals use 1,000 paired resamples with seed 1337; reported percentage reductions recompute the ratio inside each resample. The public project repository is https://github.com/sachinkg12/RouteGuard ; the frozen camera-ready claim manifest, automated recomputation receipt from a separate verification script, tables, text-free per-ticket vectors, and code snapshot are archived as a versioned series at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22609128 . The supplement pins the verified x86-64/Python 3.14 environment because estimator refits can vary slightly across architectures; the frozen prediction vectors remain the audit record. V Results V-A Base-classifier predictive performance We compare four non-LLM baselines against eight prompted hosted LLM configurations (Table III ). Among non-LLM baselines the fine-tuned encoder is strongest. DistilBERT reaches accuracy 0.877 and macro-F1 0.874 on the full 9,567-ticket test set after two epochs of training on a single GPU with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. The next non-LLM baseline is a sigmoid-calibrated linear SVM over TF-IDF features (accuracy 0.863 , macro-F1 0.864 ), followed by the TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline (0.847 / 0.842) and a TF-IDF random forest (0.818 / 0.806). The best prompted LLM is Claude Haiku 4.5 with k = 3 k{=}3 few-shot prompting at 0.477 / 0.459 0.477/0.459 . GPT-4o-mini few-shot follows (0.459 / 0.450), then Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct few-shot (0.447 / 0.454) and Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite zero-shot (0.378 / 0.284). On the common 1,000-ticket subset, DistilBERT reaches 0.879 and Haiku few-shot 0.477, so the measured gap is not caused by different test examples. It is not, however, a pure capability comparison: the trained models learn the taxonomy from 33,486 labeled tickets, whereas the prompted LLMs receive label names and, at most, 24 examples without category definitions. Ambiguous labels such as Miscellaneous , Internal Project , and Administrative rights make that distinction material. We therefore scope the result to these training and prompt-information regimes. Few-shot prompting helps three of the four LLMs but hurts Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite by 12.3 percentage points. Inspection of the raw outputs shows that the model often emits a conversational preamble ( “I’ll classify the ticket and return the JSON.” ) that uses up the output budget before any JSON is emitted, which produces a 15.1 % parse-error rate. 2 2 2 This low few-shot result is sensitive to the joint prompt/output-budget configuration: on the ablation subsample, switching from v1 /64 to the stricter v2 /128 configuration eliminates the parse failures and raises Llama few-shot accuracy from 0.245 to 0.320 (Table IX ). Our evaluation lands in the same mixed picture for the IT-ticket domain. IT ticket classification. Automated routing of support tickets has a long applications-track history [ 22 , 23 ] but is rarely evaluated under explicit cost models or with abstention. Our framework is structured as a deferral layer that could be integrated into an IT service management pipeline rather than as a new classifier. III Method III-A Problem setup Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} be the space of ticket texts and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} a set of K K disjoint downstream queues. A base classifier h : 𝒳 → 𝒴 h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} emits a label. The policy-wrapped decision d : 𝒳 → 𝒴 ∪ { ⊥ } d:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\cup\{\bot\} either routes h ⁡ ( x ) h(x) or abstains ( ⊥ \bot ); abstained tickets go to a human triager. Each decision incurs one of three costs: c ok c_{\mathrm{ok}} (correct auto-route), c triage c_{\mathrm{triage}} (human triage), and c wrong c_{\mathrm{wrong}} (incorrect auto-route). The expected per-ticket cost is 𝔼 ⁡ [ c ] = \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c]={} ℙ ( ⊥ ) c triage + ℙ ( correct , ¬ ⊥ ) c ok \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\bot)c_{\mathrm{triage}}+\mathbb{P}(\text{correct},\neg\bot)c_{\mathrm{ok}} (1) + ℙ ( wrong , ¬ ⊥ ) c wrong . \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}(\text{wrong},\neg\bot)c_{\mathrm{wrong}}. Our primary analysis uses ( c ok , c triage , c wrong ) = ( 0 , 1 , 5 ) (c_{\mathrm{ok}},c_{\mathrm{triage}},c_{\mathrm{wrong}})=(0,1,5) . These values are illustrative rather than calibrated to any single organization, but they encode the qualitative ordering that motivates abstention: a misroute is costlier than a human triage because it still incurs the triage after a delayed hand-off plus rework, whereas a correct auto-route is effectively free. Because the ratio is an assumption rather than a measured quantity, every deployment conclusion is conditional on it. Equation ( 2 ) shows how local costs determine the routing threshold; an organization must estimate its own triage and misroute costs before use. As a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, we also cross c triage ∈ { 0.5 , 1 , 1.5 , 2 } c_{\mathrm{triage}}\in\{0.5,1,1.5,2\} with c wrong ∈ { 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 } c_{\mathrm{wrong}}\in\{2,5,10,20\} while fixing c ok = 0 c_{\mathrm{ok}}=0 . The ( 2 , 2 ) (2,2) pair is an equal-cost boundary; the other 15 pairs retain c wrong > c triage c_{\mathrm{wrong}}>c_{\mathrm{triage}} . III-B Predictors We evaluate four non-LLM baselines and four prompted LLMs. Non-LLM baselines. TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) uni- and bi-gram features feed three classifiers. Logistic regression and linear support vector machine (SVM) cap the vocabulary at 100,000 features; random forest caps it at 50,000. The headline baseline is multiclass logistic regression (LR; L2 regularization, C = 1.0 C{=}1.0 ). The linear SVM head is a one-vs-rest linear support vector classifier (SVC) wrapped in sigmoid-calibrated probability outputs. The random forest head uses 300 trees with default depth. Separately, the fourth baseline fine-tunes DistilBERT ( distilbert-base-uncased ) on tokenized ticket text from the full training split for two epochs with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. All four are fit on the same train split. LLM predictors. Each LLM is queried per ticket with a structured prompt (template v1 ; the strict v2 is used only in § V-D ) that lists the allowed labels, the ticket text, and an instruction to return JSON {"label": ..., "confidence": ...} . Few-shot variants prepend k = 3 k{=}3 exemplars per class (24 in total, class-balanced across the eight categories), drawn only from the training split. The main prompts contain label names and examples but no natural-language category definitions; the comparison therefore characterizes these prompting conditions, not each LLM’s intrinsic capability. We use temperature 0 and max_tokens =64 for all main runs. Out-of-set labels are tagged as invalid; malformed JSON is tagged as a parse error. Both invalid labels and parse errors are scored as incorrect predictions and assigned confidence 0; the threshold policies defer such rows rather than auto-route them, while always_route , by definition, routes them and incurs c wrong c_{\mathrm{wrong}} . The four models are GPT-4o-mini [ 24 ] , Claude Haiku 4.5 [ 25 ] , Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 26 ] , and Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite [ 27 ] . GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku are queried through their vendor APIs. 1 1 1 For reproducibility, the proprietary endpoints and query date were: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 , both queried on 2026-05-22. The Anthropic model is a dated snapshot; the OpenAI alias resolves to the provider’s then-current gpt-4o-mini snapshot, so those results reflect the endpoint state on that date. The open-weights models use Together AI endpoints Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite , provider-documented at query time as 8-bit floating point (FP8) and 4-bit integer (INT4), respectively; precision is absent from our saved responses and is not independently verified. We re-run the model families through DeepInfra (provider-documented bfloat16, or BF16) as a cross-provider check that does not isolate quantization; our conclusions are unchanged (§ V-E ). III-C Confidence and rejection scores We evaluate probability estimates and ranking signals separately. Model-reported. For a non-LLM baseline this is the maximum class-probability estimate returned by that model: multinomial probabilities for logistic regression, sigmoid-calibrated outputs for the SVM, tree-vote fractions for the random forest, and softmax for DistilBERT. For LLMs it is the confidence field parsed from the JSON output. Cross-predictor agreement. Given M M predictors evaluated on the same ticket, the agreement-confidence for the primary predictor is the fraction of the M M predictors that emit the same label. No held-out labels are used to compute this score at application time. In our mixed configuration M = 9 M{=}9 : the four LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings (eight prompted variants) plus the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline. Because this pool mixes the eight LLM variants with the stronger classical baseline, an LLM’s agreement partly reflects concordance with a more accurate supervised predictor, not peer consensus alone. We therefore also report an LLM-only M = 8 M{=}8 control. Operational trade-off: agreement requires running all M M predictors at inference. Because the pool is heterogeneous, its dollar cost and latency depend on the endpoints and are not necessarily M × M{\times} those of the primary alone. Isotonic incurs one calibration-time pass per prompted predictor and a constant-time lookup at inference. Isotonic regression on a held-out calibration split. LLM-emitted confidence fields are bounded in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] but are not logits, so parametric Platt or temperature scaling do not apply cleanly. We instead fit one isotonic regression per prompted LLM condition on the calibration split: pairs { ( c i , 𝟏 [ y ^ i = y i ] ) } \{(c_{i},\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}])\} of raw confidence and ground-truth correctness, mapped via sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression [ 28 ] (monotone non-decreasing, output clipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ) into a recalibration c ↦ Pr ^ ​ ( correct ) c\mapsto\hat{\Pr}(\text{correct}) . For each LLM predictor we fit on a stratified 500-ticket subsample of the calibration split (4,000 calibration queries across the 8 prompted variants). Calibration and test splits are disjoint : the isotonic mapping is learned only from calibration pairs and applied unchanged to test confidences. ECE is computed with 10 equal-width bins on test predictions. Discrimination metrics. ECE measures probability-level calibration but not whether confidence ranks correct predictions above errors. We therefore report correctness AUROC (ties receive half credit) and area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC; lower is better). Since LLM scores contain many ties, our AURC adds each equal-score group as a block and integrates the right-continuous risk step, avoiding arbitrary ordering within ties. Nontrivial rejection comparators. For TF-IDF + LR we also use the top-two probability margin p ( 1 ) − p ( 2 ) p_{(1)}-p_{(2)} and normalized inverse entropy 1 − H ⁡ ( p ) / log ⁡ K 1-H(p)/\log K . Each score’s threshold is selected on calibration over a 0.01-spaced grid in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and then evaluated once on test. III-D Abstention policies For the primary non-LLM analysis we compare always_route (route every ticket) with threshold@ τ \tau for τ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 , 0.8 , 0.9 } \tau\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} (route if conf ≥ τ \text{conf}\geq\tau , defer otherwise). Where stated, we also use the trivial always_defer reference policy, which defers every ticket at cost c triage c_{\mathrm{triage}} by construction. It appears in the LLM break-even comparison and the post-hoc cost grid; the primary non-LLM analysis uses always_route as its baseline. Cross-predictor agreement enters our experiments only as a confidence estimator (above), not as a deferral policy. Threshold selection. Non-LLM operating points are selected on the calibration split under the configured cost model. The best threshold over the stated grid, τ ∗ = arg ⁡ min τ ​ 𝔼 calib ​ [ c ∣ τ ] \tau^{*}=\arg\min_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{\text{calib}}[c\mid\tau] , is then evaluated once on the held-out test split. For the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline this procedure selects τ ∗ = 0.60 \tau^{*}=0.60 (calibration costs at τ ∈ { 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 , 0.8 , 0.9 } \tau\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\} are { 0.493 , 0.461 , 0.477 , 0.537 , 0.654 } \{0.493,0.461,0.477,0.537,0.654\} ). Calibration and test splits are disjoint by construction. For each post-hoc cost-sensitivity setting, we select on calibration among always_route , always_defer , and thresholds from 0.01 to 0.99 in steps of 0.01, then evaluate the frozen choice once on test. For exact calibration-cost ties, the deterministic order is always_route , then always_defer , then the smallest threshold among tied threshold policies. For LLMs we do not select a threshold on test. If an isotonic score is interpreted as p = Pr ⁡ ( correct ) p=\Pr(\mathrm{correct}) , auto-routing is cost-preferred when p ​ c ok + ( 1 − p ) ​ c wrong ≤ c triage , pc_{\mathrm{ok}}+(1-p)c_{\mathrm{wrong}}\leq c_{\mathrm{triage}}, (2) which gives the fixed break-even threshold p ≥ 0.80 p\geq 0.80 under ( 0 , 1 , 5 ) (0,1,5) . Raw verbalized scores are not treated as probabilities for policy optimization. III-E Modular evaluation pipeline Predictors, confidence estimators, abstention policies, and the cost model are separated by interfaces. Registry-based predictor addition does not require changing the evaluator; other extension types require explicit builder or policy-set wiring in the current code. Fig. 1 shows the flow. Ticket text Classifier Confidence estimator Abstention policy Auto-route Human triage high conf. low conf. Fig. 1: Evaluation pipeline from ticket text to auto-routing or human triage, with prediction, confidence estimation, and abstention separated. IV Experimental Setup IV-A Dataset and splits We use the public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset [ 29 ] : 47,837 tickets, 8 categories ( Access , Administrative rights , HR Support , Hardware , Internal Project , Miscellaneous , Purchase , Storage ), median ticket length 175 characters, maximum/minimum class size 13,617 / 1,760 ( 7.74 × 7.74\times imbalance; Fig. 2 ). We use a stratified 70/10/20 train/calibration/test split (Table I ). Few-shot exemplars are drawn only from the training split. The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle under its posted terms. We use that preprocessed public release. The complete dataset and per-ticket text arrays are not redistributed in the camera-ready artifacts; only three brief illustrative excerpts from the public dataset are quoted in Section V-F . Each dataset row pairs a short internal IT request with a category label. TABLE I: Dataset summary (public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset). Property Value # tickets 47,837 # classes 8 Train / Calib. / Test 33,486 / 4,784 / 9,567 Median ticket length (chars) 175 Class imbalance (max/min) 7.74 × 7.74\times IV-B Test subsample for LLM predictors Per-call API budget makes evaluating all four LLMs on the full 9,567-ticket test set impractical. The 8 LLM configurations alone issue 8,000 8{,}000 test queries on the subsample described below, and scaling to the full test set would multiply that by an order of magnitude. LLMs are therefore evaluated on a stratified 1,000-ticket subsample (seed 42). To assess whether that subset preserves the non-LLM baseline ordering, we re-evaluate every non-LLM baseline on the same 1,000-ticket subsample (Table II ). Subsample and full-test numbers differ by at most 1.6 percentage points for every baseline. The strongest non-LLM baseline (DistilBERT) reaches 0.879 accuracy on the subsample, versus 0.477 for the best LLM on the same tickets, confirming the same ordering on identical examples. TABLE II: Non-LLM baselines on the LLM test subset ( n = 1,000 n=1{,}000 ). Baseline (on 1,000-ticket subsample) Acc. Macro-F1 ECE-raw TF-IDF + LR 0.847 0.842 0.111 TF-IDF + Linear SVM 0.867 0.869 0.056 TF-IDF + Random Forest 0.804 0.791 0.172 DistilBERT (fine-tuned) 0.879 0.883 0.043 IV-C Reproducibility Runs save configuration, seeds, dataset and split hashes, package versions, and per-ticket outputs. Intervals use 1,000 paired resamples with seed 1337; reported percentage reductions recompute the ratio inside each resample. The public project repository is https://github.com/sachinkg12/RouteGuard ; the frozen camera-ready claim manifest, automated recomputation receipt from a separate verification script, tables, text-free per-ticket vectors, and code snapshot are archived as a versioned series at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22609128 . The supplement pins the verified x86-64/Python 3.14 environment because estimator refits can vary slightly across architectures; the frozen prediction vectors remain the audit record. V Results V-A Base-classifier predictive performance We compare four non-LLM baselines against eight prompted hosted LLM configurations (Table III ). Among non-LLM baselines the fine-tuned encoder is strongest. DistilBERT reaches accuracy 0.877 and macro-F1 0.874 on the full 9,567-ticket test set after two epochs of training on a single GPU with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. The next non-LLM baseline is a sigmoid-calibrated linear SVM over TF-IDF features (accuracy 0.863 , macro-F1 0.864 ), followed by the TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline (0.847 / 0.842) and a TF-IDF random forest (0.818 / 0.806). The best prompted LLM is Claude Haiku 4.5 with k = 3 k{=}3 few-shot prompting at 0.477 / 0.459 0.477/0.459 . GPT-4o-mini few-shot follows (0.459 / 0.450), then Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct few-shot (0.447 / 0.454) and Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite zero-shot (0.378 / 0.284). On the common 1,000-ticket subset, DistilBERT reaches 0.879 and Haiku few-shot 0.477, so the measured gap is not caused by different test examples. It is not, however, a pure capability comparison: the trained models learn the taxonomy from 33,486 labeled tickets, whereas the prompted LLMs receive label names and, at most, 24 examples without category definitions. Ambiguous labels such as Miscellaneous , Internal Project , and Administrative rights make that distinction material. We therefore scope the result to these training and prompt-information regimes. Few-shot prompting helps three of the four LLMs but hurts Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite by 12.3 percentage points. Inspection of the raw outputs shows that the model often emits a conversational preamble ( “I’ll classify the ticket and return the JSON.” ) that uses up the output budget before any JSON is emitted, which produces a 15.1 % parse-error rate. 2 2 2 This low few-shot result is sensitive to the joint prompt/output-budget configuration: on the ablation subsample, switching from v1 /64 to the stricter v2 /128 configuration eliminates the parse failures and raises Llama few-shot accuracy from 0.245 to 0.320 (Table IX ). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.31656 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning Authors: Ali Najar , Hosein Hasani , Amir Kooshan Fattah , Yasamin Rajabi , Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah View a PDF of the paper titled METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning, by Ali Najar and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL. items.content: Metta : Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning Ali Najar Hosein Hasani Amir Kooshan Fattah Affiliation: Yasamin Rajabi Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah Affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering Affiliation: Sharif University of Technology Affiliation: {ali.najjar82,hosein.hasani,amir.hesari82, Email: Yasamin.rajabi53,soleymani}@sharif.edu Abstract Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation ( Metta ) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, Metta achieves a success rate over 50 % 50\% while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that Metta provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) studies how agents learn to make sequential decisions through interaction with an environment, using rewards as feedback to improve future behavior ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) . Despite strong performance in fixed environments, standard RL methods often require large amounts of data to adapt to new tasks and generalize poorly under environment shifts ( Packer et al., 2018 ; Cobbe et al., 2019 ) . Meta-reinforcement learning addresses this limitation by training agents over a distribution of tasks so they can use past training experience to adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction at meta-test time ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2016 ; Finn et al., 2017 ; Rakelly et al., 2019 ) . A fundamental problem in meta-RL is representing task evidence collected during interaction with the environment ( Humplik et al., 2019 ; Zintgraf et al., 2021 ) . Black-box sequence-based agents learn this representation directly from trajectories using internal dynamics ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2016 ; Mishra et al., 2018 ; Alver and Precup, 2021 ) . Latent-context methods instead make task inference more explicit by inferring a task variable or belief from collected experience ( Humplik et al., 2019 ; Rakelly et al., 2019 ; Zintgraf et al., 2021 ) . Yet despite their differences, most approaches still rely on compressed task representations, which may restrict their capacity in meta-RL settings where task evidence may be sparse, delayed, or unevenly distributed across episodes. Once experience is compressed into a latent task representation, the policy cannot easily recover specific past evidence that later becomes important. Figure 1: Exploration behavior on a sparse-reward PointMaze task ( Fu et al., 2020 ) across adaptation episodes. Trajectories are shown for Episodes 1 1 , 2 2 , 5 5 , and 10 10 of the same task. As interaction proceeds, Metta explores new regions and reduces repeated trajectories across episodes, suggesting more effective reuse of past exploration evidence in long-context adaptation. TrMRL ( Melo, 2022 ) is difficult to scale to long multi-episode settings, while ECET ( Shala et al., 2025 ) is limited by its short within-episode context. Transformers offer a natural alternative because self-attention enables associative retrieval over past interactions and supports long-range dependency modeling without relying on recurrent state compression ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Melo, 2022 ; Shala et al., 2025 ) . This makes them well suited to cross-episode meta-RL, where useful evidence may appear far back in the trial ( Mishra et al., 2018 ; Shala et al., 2025 ; Melo, 2022 ) . However, standard self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Duman Keles et al., 2023 ) , making long adaptation horizons increasingly expensive in online RL settings. Prior work also showed that transformer optimization in reinforcement learning can be unstable due to exploration dynamics and non-stationary training signals ( Parisotto et al., 2019 ) . In online meta-RL, the effective context grows with both the episode horizon and the number of adaptation episodes, making full-history attention increasingly expensive in memory and computation. As a result, transformer-based agents often face a trade-off between retaining long histories and remaining computationally practical. The computational overhead of full-history attention has motivated a recent shift toward modern linear recurrent models and neural memory architectures ( Gu et al., 2021 ; Smith et al., 2022 ; Gu and Dao, 2023 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . Instead of attending over the full history, these methods update an adaptive memory state online while preserving linear sequence complexity. Recent work suggests that recurrence need not be limited to a small passive hidden state and can instead be equipped with expressive state dynamics or trainable memory modules, allowing models to store information over long horizons while preserving linear sequence complexity ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . In particular, Test-Time Training (TTT) ( Sun et al., 2025 ) treats memory as a trainable module that can be updated continually during inference, turning sequence processing from passive state compression into adaptive memory updating. This has led to promising results in settings where long-range information is essential, including language modeling, time series, genomics, novel-view synthesis, and video generation ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Behrouz et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Dalal et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation ( Metta ), which leverages TTT layers ( Sun et al., 2025 ) as a modern neural memory module to gather task evidence from long-range interaction sequences in meta-RL. Besides this within-episode memory module, which provides fine-grained episode-level memories, we also use a coarse-grained aggregation mechanism that combines summaries across episodes. Thus, in addition to the classical slow and fast learning processes in meta-RL, our fast adaptation phase separates within-episode adaptation from cross-episode evidence aggregation, allowing the policy to condition on longer meta-test histories without relying on quadratic computation over agent interaction steps. Our experiments across locomotion, manipulation, and navigation benchmarks show that Metta improves fast adaptation in both standard and long-context meta-RL settings. Interestingly, the relative gain over existing methods is especially notable when generalizing to unseen held-out Meta-World task families that are not encountered during meta-training. This provides evidence of task-family-level out-of-distribution generalization, where adaptation transfers to task families not observed during meta-training. This suggests that neural memory modules can support adaptation beyond the task families observed during training. In addition, Metta achieves these improvements with substantially lower training cost than transformer-based meta-RL methods, while preserving linear sequence complexity over long horizons. Figure 1 illustrates the role of neural memory in long-context sparse-reward settings. Metta explores more broadly while reducing repeated trajectories across episodes, suggesting more effective reuse of information gathered during earlier episodes. Compared with EMA, attention-based retrieval is more expressive because it can learn which previous episode summaries contain the most relevant task information. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on standard meta-RL benchmarks covering locomotion, manipulation, and navigation tasks. We evaluate continuous-control adaptation on MuJoCo HalfCheetahVel ( Todorov et al., 2012 ) , where the agent must infer the target velocity from interaction. We use a limited training budget to compare how efficiently each method adapts under restricted environment interaction. Next, we evaluate robotic manipulation on ML1, ML10, and ML45 from the Meta-World benchmark ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . In ML1, following the standard baseline convention, goal coordinates are masked and must be inferred through interaction. ML10 and ML45 span multiple task families with disjoint train and test splits, allowing us to evaluate generalization to families not observed during meta-training. We view this as a form of task-family-level OOD evaluation, since the held-out test families are encountered only at meta-test time. In these settings, goal coordinates are included in the observation, while the task family remains fixed within each trial. During multi-class training, each rollout batch assigns environments to task classes in a balanced way and then samples a task variation within each class. Finally, we use PointMaze ( Fu et al., 2020 ) with sparse rewards (only at the goal position) to evaluate long-context adaptation. In this environment, the agent may need to explore for many steps before receiving useful feedback, making it important to preserve information from earlier parts of the trajectory. This benchmark directly tests whether meta-RL methods can benefit from long context. (a) MuJoCo HalfCheetahVel. (b) Sparse-reward PointMaze. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation ( Metta ), which leverages TTT layers ( Sun et al., 2025 ) as a modern neural memory module to gather task evidence from long-range interaction sequences in meta-RL. Besides this within-episode memory module, which provides fine-grained episode-level memories, we also use a coarse-grained aggregation mechanism that combines summaries across episodes. Thus, in addition to the classical slow and fast learning processes in meta-RL, our fast adaptation phase separates within-episode adaptation from cross-episode evidence aggregation, allowing the policy to condition on longer meta-test histories without relying on quadratic computation over agent interaction steps. Our experiments across locomotion, manipulation, and navigation benchmarks show that Metta improves fast adaptation in both standard and long-context meta-RL settings. Interestingly, the relative gain over existing methods is especially notable when generalizing to unseen held-out Meta-World task families that are not encountered during meta-training. This provides evidence of task-family-level out-of-distribution generalization, where adaptation transfers to task families not observed during meta-training. This suggests that neural memory modules can support adaptation beyond the task families observed during training. In addition, Metta achieves these improvements with substantially lower training cost than transformer-based meta-RL methods, while preserving linear sequence complexity over long horizons. Figure 1 illustrates the role of neural memory in long-context sparse-reward settings. Metta explores more broadly while reducing repeated trajectories across episodes, suggesting more effective reuse of information gathered during earlier episodes. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on standard meta-RL benchmarks covering locomotion, manipulation, and navigation tasks. We evaluate continuous-control adaptation on MuJoCo HalfCheetahVel ( Todorov et al., 2012 ) , where the agent must infer the target velocity from interaction. Barron , Dan Gnanapragasam , Michael Tschannen View a PDF of the paper titled A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy, by Jonathan T. Barron and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $\epsilon$ hyperparameter. A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy Jonathan T. Barron Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: barron@google.com Dan Gnanapragasam Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: nanabyte@google.com Michael Tschannen Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: tschannen@google.com Abstract Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse , rounds the target logit’s gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation , occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed “Slingshot” phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam’s ϵ \epsilon hyperparameter. 1 Introduction (a) Softmax Collapse: | g t | |g_{t}| vs. margin m m . (b) Softmax Cancellation: ‖ ∇ 𝐳 S ℒ ‖ 2 \|

Barron Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: barron@google.com Dan Gnanapragasam Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: nanabyte@google.com Michael Tschannen Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: tschannen@google.com Abstract Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse , rounds the target logit’s gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.31639 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation Authors: Gabriele Dominici , Teague McMillan , Fazl Barez , Marc Langheinrich , Martin Gjoreski View a PDF of the paper titled Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation, by Gabriele Dominici and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning. items.content: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation Gabriele Dominici † † thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: Università della Svizzera Italiana Email: gabriele.dominici@usi.ch Teague McMillan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: ETH Zurich Email: tmcmillan@ethz.ch Fazl Barez Affiliation: University of Oxford Email: fazl@robots.ox.ac.uk Marc Langheinrich Affiliation: Università della Svizzera Italiana Email: marc.langheinrich@usi.c Martin Gjoreski Affiliation: Università della Svizzera Italiana Email: martin.gjoreski@usi.ch Abstract Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT , an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where user trust is crucial ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . Here, non-experts frequently rely on LLM-generated rationales, treating them as transparent windows into the model’s decision-making ( Barez et al., 2025 ) . However, this trust is often misplaced. While techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) , and Chain of Thought (CoT) ( Wei et al., 2023 ) produce highly plausible text, they optimize for human preference rather than mechanistic transparency. Consequently, these explanations are frequently unfaithful to the model’s internal logic ( Mayne et al., 2026 ; Matton et al., 2025 ; Turpin et al., 2023 ; Lanham et al., 2023 ) . Alarmingly, even researchers sometimes misuse these persuasive post-hoc rationalizations with true explanations ( Barez et al., 2025 ) . This fundamental disconnect is a critical barrier to safe deployment. Specifically, standard CoT prompting suffers from severe causal opacity driven by attention leakage, the phenomenon where dense, global attention mechanisms allow a model to implicitly bleed information across its entire context window rather than strictly depending on preceding logical steps. Because of this leakage, generated reasoning may appear perfectly logical while remaining entirely disconnected from the final prediction. For instance, Turpin et al. (2023) demonstrate that when provided with subtle context biases or unstated hints, models will heavily exploit these heuristics to derive an answer, yet completely omit them from their generated explanations, fabricating a step-by-step rationale that was never utilized. Furthermore, Lanham et al. (2023) reveal that actively modifying, degrading, or intervening on early CoT steps often yields surprisingly little impact on the downstream output. Together, these phenomena prove that standard autoregressive reasoning frequently acts as a superficial justification, rather than a sequence of causally relevant steps that drive the model’s behavior. Information Leakage via Attention ( Lanham et al., 2023 ; Radhakrishnan et al., 2023 ) : In standard autoregressive generation, the Transformer’s attention mechanism allows every generated token to attend to all preceding tokens. Specifically, we aim to answer the following research questions: • RQ1 (Performance): Does enforcing a strict causal graph degrade task accuracy compared to standard CoT? • RQ2 (Faithfulness): Are the intermediate steps genuine drivers of the generation? We evaluate CausalCoT across performance, faithfulness, and intervenability using diverse benchmarks. We first use GPQA ( Rein et al., 2023 ) , a graduate-level science dataset, to ensure our model maintains competitive reasoning capabilities. Next, we incorporate MedQA ( Jin et al., 2020 ) to test multi-step clinical deduction in high-stakes domains. Finally, we leverage the Counterfactual Simulatability Suite (CF Suite) ( Mayne et al., 2026 ) across health, business, and ethics to quantify causal transparency and responsiveness to interventions. Combined, these benchmarks provide a robust foundation for assessing both task accuracy and model interpretability. Models and Baselines. We evaluate three families of models (Gemma 3, GPT-5.4, and Claude 4.5/4.6) across varying parameter scales. We compare CausalCoT against standard CoT prompting and Factored Decomposition ( Radhakrishnan et al., 2023 ) . Factored Decomposition isolates reasoning by breaking queries into sub-questions and evaluating them in restricted context windows. However, it suffers from two structural flaws: intermediate steps lack explicit parental routing, and the final prediction concatenates all generated text, reintroducing pervasive attention leakage. CausalCoT resolves these vulnerabilities by enforcing a DAG architecture, guaranteeing pure context isolation. Further details on baseline mechanics and comparison with CausalCoT are further explained in Appendix C . Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate our three research questions using the following metrics: • Predictive Performance (RQ1): We report standard Accuracy (Acc) to determine if CausalCoT’s strict DAG constraints degrade foundational problem-solving capabilities. We also report Pass@3 (the probability of generating at least one correct answer across three independent inferences). Because CausalCoT strictly enforces the generated topology, a malformed initial graph guarantees predictive failure. We therefore evaluate whether multi-sample generation mitigates zero-shot planning bottlenecks by providing multiple opportunities to produce a valid response. • Faithfulness and Predictability (RQ2): To quantify the causal influence of intermediate reasoning, we adapt established step-perturbation methodologies ( Lanham et al., 2023 ) . By injecting targeted errors using a frontier model (GPT-5.4) into intermediate nodes, we measure the frequency of downstream answer changes. To distinguish genuine causal adherence from arbitrary perturbation instability, we introduce a Predictable Change metric. This metric relies on an LLM judge that determines the logical downstream implication of each injected error, accounting for instances where a perturbation is insufficient to alter the final label. We then evaluate whether the model’s corrupted conclusion matches this counterfactual target, confirming that downstream predictions predictably adhere to the modified premise. • Test-Time Intervenability (RQ3): To evaluate the practical utility of our framework’s "human-in-the-loop" capabilities, we simulate expert interventions using a frontier proxy model (GPT-5.4) tasked with identifying and correcting erroneous reasoning steps. Both CausalCoT and Factored Decomposition support multi-level interventions, allowing the proxy to explicitly correct either an initial sub-question (planning) or a generated intermediate answer (execution). However, CausalCoT’s strict DAG topology provides the routing necessary to propagate these surgical edits to downstream dependent steps. On the other hand, CoT supports only the correction of intermediate steps. By measuring downstream predictive improvements across an intervention budget of k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } k\in\{1,2,3\} , we quantify how efficiently these edits correct the model’s reasoning. 5 Results 5.1 RQ1: Predictive Accuracy CausalCoT maintains competitive accuracy, absorbing an expected performance trade-off to enable strict causal isolation (Table 1 ). As shown in Table 1 , our framework generally preserves competitive overall accuracy with only a minor reduction of 1.05 to 6.38 percentage points (p.p.) in average accuracy on different datasets compared to the best-performing baselines. This slight degradation is a direct consequence of enforcing the DAG structure and removing dense attention pathways, which prevents the model from exploiting the spurious global correlations that typically inflate autoregressive accuracy

By decoupling the reasoning plan from its execution, users can actively interact with and steer the model’s logic at multiple stages: • Structural Auditing and Test-Time Interventions: Before reasoning begins, the generated DAG 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) is fully exposed for a priori inspection. Experts can rectify flawed logic, value misalignments, or missing steps by adding or removing sub-questions v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} , modifying context, or redefining edges ℰ \mathcal{E} . Inspired by concept interventions in interpretable architectures ( Koh et al., 2020 ; Dominici et al., 2024 ) , experts can also perform test-time surgical corrections on incorrect or hallucinated intermediate nodes; due to topological isolation, only downstream descendants require recomputation. Unlike standard autoregressive CoT, where dense attention causes localized edits to trigger unpredictable cascades that destabilize reasoning, CausalCoT enables predictable, efficient steering to improve final predictive performance. • Faithful Counterfactual Simulation: The forced Markovian property natively supports counterfactual simulations via explicit causal interventions (conceptually equivalent to Pearl’s d ​ o do -operator, e.g., d ​ o ​ ( v i = x ) do(v_{i}=x) ). Users can cleanly intervene on the value produced by a node (or on the information in the input), and dynamically propagate these changes through the graph (keeping it fixed). Since the environment is sealed against non-causal leakage and the ancestors of v v are dropped from every downstream context and cannot re-enter the resulting final answer, Y Y is a faithful reflection of the counterfactual intervention, under the same generated graph. 4 Experiments We design our experiments to evaluate the efficacy, faithfulness, and intervenability of CausalCoT compared to standard autoregressive reasoning. Specifically, we aim to answer the following research questions: • RQ1 (Performance): Does enforcing a strict causal graph degrade task accuracy compared to standard CoT? • RQ2 (Faithfulness): Are the intermediate steps genuine drivers of the generation? Specifically, if an intermediate reasoning step is modified, does the model structurally rely on it, and does the final prediction shift in a predictable direction? • RQ3 (Intervenability): Can CausalCoT reliably integrate test-time interventions to correct intermediate reasoning steps? All the remaining information about the experimental settings such as hyperparameters, dataset splits and additional information are defined in Appendix F , while the used prompts in Appendix I . 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate CausalCoT across performance, faithfulness, and intervenability using diverse benchmarks. We first use GPQA ( Rein et al., 2023 ) , a graduate-level science dataset, to ensure our model maintains competitive reasoning capabilities. Next, we incorporate MedQA ( Jin et al., 2020 ) to test multi-step clinical deduction in high-stakes domains. Finally, we leverage the Counterfactual Simulatability Suite (CF Suite) ( Mayne et al., 2026 ) across health, business, and ethics to quantify causal transparency and responsiveness to interventions. Combined, these benchmarks provide a robust foundation for assessing both task accuracy and model interpretability. Models and Baselines. We evaluate three families of models (Gemma 3, GPT-5.4, and Claude 4.5/4.6) across varying parameter scales. We compare CausalCoT against standard CoT prompting and Factored Decomposition ( Radhakrishnan et al., 2023 ) . Factored Decomposition isolates reasoning by breaking queries into sub-questions and evaluating them in restricted context windows. However, it suffers from two structural flaws: intermediate steps lack explicit parental routing, and the final prediction concatenates all generated text, reintroducing pervasive attention leakage. CausalCoT resolves these vulnerabilities by enforcing a DAG architecture, guaranteeing pure context isolation. Further details on baseline mechanics and comparison with CausalCoT are further explained in Appendix C . Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate our three research questions using the following metrics: • Predictive Performance (RQ1): We report standard Accuracy (Acc) to determine if CausalCoT’s strict DAG constraints degrade foundational problem-solving capabilities. We also report Pass@3 (the probability of generating at least one correct answer across three independent inferences). Because CausalCoT strictly enforces the generated topology, a malformed initial graph guarantees predictive failure. We therefore evaluate whether multi-sample generation mitigates zero-shot planning bottlenecks by providing multiple opportunities to produce a valid response. • Faithfulness and Predictability (RQ2): To quantify the causal influence of intermediate reasoning, we adapt established step-perturbation methodologies ( Lanham et al., 2023 ) . By injecting targeted errors using a frontier model (GPT-5.4) into intermediate nodes, we measure the frequency of downstream answer changes. To distinguish genuine causal adherence from arbitrary perturbation instability, we introduce a Predictable Change metric. This metric relies on an LLM judge that determines the logical downstream implication of each injected error, accounting for instances where a perturbation is insufficient to alter the final label. We then evaluate whether the model’s corrupted conclusion matches this counterfactual target, confirming that downstream predictions predictably adhere to the modified premise. • Test-Time Intervenability (RQ3): To evaluate the practical utility of our framework’s "human-in-the-loop" capabilities, we simulate expert interventions using a frontier proxy model (GPT-5.4) tasked with identifying and correcting erroneous reasoning steps. Both CausalCoT and Factored Decomposition support multi-level interventions, allowing the proxy to explicitly correct either an initial sub-question (planning) or a generated intermediate answer (execution). However, CausalCoT’s strict DAG topology provides the routing necessary to propagate these surgical edits to downstream dependent steps. On the other hand, CoT supports only the correction of intermediate steps. By measuring downstream predictive improvements across an intervention budget of k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } k\in\{1,2,3\} , we quantify how efficiently these edits correct the model’s reasoning. 5 Results 5.1 RQ1: Predictive Accuracy CausalCoT maintains competitive accuracy, absorbing an expected performance trade-off to enable strict causal isolation (Table 1 ). As shown in Table 1 , our framework generally preserves competitive overall accuracy with only a minor reduction of 1.05 to 6.38 percentage points (p.p.) in average accuracy on different datasets compared to the best-performing baselines. This slight degradation is a direct consequence of enforcing the DAG structure and removing dense attention pathways, which prevents the model from exploiting the spurious global correlations that typically inflate autoregressive accuracy

items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.31667 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning Authors: Mahdi Salmani , Adel Javanmard , Devansh Gupta , Meisam Razaviyayn View a PDF of the paper titled Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning, by Mahdi Salmani and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.
