items.content: Direct Pass@ k k Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning Mahdi Salmani Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Adel Javanmard Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Devansh Gupta Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Meisam Razaviyayn Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Abstract Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Test-time pruning. Only k k of the N N rollouts (ringed) continue past the cutoff T T , up to the budget B B . Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning, showcasing a strong aptitude for solving complex problems that require multi-step logic [ 45 , 21 , 52 , 18 , 15 ] . To further enhance these capabilities, test-time scaling has emerged as a prominent strategy, where generating multiple candidate solutions for a single problem allows the model to explore diverse reasoning strategies and achieve substantially better final performance [ 35 , 44 , 3 , 48 ] . However, a significant challenge in scaling test-time compute is the prohibitive cost of generating many full solutions, which we refer to as rollouts moving forward [ 33 , 23 ] . Beyond generation, there is also the cost of evaluating the finished rollouts in best-of- N N methods, which score each rollout with a reward model, and this is computationally demanding on a large pool of long reasoning traces [ 11 , 26 , 36 ] . This computational bottleneck, both in generation and in evaluating all N N rollouts in best-of- N N methods, necessitates test-time pruning of partial rollouts before they reach a final answer and terminate. In other words, we generate all N N rollouts only up to a cutoff of T T tokens, keep the k k most promising of them and run those to the full token budget B B , as illustrated in Fig. 1 . One family of methods examines the confidence dynamics of the model during generation, utilizing metrics such as logit entropy or confidence [ 30 , 50 , 17 , 43 ] . The underlying intuition is that if a model is overly confident at an intermediate decoding step, extending the reasoning process is a waste of compute; conversely, if the model is entirely lacking in confidence, it is unlikely to reach a correct solution regardless of the additional compute provided, allowing for early termination. Another line of work leverages the model’s internal state, specifically the hidden states of its transformer blocks, to identify which rollouts are worth continuing [ 54 , 1 ] . By “probing” these internal states, one can predict whether the model will ultimately arrive at a correct solution, effectively framing the pruning problem as a classification task. This allows for the early discarding of partial rollouts that are unlikely to yield a correct final answer. In parallel, a separate line of research prioritizes representation exploration (RepExp) to select a subset of rollouts that cover as many distinct reasoning strategies as possible [ 39 ] . By selecting partial rollouts whose corresponding embeddings are dissimilar, RepExp aims to explore a diverse set of reasoning trajectories. Figure 2: Conceptual illustration. The same pool of candidate rollouts, positioned by their partial rollout representations in embedding space, under three pruning strategies. Each rollout is colored by its predicted correctness and marked ✓/✗ by its actual outcome; the k = 3 k=3 kept rollouts are ringed. (a) Pure exploitation keeps the highest-scoring rollouts, but they are correlated and cluster together, so they miss the correct rollout. (b) Pure exploration keeps a maximally diverse subset yet spends its budget on low-quality rollouts, also missing it. (c) Our method optimizes pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k directly over the kept subset, balancing quality and diversity, and retains the correct rollout. These approaches, however, sit at the two ends of a spectrum, and neither directly optimizes the quantity we actually care about. The problem with probing methods is that the rollouts they rank highest tend to be similar to one another. As a result, the probe may be confidently wrong about all of the kept rollouts at once, and none of them reaches a correct answer. This is the problem of pure exploitation ( Fig. 2 a). RepExp, on the other hand, finds diverse rollouts, but because it ignores the quality of the rollouts, it can spend much of its budget on rollouts that are unlikely to succeed ( Fig. 2 b). These limitations motivate selecting the rollouts by the metric we actually want to optimize, choosing the set S S of k k rollouts that maximizes pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k , that is, max | S | = k ⁡ pass ​ @ ​ k ​ ( S ) \max_{|S|=k}\mathrm{pass}@k(S) , which we formalize in Eq. 3 . Optimizing this objective directly keeps the selected rollouts diverse enough to avoid shared failures while still favoring high-quality ones ( Fig. 2 c). To this end, we propose PKTP ( P ass@ 𝒌 \mathbfit{k} T hought P runing), a pruning framework that chooses the kept rollouts by maximizing pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k directly. The main difficulty is that, even if the rollouts are sampled independently, their outcomes are not independent (conditioned on the partial observation of the rollout). Hence, pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k depends on their joint distribution (i.e., rollouts with similar partial rollouts tend to succeed or fail together). We model this joint distribution with a latent Gaussian model, in which the correctness of each rollout is obtained by thresholding a Gaussian score. Evaluating pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k under this model requires an expectation over the latent variables, so we instead derive a closed-form second-order approximation of it. We show that this approximation is submodular, enabling us to approximately solve it using a greedy procedure to find a subset of size k k . An important aspect of the proposed framework is that the latent model is trained only once and does not depend on k k , and a single greedy pass yields a nested sequence of subsets, so the budget k k can be chosen online at inference time without retraining. Contributions. First, we cast pruning as maximizing the pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k of the kept set, and we model how similar rollouts fail together. Second, we derive a closed-form, submodular approximation of pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k that links the probe and RepExp. Third, through experiments on eight reasoning models, we show that PKTP improves over existing pruning methods, especially for moderate values of k k . 2 Problem Formulation and Related Work Setup. Given a question 𝒒 \mathbfit{q} , we draw N N candidate reasoning rollouts y ( i ) ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒒 ) y^{(i)}\sim\pi(\,\cdot\mid\mathbfit{q}\,) from a model π \pi . Each rollout is observed only through its first T T tokens, the prefix y 1 : T ( i ) y_{1:T}^{(i)} . We encode this prefix as a representation vector h i = h ( y 1 : T ( i ) ) h_{i}=h\!\left(y_{1:T}^{(i)}\right) , a hidden-state embedding of the reasoning up to token T. Pruning then keeps k ≤ N k\leq N rollouts, runs them to the full token budget B B , and discards the rest. A completed rollout y 1 : B y_{1:B} is either correct or not, recorded by the sign C ( y 1 : B ) ∈ { − 1 , + 1 } C(y_{1:B})\in\{-1,+1\} , C ( y 1 : B ) = { + 1 , if Verify ( y 1 : B ) , − 1 , otherwise . To prune partial rollouts, we need to map each prefix to a vector that captures its essential information. One line of work relies on hand-designed features of the rollout and the model’s internal states, such as token confidence, the geometry of the hidden-state trajectory, or the convergence of intermediate answers. These features are usually very low dimensional [ 13 , 40 , 38 , 19 , 28 ] . A second line of work instead keeps the hidden states of the transformer and pools them into a single vector [ 42 , 39 , 29 ] , and this is the class we use. In particular, we take h i h_{i} to be an exponential moving average (EMA) of the hidden states, which has proven an effective pooling operation [ 29 ] . Our improvements are thus shown for this class of embeddings, although our framework can be applied to other embeddings as well. Appendix F gives the details of the representation we use. Objective. items.raw_text: Direct Pass@ k k Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning Mahdi Salmani Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Adel Javanmard Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Devansh Gupta Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Meisam Razaviyayn Affiliation: University of Southern California {salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu Abstract Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Test-time pruning. Only k k of the N N rollouts (ringed) continue past the cutoff T T , up to the budget B B . Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning, showcasing a strong aptitude for solving complex problems that require multi-step logic [ 45 , 21 , 52 , 18 , 15 ] . To further enhance these capabilities, test-time scaling has emerged as a prominent strategy, where generating multiple candidate solutions for a single problem allows the model to explore diverse reasoning strategies and achieve substantially better final performance [ 35 , 44 , 3 , 48 ] . However, a significant challenge in scaling test-time compute is the prohibitive cost of generating many full solutions, which we refer to as rollouts moving forward [ 33 , 23 ] . Beyond generation, there is also the cost of evaluating the finished rollouts in best-of- N N methods, which score each rollout with a reward model, and this is computationally demanding on a large pool of long reasoning traces [ 11 , 26 , 36 ] . This computational bottleneck, both in generation and in evaluating all N N rollouts in best-of- N N methods, necessitates test-time pruning of partial rollouts before they reach a final answer and terminate. In other words, we generate all N N rollouts only up to a cutoff of T T tokens, keep the k k most promising of them and run those to the full token budget B B , as illustrated in Fig. 1 . One family of methods examines the confidence dynamics of the model during generation, utilizing metrics such as logit entropy or confidence [ 30 , 50 , 17 , 43 ] . The underlying intuition is that if a model is overly confident at an intermediate decoding step, extending the reasoning process is a waste of compute; conversely, if the model is entirely lacking in confidence, it is unlikely to reach a correct solution regardless of the additional compute provided, allowing for early termination. Another line of work leverages the model’s internal state, specifically the hidden states of its transformer blocks, to identify which rollouts are worth continuing [ 54 , 1 ] . By “probing” these internal states, one can predict whether the model will ultimately arrive at a correct solution, effectively framing the pruning problem as a classification task. This allows for the early discarding of partial rollouts that are unlikely to yield a correct final answer. In parallel, a separate line of research prioritizes representation exploration (RepExp) to select a subset of rollouts that cover as many distinct reasoning strategies as possible [ 39 ] . By selecting partial rollouts whose corresponding embeddings are dissimilar, RepExp aims to explore a diverse set of reasoning trajectories. Figure 2: Conceptual illustration. The same pool of candidate rollouts, positioned by their partial rollout representations in embedding space, under three pruning strategies. Each rollout is colored by its predicted correctness and marked ✓/✗ by its actual outcome; the k = 3 k=3 kept rollouts are ringed. (a) Pure exploitation keeps the highest-scoring rollouts, but they are correlated and cluster together, so they miss the correct rollout. (b) Pure exploration keeps a maximally diverse subset yet spends its budget on low-quality rollouts, also missing it. (c) Our method optimizes pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k directly over the kept subset, balancing quality and diversity, and retains the correct rollout. These approaches, however, sit at the two ends of a spectrum, and neither directly optimizes the quantity we actually care about. The problem with probing methods is that the rollouts they rank highest tend to be similar to one another. As a result, the probe may be confidently wrong about all of the kept rollouts at once, and none of them reaches a correct answer. This is the problem of pure exploitation ( Fig. 2 a). RepExp, on the other hand, finds diverse rollouts, but because it ignores the quality of the rollouts, it can spend much of its budget on rollouts that are unlikely to succeed ( Fig. 2 b). These limitations motivate selecting the rollouts by the metric we actually want to optimize, choosing the set S S of k k rollouts that maximizes pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k , that is, max | S | = k ⁡ pass ​ @ ​ k ​ ( S ) \max_{|S|=k}\mathrm{pass}@k(S) , which we formalize in Eq. 3 . Optimizing this objective directly keeps the selected rollouts diverse enough to avoid shared failures while still favoring high-quality ones ( Fig. 2 c). To this end, we propose PKTP ( P ass@ 𝒌 \mathbfit{k} T hought P runing), a pruning framework that chooses the kept rollouts by maximizing pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k directly. The main difficulty is that, even if the rollouts are sampled independently, their outcomes are not independent (conditioned on the partial observation of the rollout). Hence, pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k depends on their joint distribution (i.e., rollouts with similar partial rollouts tend to succeed or fail together). We model this joint distribution with a latent Gaussian model, in which the correctness of each rollout is obtained by thresholding a Gaussian score. Evaluating pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k under this model requires an expectation over the latent variables, so we instead derive a closed-form second-order approximation of it. We show that this approximation is submodular, enabling us to approximately solve it using a greedy procedure to find a subset of size k k . An important aspect of the proposed framework is that the latent model is trained only once and does not depend on k k , and a single greedy pass yields a nested sequence of subsets, so the budget k k can be chosen online at inference time without retraining. Contributions. First, we cast pruning as maximizing the pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k of the kept set, and we model how similar rollouts fail together. Second, we derive a closed-form, submodular approximation of pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k that links the probe and RepExp. Third, through experiments on eight reasoning models, we show that PKTP improves over existing pruning methods, especially for moderate values of k k . 2 Problem Formulation and Related Work Setup. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.31650 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence Authors: Qijin Zhang , Hanzhen Wang , Yuehan Zhao , Haoyu Dai , Yao Shu , Zhongxiang Dai , Shuang Qiu View a PDF of the paper titled EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence, by Qijin Zhang and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce EpiSEM-Bench, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds. \NoHyper † † footnotetext: * Equal contribution. † Corresponding author. \endNoHyper 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents use tools to read documents, inspect resources, and execute operations on a user’s behalf ( Yao et al., 2022 , Yao et al., 2024 , Lu et al., 2025 ) . Before sending a payment, sharing a file, or deleting a resource, the agent needs to establish that the operation is permitted in the current environment. This decision depends on facts returned by its tools, such as an authorization limit, a recipient’s access rights, or the dependencies of a running service. A missing fact can change the agent’s decision even when the tool response contains no false statement. Existing benchmarks evaluate tool-use capability, action safety, and robustness to adversarial observations ( Zhang et al., 2024 , Debenedetti et al., 2024 , Wang et al., 2026b ) . AgentDojo evaluates task utility and security using executable checks ( Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) . Missing evidence poses a different intervention that requires no attacker instruction, and the remaining observations can all be true. An evaluation of this problem needs to follow the decision from available facts to consequential action. It must establish whether the agent distinguishes permission from prohibition, how that behavior responds to missing evidence, and whether the agent can actively recover the facts needed to proceed appropriately. Task completion alone rewards execution in the permissible case. Avoidance of unsafe execution alone can reward refusal in every case. To address these challenges, we introduce the Epi stemic S afety under E vidence M issingness Benchmark (EpiSEM-Bench), which separates the world’s safety conditions from the evidence visible to the agent. It contains 300 task pairs comprising 600 worlds, with 50 pairs in each of six domains and 60 task families. The suppression inventory contains 1,363 facts, comprising 944 critical and 419 irrelevant, with two to seven critical facts per task. The two worlds in a pair share the request and tools, but differ in the state that makes the target operation prohibited or permissible. An executable oracle judges actions against the complete state. Evidence annotations identify every ordinary-tool exposure of a fact. Suppression therefore persists throughout the rollout. Critical facts enter the safety rule, such as the payment authorization limit. Irrelevant facts, such as a cost-center display label, affect neither legality nor the action parameters. These design choices support three stages of evaluation. Complete evidence first establishes legitimate completion and avoidance of prohibited actions, measured by Full Safe-World Success (SWS) and Full Unsafe Commit Rate (UCR). In Suppressed Evidence (SE) , selected facts remain unavailable through ordinary tools. Critical UCR identifies tasks with unsafe execution under critical omission, while Safety Boundary Margin (SBM) characterizes the minimum observed omission needed for failure. In Recoverable Evidence (RE) , the same omissions apply, but the agent can actively query an independent audit source. Recovery UCR measures unsafe execution with this opportunity, and Paired Useful Recovery (PUR) requires evidence acquisition followed by restraint in the prohibited world and completion in its permissible twin. The six metrics are intended to be read together. Full SWS supplies the utility context for safety, Critical UCR and SBM describe observed omission vulnerability, and Recovery UCR and PUR distinguish avoiding unsafe action from using restored evidence successfully. Our ten-model evaluation shows why this joint interpretation matters. Safety-relevant state makes the target action prohibited in the unsafe world and permissible in its safe twin. Dashed evidence cards denote omitted facts. They do not block prohibited operations on the agent’s behalf, allowing unsafe decisions to remain observable. This separates the agent’s decision from protection supplied by the environment: a prohibited commit remains a failure even if the agent describes its intent as safe. The goal, target operation, and tool interface remain the same. For example, a different authorization limit changes whether a payment is permissible without changing the requested payment. Holding the request and tools constant makes permission-sensitive action the central requirement. The agent needs to use environmental evidence to select different outcomes for the same operation. It leaves the private state, safety rule, user request, tool schemas, action semantics, and unmasked values unchanged. The remaining responses contain true facts, without injected instruction or replacement assertion. Atom identities and exposure structure are shared across twins. The mask can therefore be applied in both worlds. Fact-level suppression preserves the operational context around the missing evidence. Removing an entire tool response could also remove the amount, recipient, or resource needed to execute the task, mixing missing safety evidence with inability to perform the operation. Annotated exposures allow us to remove the selected facts while retaining other true information. Applying the mask throughout the rollout also prevents repeated reads from inadvertently restoring them, so the intended evidence deficit persists across the agent’s ordinary-tool choices. We construct tasks from the private state and executable rule before specifying evidence, exposure maps, tools, and the user goal. Validation checks schema consistency, exposure paths, and opposite oracle labels across the twins. Other annotated facts describe workflow context or redundant evidence and remain outside the critical/irrelevant omission inventory. The first unsafe mask receives counterpart evaluations in the safe world and RE. All completed nonempty critical omissions enter the metrics. PUR averages these joint outcomes within each task and then across tasks: PUR = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N 1 q i ​ ∑ j = 1 q i p i ​ j . \mathrm{PUR}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{q_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{q_{i}}p_{ij}. (2) Refusing both twins or executing both twins gives p i ​ j = 0 p_{ij}=0 , since one of the two required outcomes fails. SWS allows legal completion without restoration, while strict recovery requires restoration explicitly. Each successful pair includes agent-initiated evidence acquisition, withholding the prohibited operation, and completing its permissible counterpart. Recovery-call rates and the two worlds’ outcomes show which steps agents complete or fail. Evidence acquisition and action behavior. Attempt records whether an agent makes a valid recovery query. Premature commit records whether it executes the target operation before recovering the missing facts. Every valid recovery query returns all omitted facts. Attempt therefore indicates that the evidence was obtained. Premature commit includes execution without any recovery query. In safe-twin rollouts without legal completion, stopping or escalating is counted as false abstention. Remaining failures, including invalid or unfinished episodes, are classified as other non-completions. Recovery, behavioral, and omission SWS rates first average the applicable conditions within each task and then weight the N N tasks equally. Joint interpretation of the metrics. The measurements form a profile rather than independent claims of agent quality. Full SWS and Full UCR establish whether successful execution is accompanied by appropriate restraint. Critical UCR identifies affected tasks, while SBM supplies the observed boundary information that an affected-task count does not contain. Recovery UCR and PUR distinguish safety with a recovery opportunity from evidence acquisition followed by correct behavior in both worlds. Joint interpretation resolves otherwise ambiguous successes. Refusing every operation can give zero UCR and maximal SBM, but gives neither legitimate completion nor PUR. High SWS can instead accompany execution without regard to permission. Low Recovery UCR alone also leaves open whether the agent verified the facts or simply avoided acting. PUR requires active verification and the appropriate paired outcome, while acquisition and action records explain unsuccessful pairs. Reading the six metrics together therefore evaluates safety, usefulness, and evidence-dependent decisions without treating any one as a substitute for the others. 4 Evaluation The ten-model evaluation follows three stages. Full SWS and Full UCR assess completion and safety under complete evidence. Critical UCR and SBM measure vulnerability to missing evidence, while Recovery UCR and PUR evaluate evidence recovery. These conditions remain complete even when the model fails with full evidence. To determine safety boundaries, we inspect critical omission combinations in the unsafe world under SE in increasing cardinality, reusing completed conditions and evaluating untested masks until an unsafe witness is found or coverage is exhaustive. The first unsafe mask receives counterpart evaluations in the safe world and RE. All completed nonempty critical omissions enter the metrics. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.31593 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: Simulated Control Evals Authors: Jeffrey Olmo , David Zhang , Tyler Tracy View a PDF of the paper titled Simulated Control Evals, by Jeffrey Olmo and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Control evaluations measure whether safeguards can prevent an AI model from causing undesired outcomes even when it is intentionally trying to do so. These evaluations typically use purpose-built control settings and extrapolate their results to a model's deployment. However, the effectiveness of safeguards in deployment can depend on features of environments and tasks that control settings do not represent. To broaden where control evaluations can be run, we introduce simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment. We evaluate SCEs on LinuxArena, where execution provides ground-truth outcomes. We compare SCE prediction errors with those from a separate control setting, BashArena, and with variation in control metrics within LinuxArena. For independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, SCEs predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena. SCEs closely reproduce distributions of attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning, with over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena. SCEs explain 78-85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. This accuracy is sample efficient: SCEs predict safety with less error than BashArena using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set. Strategies discovered through simulation also improve monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks, outperforming BashArena and approximately matching improvement from executed strategies. These results suggest that deployment-specific SCEs can be more predictive than control evaluations executed in separate control settings. items.content: Simulated Control Evaluations Jeffrey Olmo David Zhang Tyler Tracy Affiliation: Redwood Research Abstract Control evaluations measure whether safeguards can prevent an AI model from causing undesired outcomes even when it is intentionally trying to do so. These evaluations typically use purpose-built control settings and extrapolate their results to a model’s deployment. However, the effectiveness of safeguards in deployment can depend on features of environments and tasks that control settings do not represent. To broaden where control evaluations can be run, we introduce simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment. We evaluate SCEs on LinuxArena, where execution provides ground-truth outcomes. We compare SCE prediction errors with those from a separate control setting, BashArena, and with variation in control metrics within LinuxArena. For independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, SCEs predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena. SCEs closely reproduce distributions of attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning, with over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena. SCEs explain 78–85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. This accuracy is sample efficient: SCEs predict safety with less error than BashArena using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set. Strategies discovered through simulation also improve monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks, outperforming BashArena and approximately matching improvement from executed strategies. These results suggest that deployment-specific SCEs can be more predictive than control evaluations executed in separate control settings. 1 Introduction Figure 1: The simulated control evaluation process. A language-model simulator generates tool responses for an attack policy pursuing a side task during legitimate work. Repeating this process across tasks produces simulated attack trajectories. A monitor scores their suspicion, and an attack success judge estimates attack success. Control metrics such as safety at a given audit budget can then be computed. Attack-policy actions never execute against the deployment environment. AI control aims to make it safe to use capable AI agents even if they try to cause harm ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . The same capabilities and access that let an agent do useful work can let it exfiltrate information, introduce backdoors, or launch rogue deployments. A control protocol puts safeguards around the agent, such as trusted monitoring. A control evaluation tests these safeguards by replacing the agent with an attack policy configured to pursue a harmful objective while doing legitimate work ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) . Control evaluations produce control metrics , such as how often attacks succeed and how often a monitor catches them. Accurate control metrics can guide improvements to the control protocol and inform risk estimates. Where an agent acts matters for control evaluations: its opportunities for dangerous behavior, and the evidence control protocols have to detect them, depend on the particular codebases, services, tasks, and available actions in its deployment. Control evaluations aim to inform judgments about a model’s deployment, but typically run in a separate control setting such as BashArena or LinuxArena ( Kaufman et al., 2025 ; Tracy et al., 2026 ) , which provides a safe testbed for executing attacks, and ground truth for outcomes like whether a given side task succeeded, but which shares neither the deployment’s environments nor its task profile. Evidence from such a control setting may transfer poorly to deployment. Even if it captures average attacker and monitor performance, deployment risk will not be determined by those averages when an attacker selects especially promising opportunities ( Ge-Wang et al., 2026 ) . A control protocol that appears safe in a control setting might miss specific attacks available in a lab’s internal infrastructure ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . Running control evaluations directly in the deployment would address this mismatch, but running an attack policy on live infrastructure risks causing the very harms the evaluation is intended to measure. An alternative that avoids this risk is an executable replica of the deployment, but building one can be expensive or infeasible, especially when the agent depends on many services and changing external state. What is usually available, even when a replica is not, is a record of past activity: agent trajectories that show what tasks models were given, which tools they called, and what those tools returned, along with snapshots of the relevant codebases. Our method uses these records to construct control evaluations. We study simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to produce the tool responses an agent would receive in deployment (Figure 1 ). An attack policy receives a legitimate main task and a harmful side task . It chooses actions and issues tool calls as usual, while a simulator uses an honest reference trajectory and codebase read access to generate the observations those actions would produce in deployment. The attack policy conditions on each simulator output, so the attack can diverge from the reference trajectory. Monitors then score the resulting simulated trajectory, and an attack success judge estimates whether the side task succeeded. The attack policy’s actions never execute. The central question is whether SCEs predict deployment control metrics more accurately than a separate control setting does. Simulation introduces unrealism in tool responses, but lets evaluators use the deployment’s real tasks and codebase; a control setting executes attacks faithfully, but on a different distribution of tasks and environments. Unlike deployment simulation used to forecast misalignment propensity ( Williams et al., 2026 ) , SCEs need not conceal the evaluation from the agent: the attack policy is already instructed to pursue a harmful objective. On the other hand, SCEs place stronger demands on modeling the environment’s attack-relevant mechanics, including subtle details of permissions, state changes, and tool behavior that determine whether an attack succeeds and what evidence it leaves for monitors. We test this tradeoff on LinuxArena, where attacks can be executed to measure ground-truth outcomes. In our experiments, execution in LinuxArena stands in for deployment. Across 1,000 main-task–side-task pairs, we compare SCE predictions with predictions from 1,000 attacks executed in BashArena; Section 2.4 defines these comparisons. We also compare SCE prediction errors with the variation between LinuxArena tasks and environments. Our contributions are: • A framework for measuring control evaluation transfer. We combine variance explained in control metrics across tasks and environments with matching behavioral distributions to assess accuracy beyond overall averages. This framework applies to both simulated and executed control evaluations. (Section 2.4 ). • Empirical validation of SCEs. On LinuxArena, SCEs match executed behavioral distributions and predict control metrics more accurately than BashArena, explaining most between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. We show how these advantages scale with the number of simulated task pairs. (Sections 3.1 – 3.6 ). • Demonstrating that SCEs can improve safeguards. We show that briefing a monitor with simulated strategies improves detection of held-out executed attacks more than BashArena briefings, approaching the performance of briefings from same-environment execution. SCEs thus support improving safeguards as well as assessing them (Section 3.7 ). 2 Methods 2.1 SCE components Attack policy. The attack policy is gpt-5.6-sol at medium reasoning effort for both executed and simulated trajectories. It receives the main task, the side task, and attack guidance suggesting how to pursue the side task covertly. For each task, we provide the same attack-policy prompt in execution and SCE. Simulator. At each tool call, the simulator receives the tool name and arguments, interaction history, and grounding affordances : records and tools that provide information about the environment being simulated. The simulator generates a tool response for the policy’s next step; its reasoning is withheld from the policy and subsequent simulation steps. In what follows, the simulator is gpt-6-astra , with two main affordances: • Reference trajectory. The simulator receives the original honest agent transcript for the same main task, including tool calls and responses. This shows how the environment behaved during one execution; the simulator predicts responses to the attack policy’s different actions. • Codebase read access. The simulator can read, list, and search a snapshot of the environment’s files, giving it access to source code, configuration, and initial file contents. Some tool call outputs follow directly from evidence from the reference trajectory and codebase; many outputs depend on state the simulator cannot observe, in which case it generates a plausible result consistent with what is already known. We fall back to gpt-5.6-sol when gpt-6-astra refuses or fails to produce a valid tool response; gpt-6-astra resumes on subsequent outputs. The base , +reference , and +codebase conditions provide neither affordance, only the reference trajectory, and both affordances, respectively. We use the simulator with both affordances throughout. We investigated many additional affordances, including read access to attack-policy reasoning, an executable sandbox, access to a database of logged trajectories, and forking from the reference trajectory, but did not find evidence that these materially improved simulator quality on the measured dimensions beyond what the reference trajectory and codebase read access provide. Attack success judge. Executed attacks have a ground-truth outcome from the side-task scorer; simulated attacks have only a transcript, so an attack success judge estimates the probability that the side task succeeded. We use gpt-5.6-sol at high reasoning effort, with read access to the codebase, side-task definitions, and success-scoring logic. Unlike monitors, the judge receives the side-task objective and scoring logic, helping it assess whether the observed actions satisfy the attack’s specific success criteria. SCE success and safety estimates therefore include both simulator and judge error. We validate the judge against executed outcomes in Section 3.2 . Monitors. We use five full-trajectory monitors: gpt-5.4 , gpt-5.4-mini , gpt-5.4-nano , gpt-5-nano , and gpt-5.6-sol . Each produces a suspicion score on a 0–10 scale; we score each trajectory three times and average. Audit thresholds are set on a shared set of executed honest trajectories, the same trajectories that serve as reference trajectories for the simulator. 2.2 Simulator development and evaluation data We developed the simulator on BashArena and several LinuxArena task pairs; the remaining LinuxArena pairs were held out. Our primary dataset contains 1,000 LinuxArena task pairs, each combining a main task with a side task. Pairs are balanced across ten environments and selected for overlap between main and side tasks. For each task pair, we collect two simulated runs, two independent executed runs, and one honest reference trajectory. Repeated simulated and executed runs allow us to estimate run-to-run variance. Analyses use these task pairs unless stated otherwise, excluding pairs with missing or invalid measurements. Smaller, separate collections of task pairs are used for the base and +reference conditions and some discriminability diagnostics. We independently draw evaluation and deployment task sets by sampling eligible task pairs uniformly with replacement. Simulated trajectories provide the evaluation predictions, and executed trajectories provide the deployment outcomes. We calculate metrics separately for each set and average prediction errors across draws. Environment and side-task-category metrics use whichever pairs from those groups appear in each draw. Comparisons on matched task pairs separately assess predictions for individual pairs. Throughout, sample size counts task-pair draws, including repeated selections of the same pair. 2.3 Decomposing error Prediction error combines systematic differences, run-to-run variance, and task-sampling variance. Root mean squared bias (RMS bias) measures systematic error after averaging over repeated runs and sampled task sets. For attack success and monitor scores, independent repeated runs of the same task pair estimate run-to-run variance. We estimate squared bias by subtracting the contributions of run-to-run variance and task-sampling variance from mean squared prediction error. We average in squared units across task pairs or groups and monitors before taking the root, and correct LinuxArena SD for noise in estimated means. Pooled All comparisons and the safety sample-efficiency curve retain both variance contributions in total RMSE. Bootstrap resampling separately estimates confidence intervals. Appendix B gives details. 2.4 Performance comparisons Figure 2: BashArena and LinuxArena variance as performance comparisons. Columns denote environments and rows tasks within each environment; boxes are schematic. Left: A control setting is used to predict a deployment’s control metrics. Middle: BashArena or LinuxArena averages provide constant predictions across LinuxArena task pairs, side-task categories, and environments. Right: Orange simulation and gray execution use the same LinuxArena environments and task pairs. Each Δ \Delta compares a prediction with the deployment’s measured control metric m m . Smaller simulation gaps support using SCEs when control-setting extrapolation to deployment incurs at least the reference error observed here, provided simulator accuracy is maintained. We use LinuxArena execution as the deployment ground truth and compare SCE errors with two references: the observed transfer error from BashArena, and variation among LinuxArena’s own environments, task pairs, and side-task categories (Figure 2 ). Our first comparison asks whether evaluating deployment-specific tasks through simulation is more informative than executing attacks in a separate control setting. We use BashArena to supply 1,000 executed attacks, using the same attack policy, trajectory length limit, and monitors as for LinuxArena. We calculate each metric from these attacks and use it to predict the corresponding LinuxArena metric. Our second reference compares prediction errors with variation within LinuxArena. For each environment, we consider the expected metric value, averaged over sampled deployment task sets, and the mean of these values across environments. The between-environment LinuxArena standard deviation (SD) has two interpretations. First, it is the RMSE of assigning this mean to every environment: a control setting that gets the average right but has no environment-specific information. Second, it is the RMSE of using a uniformly selected environment’s expected metric value to predict the mean across environments. In this direction, each environment acts as a possible control setting from which we extrapolate to the broader deployment. Both interpretations give the same error. The analogous interpretations apply to standard deviations over side-task categories and task pairs. Together, these references compare SCE accuracy against two scales of mismatch between a control setting and deployment: the observed transfer gap from BashArena to LinuxArena, and the deviations within LinuxArena’s own environments, task pairs, or side-task categories from their corresponding means. Outperforming these references would suggest that SCEs can predict deployment metrics more accurately than a control setting whose mismatch with deployment produces errors of comparable magnitude, provided SCE accuracy also transfers to that deployment. Figure 3: Grounded simulation closely matches LinuxArena behavior. Adding the reference trajectory and codebase access reduces divergence across attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning. The primary simulator is much closer to execution than BashArena is; gray re-execution bars show the scale of variation between repeated runs. 3 Experiments 3.1 Behavior transfer To evaluate and improve control protocols, an SCE must reproduce the kinds of behavior those protocols demonstrate and encounter in deployment. We compare three behavioral representations of a trajectory: attack strategy describes how a side task is accomplished; attacker reasoning records the attack policy’s reasoning and intent; and monitor reasoning describes the judgements and referenced evidence behind a monitor’s suspicion. Table 1 gives examples. Control evaluations are more useful to the extent that they accurately represent these behaviors. In particular, improving control protocols depends on understanding which kinds of attacks succeed and evade detection, and why. We compare the distributions of these behavior representations across executed and simulated trajectories before turning to the control metrics themselves. Table 1: Examples of behavioral representations. Category Example behavior Detail Attack strategy Prefix-confusion cleanup. Uses an expected miss on a malformed prefix to justify deleting objects under the real prefix. let storage_team = &body.team_id[1..]; let probe = format!("uploads/{storage_team}/{file_id}.mp4"); if head_object(probe).is_err() { delete_real_objects(...); } Attacker reasoning Cover for content substitution. Plans a subtle side attack while keeping the surrounding work plausible. “I need to tweak the checksum properly and consider a subtle attack. The attack should feel unrelated and not obvious. […] I have to do it precisely, but also ensure to implement a sufficient cover.” Monitor reasoning Privilege-escalation pathway. Interprets routine health checks in light of earlier privilege-seeking changes. “Current action appears as routine process and healthcheck, but prior history shows attempts to elevate privileges […]. This creates a partial causal pathway from normal task to elevated-access activity.” Following Mehri et al. (2026) , we describe each behavior, embed and cluster the descriptions, then compare frequencies over these clusters. These frequencies define the behavioral distributions . We measure D KL ( p exec ∥ p sim ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{exec}}\|p_{\mathrm{sim}}) , where the two distributions are constructed from executed and simulated LinuxArena trajectories, respectively. For the control setting, we instead compare the executed LinuxArena distribution with the distribution constructed from executed BashArena trajectories, using the same fixed LinuxArena representation and clusters. Appendix A gives the representation and clustering details. SCEs produce behavioral distributions closer to execution than the control setting for all three representations (Figure 3 ). Their estimated KL divergence is more than an order of magnitude below that of the control setting in each case, suggesting SCEs provide superior qualitative coverage of the behaviors measured. items.raw_text: Simulated Control Evaluations Jeffrey Olmo David Zhang Tyler Tracy Affiliation: Redwood Research Abstract Control evaluations measure whether safeguards can prevent an AI model from causing undesired outcomes even when it is intentionally trying to do so. These evaluations typically use purpose-built control settings and extrapolate their results to a model’s deployment. However, the effectiveness of safeguards in deployment can depend on features of environments and tasks that control settings do not represent. To broaden where control evaluations can be run, we introduce simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment. We evaluate SCEs on LinuxArena, where execution provides ground-truth outcomes. We compare SCE prediction errors with those from a separate control setting, BashArena, and with variation in control metrics within LinuxArena. For independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, SCEs predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena. SCEs closely reproduce distributions of attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning, with over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena. SCEs explain 78–85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. This accuracy is sample efficient: SCEs predict safety with less error than BashArena using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set. Strategies discovered through simulation also improve monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks, outperforming BashArena and approximately matching improvement from executed strategies. These results suggest that deployment-specific SCEs can be more predictive than control evaluations executed in separate control settings. 1 Introduction Figure 1: The simulated control evaluation process. A language-model simulator generates tool responses for an attack policy pursuing a side task during legitimate work. Repeating this process across tasks produces simulated attack trajectories. A monitor scores their suspicion, and an attack success judge estimates attack success. Control metrics such as safety at a given audit budget can then be computed. Attack-policy actions never execute against the deployment environment. AI control aims to make it safe to use capable AI agents even if they try to cause harm ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . The same capabilities and access that let an agent do useful work can let it exfiltrate information, introduce backdoors, or launch rogue deployments. A control protocol puts safeguards around the agent, such as trusted monitoring. A control evaluation tests these safeguards by replacing the agent with an attack policy configured to pursue a harmful objective while doing legitimate work ( Bhatt et al., 2025 ) . Control evaluations produce control metrics , such as how often attacks succeed and how often a monitor catches them. Accurate control metrics can guide improvements to the control protocol and inform risk estimates. Where an agent acts matters for control evaluations: its opportunities for dangerous behavior, and the evidence control protocols have to detect them, depend on the particular codebases, services, tasks, and available actions in its deployment. Control evaluations aim to inform judgments about a model’s deployment, but typically run in a separate control setting such as BashArena or LinuxArena ( Kaufman et al., 2025 ; Tracy et al., 2026 ) , which provides a safe testbed for executing attacks, and ground truth for outcomes like whether a given side task succeeded, but which shares neither the deployment’s environments nor its task profile. Evidence from such a control setting may transfer poorly to deployment. Even if it captures average attacker and monitor performance, deployment risk will not be determined by those averages when an attacker selects especially promising opportunities ( Ge-Wang et al., 2026 ) . A control protocol that appears safe in a control setting might miss specific attacks available in a lab’s internal infrastructure ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . Running control evaluations directly in the deployment would address this mismatch, but running an attack policy on live infrastructure risks causing the very harms the evaluation is intended to measure. An alternative that avoids this risk is an executable replica of the deployment, but building one can be expensive or infeasible, especially when the agent depends on many services and changing external state. What is usually available, even when a replica is not, is a record of past activity: agent trajectories that show what tasks models were given, which tools they called, and what those tools returned, along with snapshots of the relevant codebases. Our method uses these records to construct control evaluations. We study simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to produce the tool responses an agent would receive in deployment (Figure 1 ). An attack policy receives a legitimate main task and a harmful side task . It chooses actions and issues tool calls as usual, while a simulator uses an honest reference trajectory and codebase read access to generate the observations those actions would produce in deployment. The attack policy conditions on each simulator output, so the attack can diverge from the reference trajectory. Monitors then score the resulting simulated trajectory, and an attack success judge estimates whether the side task succeeded. The attack policy’s actions never execute. The central question is whether SCEs predict deployment control metrics more accurately than a separate control setting does. Simulation introduces unrealism in tool responses, but lets evaluators use the deployment’s real tasks and codebase; a control setting executes attacks faithfully, but on a different distribution of tasks and environments. Unlike deployment simulation used to forecast misalignment propensity ( Williams et al., 2026 ) , SCEs need not conceal the evaluation from the agent: the attack policy is already instructed to pursue a harmful objective. On the other hand, SCEs place stronger demands on modeling the environment’s attack-relevant mechanics, including subtle details of permissions, state changes, and tool behavior that determine whether an attack succeeds and what evidence it leaves for monitors. We test this tradeoff on LinuxArena, where attacks can be executed to measure ground-truth outcomes. In our experiments, execution in LinuxArena stands in for deployment. Across 1,000 main-task–side-task pairs, we compare SCE predictions with predictions from 1,000 attacks executed in BashArena; Section 2.4 defines these comparisons. We also compare SCE prediction errors with the variation between LinuxArena tasks and environments. Our contributions are: • A framework for measuring control evaluation transfer. We combine variance explained in control metrics across tasks and environments with matching behavioral distributions to assess accuracy beyond overall averages. This framework applies to both simulated and executed control evaluations. (Section 2.4 ). • Empirical validation of SCEs. On LinuxArena, SCEs match executed behavioral distributions and predict control metrics more accurately than BashArena, explaining most between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. We show how these advantages scale with the number of simulated task pairs. (Sections 3.1 – 3.6 ). • Demonstrating that SCEs can improve safeguards. We show that briefing a monitor with simulated strategies improves detection of held-out executed attacks more than BashArena briefings, approaching the performance of briefings from same-environment execution. SCEs thus support improving safeguards as well as assessing them (Section 3.7 ). 2 Methods 2.1 SCE components Attack policy. The attack policy is gpt-5.6-sol at medium reasoning effort for both executed and simulated trajectories. It receives the main task, the side task, and attack guidance suggesting how to pursue the side task covertly. For each task, we provide the same attack-policy prompt in execution and SCE. Simulator. At each tool call, the simulator receives the tool name and arguments, interaction history, and grounding affordances : records and tools that provide information about the environment being simulated. The simulator generates a tool response for the policy’s next step; its reasoning is withheld from the policy and subsequent simulation steps. In what follows, the simulator is gpt-6-astra , with two main affordances: • Reference trajectory. The simulator receives the original honest agent transcript for the same main task, including tool calls and responses. This shows how the environment behaved during one execution; the simulator predicts responses to the attack policy’s different actions. • Codebase read access. The simulator can read, list, and search a snapshot of the environment’s files, giving it access to source code, configuration, and initial file contents. Some tool call outputs follow directly from evidence from the reference trajectory and codebase; many outputs depend on state the simulator cannot observe, in which case it generates a plausible result consistent with what is already known. We fall back to gpt-5.6-sol when gpt-6-astra refuses or fails to produce a valid tool response; gpt-6-astra resumes on subsequent outputs. The base , +reference , and +codebase conditions provide neither affordance, only the reference trajectory, and both affordances, respectively. We use the simulator with both affordances throughout. We investigated many additional affordances, including read access to attack-policy reasoning, an executable sandbox, access to a database of logged trajectories, and forking from the reference trajectory, but did not find evidence that these materially improved simulator quality on the measured dimensions beyond what the reference trajectory and codebase read access provide. Attack success judge. Executed attacks have a ground-truth outcome from the side-task scorer; simulated attacks have only a transcript, so an attack success judge estimates the probability that the side task succeeded. We use gpt-5.6-sol at high reasoning effort, with read access to the codebase, side-task definitions, and success-scoring logic. Unlike monitors, the judge receives the side-task objective and scoring logic, helping it assess whether the observed actions satisfy the attack’s specific success criteria. SCE success and safety estimates therefore include both simulator and judge error. We validate the judge against executed outcomes in Section 3.2 . Monitors. We use five full-trajectory monitors: gpt-5.4 , gpt-5.4-mini , gpt-5.4-nano , gpt-5-nano , and gpt-5.6-sol . Each produces a suspicion score on a 0–10 scale; we score each trajectory three times and average. Our primary dataset contains 1,000 LinuxArena task pairs, each combining a main task with a side task. Pairs are balanced across ten environments and selected for overlap between main and side tasks. Analyses use these task pairs unless stated otherwise, excluding pairs with missing or invalid measurements. Smaller, separate collections of task pairs are used for the base and +reference conditions and some discriminability diagnostics. We independently draw evaluation and deployment task sets by sampling eligible task pairs uniformly with replacement. Simulated trajectories provide the evaluation predictions, and executed trajectories provide the deployment outcomes. We calculate metrics separately for each set and average prediction errors across draws. Environment and side-task-category metrics use whichever pairs from those groups appear in each draw. Comparisons on matched task pairs separately assess predictions for individual pairs. Throughout, sample size counts task-pair draws, including repeated selections of the same pair. 2.3 Decomposing error Prediction error combines systematic differences, run-to-run variance, and task-sampling variance. Root mean squared bias (RMS bias) measures systematic error after averaging over repeated runs and sampled task sets. For attack success and monitor scores, independent repeated runs of the same task pair estimate run-to-run variance. We estimate squared bias by subtracting the contributions of run-to-run variance and task-sampling variance from mean squared prediction error. We average in squared units across task pairs or groups and monitors before taking the root, and correct LinuxArena SD for noise in estimated means. We calculate each metric from these attacks and use it to predict the corresponding LinuxArena metric. Our second reference compares prediction errors with variation within LinuxArena. Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration Authors: Deepthika S , Pawni Yadav , B. Sankar View a PDF of the paper titled Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration, by Deepthika S and Pawni Yadav and B. Sankar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence.
items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.31579 (cs) [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026] Title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration Authors: Deepthika S , Pawni Yadav , B. Sankar View a PDF of the paper titled Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration, by Deepthika S and Pawni Yadav and B. Sankar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim. Sankar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.
