Keywords: trust calibration , sycophancy , large language models , human–AI interaction , misinformation , automation bias , metacognition , design for trust 1 Introduction For a species as social as ours, survival has never depended on the individual alone. In evolutionary biology, fitness describes an organism’s capacity to survive and reproduce in its environment; for humans, that capacity has been shaped by life in groups, where cooperation, communication and resource sharing are routine. The cognitive demands of such relationships are reflected in the unusually large primate neocortex, which has been linked to the need to track relationships within social groups ( Dunbar, 1992 ) . Food sharing illustrates the point. In many hunter-gatherer societies a successful hunt feeds more than the hunter: large, unpredictably acquired food packages tend to be widely distributed, partly because the cost of not sharing outweighs the benefit of eating alone ( Hawkes et al., 2018 ) . With repeated interaction, sharing and reciprocity become patterned, particularly where camp membership is stable ( Smith et al., 2016 ) . Cooperation among kin is explained by inclusive fitness ( Hamilton, 1964 ) , whereas cooperation among non-kin rests partly on the expectation that partners will reciprocate ( Rand and Nowak, 2013 ) . Repeated cooperation therefore produces more than an exchange of resources. It produces expectations about how others will behave, and those expectations are a basis for trust. As societies grew more complex, so did the relationships through which such expectations form. Human social networks are layered, from an intimate core of family and close friends to acquaintances at the margins, and the layers differ in contact frequency, emotional closeness, reciprocity and trust ( Dunbar, 2025 ) . Nor is trust static within a relationship. It starts from some baseline and moves as experience accumulates: perceptions of predictability grow from observing the consistency of a partner’s behaviour ( Camanto and Campbell, 2025 ) , and trust strengthens when positive expectations are confirmed and weakens when they are violated ( Lewicki et al., 2006 ) . Trust is less a fixed property of a relationship than a running account of expectation and outcome, and the degree to which A trusts B need not equal the degree to which B trusts A. Is a relationship even necessary? Not always. A patient trusts a doctor they have never met, and a passenger trusts a pilot they will never see. Non-experts routinely rely on expert knowledge they cannot verify, such as a physician’s diagnosis ( Leefmann and Lesle, 2020 ) . Such trust rests on competence, professional standards, reputation and institutions rather than on familiarity: “swift trust” forms among strangers through recognisable roles, and trust in a stockbroker is bounded by regulation rather than by acquaintance ( Lewicki et al., 2006 ) . A relationship is one basis for trust, not a prerequisite for it. Yet the trust we extend to strangers is usually cautious. We hesitate before trusting someone we have never met, not because they are untrustworthy but because we lack information about them: their history, their intentions, the relationship between us. Seen this way, an AI assistant is an extreme case. It has no personal history, no body, no reputation built through shared experience and no intentions we can read, and it is not even a stranger in the usual sense, because a stranger is at least another person. If people are wary of trusting a human being they do not know, why would they trust something that is not human at all? One answer is that such trust does not need a relationship, because it can rest instead on the kind of reliability we attribute to machines. We expect a calculator to return 4 for 2 + 2 2+2 , an ATM to dispense the right amount and a lift to stop at the chosen floor. Trust in such systems tracks the reliability of their performance and the extent to which that performance meets expectations ( McKenna et al., 2024 ) ; consistent performance reinforces trust and failures undermine it ( Parasuraman and Riley, 1997 ; de Visser et al., 2018 ) . Crucially, expectation and outcome can be compared. The function is defined, the output is verifiable, and reliability is observable across repeated use. Where expectation and outcome overlap, reliability is established; reliability confirmed over repeated trials becomes confidence; and confidence becomes trust (Figure 1 , top). Conversational AI breaks this arrangement (Figure 1 , bottom). Large language models have moved human–computer interaction from specialised, task-bound automation towards systems that act as advisers ( Henrique and Santos, 2024 ; Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . People ask them “What should I do?”, “Which option is better?” and “Can you explain this to me?”, questions without a single predetermined answer against which a response can be checked. An AI system can also be wrong while sounding coherent and certain. With a calculator, the user checks whether a function was performed correctly; with AI, the user must judge whether the information itself is accurate enough to rely on, often on a topic they are trying to learn precisely because they do not know it. Reliance on such systems is already known to be unstable: people sometimes discount good computerised advice ( Promberger and Baron, 2006 ) and, in other conditions, follow AI advice against contrary evidence and their own judgement ( Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . And if trust is built through repeated experiences of something meeting our expectations, a system that is trained to meet expectations—to sound right, to agree, to please—can meet them while being wrong. Figure 1: The calculator fallacy. Top: trust in a deterministic tool is earned through verification, because the user can compare output with expectation and accumulate evidence of reliability. Bottom: with conversational AI, the learner cannot verify, fluency and confidence stand in for reliability, and “checking” routes back to the same source, closing a loop in which trust cannot calibrate. This creates an under-studied failure mode at the intersection of two literatures. Research on trust in automation asks whether people’s trust tracks a system’s reliability ( Lee and See, 2004 ; Hoff and Bashir, 2015 ) . Research on sycophancy asks whether LLMs tailor their answers to what users want rather than to what is true ( Perez et al., 2023 ; Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Both typically treat one side of the human–AI pair as fixed. Sycophancy research, in particular, measures whether the model adapts to the user : whether it abandons a correct answer under pushback, mirrors a stated opinion or flatters the user’s self-image ( Fanous et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . The reverse direction has received far less attention: when the model holds its ground confidently and consistently, does the user adapt to the model? We call this human-side deference : the convergence of a person’s beliefs on a source’s claims irrespective of their truth. It is the mirror image of model sycophancy, and it matters because modern assistants are, by design, fluent, assertive and unhedged ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . We report HARICHAN (Human–AI Reliance in CHAt iNteractions), a controlled experiment in which the same LLM taught five science topics while covertly falsifying between none and all of its briefing facts, always with full confidence. We address five research questions: RQ1. How much planted misinformation do learners absorb as falsification rises, and does their acceptance of each stated falsehood change with the source’s overall reliability? RQ2. Does learners’ confidence distinguish what they learned correctly from what they absorbed falsely? RQ3. Does their reported trust track the assistant’s actual reliability? RQ4. How do learners check an assistant they have reason to doubt, and what happens when they push back? RQ5. Is the deference sycophancy on the model’s side or on the human’s, and how does human-side deference relate to confidence? Our contributions are fourfold. Empirically , we measure misinformation uptake across a graded range of assistant reliability in open-ended conversational learning, and we separate exposure to a falsehood from acceptance of it by coding every transcript for which facts the assistant actually stated. Methodologically , we adapt baseline-corrected sycophancy metrics from model evaluation to the human side, introducing a Human Deference Index and pairing it with metacognitive measures of confidence. Conceptually , we argue that the “calculator fallacy”—extending to a fluent, probabilistic system the trust that deterministic tools earn through verification—explains why trust cannot calibrate when error is invisible, and that trustworthiness is a property of the human–AI pair. For design , we derive strategies that make reliability legible per claim, route verification outward and evaluate trust behaviourally. 2 Related work 2.1 Trust, reliance and calibration Trust in automation is commonly defined as the attitude that an agent will help achieve one’s goals in a situation characterised by uncertainty and vulnerability ( Lee and See, 2004 ) , and in interpersonal terms as a willingness to be vulnerable that rests on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity ( Mayer et al., 1995 ) . The design goal is not more trust but calibrated trust: trust that matches a system’s actual capability ( Lee and See, 2004 ; Wischnewski et al., 2023 ) , or, in the terms of Jacovi et al. (2021) , warranted rather than unwarranted trust. Lee and See (2004) also describe resolution , the degree to which changes in capability are mirrored by changes in trust, and specificity , the degree to which trust attaches to particular functions rather than to the system as a whole. Reviews of trust measurement emphasise that trust is latent and multifaceted, that most scales are bespoke, and that behavioural measures should accompany self-report ( Gebru et al., 2022 ; Wischnewski et al., 2023 ) . Trust and distrust also appear to be distinct factors rather than two ends of one scale ( Scharowski et al., 2025 ) , and healthy distrust may require both explicit error detection and an intuitive sense of when to doubt ( Peters et al., 2026 ) . Hoff and Bashir (2015) separate dispositional, situational and learned trust and note that learned trust updates dynamically with reliability, but only when people can compare the system’s performance with their own. Experiments bear this out. Stated and observed accuracy both shape trust, but observed accuracy dominates once users can see it ( Yin et al., 2019 ) ; trust can drift away from reliability when no feedback is available ( Rittenberg et al., 2024 ) ; and displaying an AI’s case-level confidence helps calibrate trust where explanations do not ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Computational models describe trust as moving towards recent experience, cumulative trust and a prior expectation bias; without outcome feedback, the experience term cannot register failure ( Hu et al., 2019 ) . For virtual and embedded AI, high initial trust typically drops after errors are experienced ( Glikson and Woolley, 2020 ) , and trust has affective as well as cognitive roots ( Gillath et al., 2021 ; Choung et al., 2023 ) . The recurring condition across this literature is visibility: trust calibrates to what users can observe. 2.2 Overreliance and automation bias with conversational AI When verification is costly, people lean on automated aids. Automation bias, the use of automated output as a substitute for vigilant information seeking, produces commission errors even when contradictory cues are available ( Skitka et al., 1999 ; Goddard et al., 2012 ) , and it shares an attentional mechanism with complacency that affects experts and novices alike ( Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ) . Labelling advice as algorithmic increases its weight regardless of its quality ( Logg et al., 2019 ) , and AI-labelled advice can override both contextual evidence and people’s own assessments, at real cost ( Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . Appropriate reliance requires both relying on correct advice and overriding incorrect advice ( Schemmer et al., 2023 ) ; explanations can reduce overreliance when they lower the cost of verification ( Vasconcelos et al., 2023 ) but can also inflate reliance when they merely justify ( Dzindolet et al., 2003 ) . Sundar (2020) attributes part of this to a “machine heuristic”, the lay belief that machines are objective and accurate, which invites users to outsource vigilance. Large language models intensify the problem because they are fluent by default and rarely express uncertainty; users rely on their confident outputs whether or not those outputs are correct ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and overreliance on overconfident models appears across languages ( Rathi et al., 2025 ) . Users overestimate the accuracy of model answers from default explanations, and longer explanations raise confidence without improving discrimination ( Steyvers et al., 2025 ) . Model-generated explanations speed up fact-checking but mislead when the model is convincingly wrong ( Si et al., 2024 ) ; users overlooked the errors in ChatGPT answers to programming questions 39% of the time even though 52% of those answers were incorrect ( Kabir et al., 2024 ) ; and LLM-based search is fast but invites overreliance when the model errs ( Spatharioti et al., 2025 ) . First-person hedging reduces overreliance only in part ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , sources and visible inconsistencies help more than explanations ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , and combining visual and verbal uncertainty cues can sharpen subjective discrimination while worsening behavioural reliance ( Ojewale et al., 2026 ) . In conversational settings, dialogue cues increase trust even when an assistant spreads health misinformation, and only acted-upon, independent verification lowers it ( Liao and Sundar, 2026 ) . AI assistance can also make people perform better while making them worse at judging their own performance ( Fernandes et al., 2026 ) , and human confidence in themselves, rather than in the AI, often governs whether advice is adopted ( Chong et al., 2022 ) . Most of this work, however, studies single decisions with a fixed error rate. Less is known about learning from a conversational source whose reliability varies, where the learner has no independent knowledge and the only readily available check is the source itself. 2.3 Misinformation, fluency and epistemic vigilance Research on misinformation explains why confidently stated falsehoods persist. Once encoded, misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after it is retracted, and corrections work best when they supply an alternative account ( Lewandowsky et al., 2012 ) . Repetition increases perceived truth ( Hasher et al., 1977 ) , and prior knowledge offers surprisingly little protection against this illusory-truth effect ( Fazio et al., 2015 ) . Belief in misinformation is driven less by a lack of intelligence than by ordinary cognitive shortcuts, including reliance on fluency and familiarity ( Ecker et al., 2022 ) . People do possess mechanisms of epistemic vigilance that monitor the competence and benevolence of sources and the coherence of what they say ( Sperber et al., 2010 ) , and much human knowledge legitimately rests on trusting testimony we cannot check ( Hardwig, 1991 ) . These mechanisms evolved for human informants, however, and fluent machine text offers few of the signals they rely on; people form stronger and less revisable beliefs from sources that sound confident and knowledgeable ( Kidd and Birhane, 2023 ) . Access to external information can also inflate people’s sense of what they themselves know ( Fisher et al., 2015 ; Sparrow et al., 2011 ) , and offloading cognition to tools depends on metacognitive judgements that can be miscalibrated ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ) . Measuring such metacognition requires separating sensitivity (does confidence discriminate right from wrong?) from bias (is confidence too high overall?) ( Fleming and Lau, 2014 ) . 2.4 Sycophancy: the model adapts to the user Sycophancy refers to the tendency of language models to tailor responses to what users appear to want rather than to what is true. It was first documented as models repeating back users’ stated views, increasingly so at larger scales ( Perez et al., 2023 ) , and has been traced to human preference data that reward agreement and convincingly written responses over correct ones ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Models agree with users on subjective questions and follow plausible hints even on factual ones ( Ranaldi and Pucci, 2023 ) . A family of benchmarks now quantifies the behaviour. SycEval classifies answer changes under rebuttal as progressive (incorrect to correct) or regressive (correct to incorrect) and finds sycophancy in 58% of cases, with citation-based rebuttals producing the most regressive flips ( Fanous et al., 2025 ) . SYCON Bench measures how many turns a model holds its stance under sustained pressure and how often it flips ( Hong et al., 2025 ) . Adversarial scientific QA dialogues show that resistance to misleading cues depends more on alignment and reasoning than on scale ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . ELEPHANT broadens the construct to social sycophancy, the excessive preservation of the user’s face through validation, indirectness and acceptance of the user’s framing, and subtracts a human baseline to score it ( Cheng et al., 2026b ) . A psychometric Social Sycophancy Scale distinguishes uncritical agreement, obsequiousness and excitement as perceived by readers ( Rehani et al., 2026 ) . An expert survey shows that researchers share concern about sycophancy but not its boundaries ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Reinforcement learning from human feedback can also make models better at convincing human evaluators that wrong answers are right, raising evaluators’ false-positive rates ( Wen et al., 2025 ) , and training models to be warm can increase sycophancy and reduce accuracy ( Ibrahim et al., 2026 ) . The persuasive power of LLMs in conversation is itself well documented ( Salvi et al., 2025 ) . 2.5 Human consequences of sycophancy A smaller body of work traces what sycophancy does to people. In a between-subjects study, a custom GPT that never contradicted users lowered demonstrated trust, and the decline in self-reported trust was significant mainly when participants could verify answers ( Carro, 2024 ) . Sycophantic chatbots increase attitude extremity and certainty while being perceived as unbiased, an effect driven by one-sided facts rather than by validation ( Rathje et al., 2025 ) . Sycophancy decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence while users continue to prefer and trust sycophantic models ( Cheng et al., 2026a ) . Flattery combined with agreement lowers perceived authenticity, whereas agreement delivered in a neutral tone raises trust ( Sun and Wang, 2026 ) . Sycophantic assistants leave novices’ misconceptions uncorrected in problem-solving tasks without the novices noticing ( Bo et al., 2026 ) . Table 1 places our study relative to this work. Almost all of it asks whether the model adapts to the user, and measures the model. We hold the model’s behaviour fixed—confident, non-flattering and unyielding to pushback—and measure whether the user adapts to the model. Table 1: Where this study sits. Most sycophancy research varies or measures the model’s adaptation to the user; we hold a confident, non-adaptive model fixed and measure the human’s adaptation to it. Work Who adapts Participants What is measured Perez et al. (2023) ; Sharma et al. (2024) Model → \rightarrow user None / crowd raters Agreement with stated user views; preference for sycophantic answers Fanous et al. (2025) ; Hong et al. (2025) Model → \rightarrow user None Answer flips under rebuttal (progressive/regressive; turn-of-flip) Cheng et al. (2026b) ; Rehani et al. (2026) Model → \rightarrow user None / raters Social sycophancy (validation, framing, obsequiousness) Rathje et al. (2025) ; Cheng et al. (2026a) Model → \rightarrow user Large online samples Downstream attitudes, certainty, prosociality, dependence Carro (2024) ; Sun and Wang (2026) ; Bo et al. (2026) Model → \rightarrow user Online / lab Trust and performance under a sycophantic assistant Wen et al. (2025) Model → \rightarrow evaluator Expert evaluators False-positive rate when judging RLHF outputs This study User → \rightarrow model Learners, within-subjects Uptake of planted falsehoods from a confident, fixed model across five reliability levels; confidence, trust, checking, deference 2.6 Designing for calibrated trust Design research treats trustworthiness as something communicated through cues. The MATCH model distinguishes a system’s actual trustworthiness from the cues that signal it and warns that some prominent cues, such as the chatbot medium and a polished design look, are irrelevant to trustworthiness yet shape it ( Liao and Sundar, 2022 ) . Proposed remedies include cognitive forcing functions that make users commit before seeing AI output ( Buçinca et al., 2021 ) , adaptive cues delivered when over-trust is detected ( Okamura and Yamada, 2020 ) , seamful designs that expose a system’s limits rather than hide them ( Ehsan et al., 2024 ) , deliberate micro-frictions that interrupt automatic behaviour ( Cox et al., 2016 ) , and verification affordances that users act on

Such trust rests on competence, professional standards, reputation and institutions rather than on familiarity: “swift trust” forms among strangers through recognisable roles, and trust in a stockbroker is bounded by regulation rather than by acquaintance ( Lewicki et al., 2006 ) . A relationship is one basis for trust, not a prerequisite for it. Yet the trust we extend to strangers is usually cautious. We hesitate before trusting someone we have never met, not because they are untrustworthy but because we lack information about them: their history, their intentions, the relationship between us. Seen this way, an AI assistant is an extreme case. It has no personal history, no body, no reputation built through shared experience and no intentions we can read, and it is not even a stranger in the usual sense, because a stranger is at least another person. If people are wary of trusting a human being they do not know, why would they trust something that is not human at all? One answer is that such trust does not need a relationship, because it can rest instead on the kind of reliability we attribute to machines. We expect a calculator to return 4 for 2 + 2 2+2 , an ATM to dispense the right amount and a lift to stop at the chosen floor. Trust in such systems tracks the reliability of their performance and the extent to which that performance meets expectations ( McKenna et al., 2024 ) ; consistent performance reinforces trust and failures undermine it ( Parasuraman and Riley, 1997 ; de Visser et al., 2018 ) . Crucially, expectation and outcome can be compared. The function is defined, the output is verifiable, and reliability is observable across repeated use. Where expectation and outcome overlap, reliability is established; reliability confirmed over repeated trials becomes confidence; and confidence becomes trust (Figure 1 , top). Conversational AI breaks this arrangement (Figure 1 , bottom). Large language models have moved human–computer interaction from specialised, task-bound automation towards systems that act as advisers ( Henrique and Santos, 2024 ; Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . People ask them “What should I do?”, “Which option is better?” and “Can you explain this to me?”, questions without a single predetermined answer against which a response can be checked. An AI system can also be wrong while sounding coherent and certain. With a calculator, the user checks whether a function was performed correctly; with AI, the user must judge whether the information itself is accurate enough to rely on, often on a topic they are trying to learn precisely because they do not know it. Reliance on such systems is already known to be unstable: people sometimes discount good computerised advice ( Promberger and Baron, 2006 ) and, in other conditions, follow AI advice against contrary evidence and their own judgement ( Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . And if trust is built through repeated experiences of something meeting our expectations, a system that is trained to meet expectations—to sound right, to agree, to please—can meet them while being wrong. Figure 1: The calculator fallacy. Top: trust in a deterministic tool is earned through verification, because the user can compare output with expectation and accumulate evidence of reliability. Bottom: with conversational AI, the learner cannot verify, fluency and confidence stand in for reliability, and “checking” routes back to the same source, closing a loop in which trust cannot calibrate. This creates an under-studied failure mode at the intersection of two literatures. Research on trust in automation asks whether people’s trust tracks a system’s reliability ( Lee and See, 2004 ; Hoff and Bashir, 2015 ) . Research on sycophancy asks whether LLMs tailor their answers to what users want rather than to what is true ( Perez et al., 2023 ; Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Both typically treat one side of the human–AI pair as fixed. Sycophancy research, in particular, measures whether the model adapts to the user : whether it abandons a correct answer under pushback, mirrors a stated opinion or flatters the user’s self-image ( Fanous et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . The reverse direction has received far less attention: when the model holds its ground confidently and consistently, does the user adapt to the model? We call this human-side deference : the convergence of a person’s beliefs on a source’s claims irrespective of their truth. It is the mirror image of model sycophancy, and it matters because modern assistants are, by design, fluent, assertive and unhedged ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . We report HARICHAN (Human–AI Reliance in CHAt iNteractions), a controlled experiment in which the same LLM taught five science topics while covertly falsifying between none and all of its briefing facts, always with full confidence. We address five research questions: RQ1. How much planted misinformation do learners absorb as falsification rises, and does their acceptance of each stated falsehood change with the source’s overall reliability? RQ2. Does learners’ confidence distinguish what they learned correctly from what they absorbed falsely? RQ3. Does their reported trust track the assistant’s actual reliability? RQ4. How do learners check an assistant they have reason to doubt, and what happens when they push back? RQ5. Is the deference sycophancy on the model’s side or on the human’s, and how does human-side deference relate to confidence? Our contributions are fourfold. Empirically , we measure misinformation uptake across a graded range of assistant reliability in open-ended conversational learning, and we separate exposure to a falsehood from acceptance of it by coding every transcript for which facts the assistant actually stated. Methodologically , we adapt baseline-corrected sycophancy metrics from model evaluation to the human side, introducing a Human Deference Index and pairing it with metacognitive measures of confidence. Conceptually , we argue that the “calculator fallacy”—extending to a fluent, probabilistic system the trust that deterministic tools earn through verification—explains why trust cannot calibrate when error is invisible, and that trustworthiness is a property of the human–AI pair. For design , we derive strategies that make reliability legible per claim, route verification outward and evaluate trust behaviourally. 2 Related work 2.1 Trust, reliance and calibration Trust in automation is commonly defined as the attitude that an agent will help achieve one’s goals in a situation characterised by uncertainty and vulnerability ( Lee and See, 2004 ) , and in interpersonal terms as a willingness to be vulnerable that rests on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity ( Mayer et al., 1995 ) . The design goal is not more trust but calibrated trust: trust that matches a system’s actual capability ( Lee and See, 2004 ; Wischnewski et al., 2023 ) , or, in the terms of Jacovi et al. (2021) , warranted rather than unwarranted trust. Lee and See (2004) also describe resolution , the degree to which changes in capability are mirrored by changes in trust, and specificity , the degree to which trust attaches to particular functions rather than to the system as a whole. Reviews of trust measurement emphasise that trust is latent and multifaceted, that most scales are bespoke, and that behavioural measures should accompany self-report ( Gebru et al., 2022 ; Wischnewski et al., 2023 ) . Trust and distrust also appear to be distinct factors rather than two ends of one scale ( Scharowski et al., 2025 ) , and healthy distrust may require both explicit error detection and an intuitive sense of when to doubt ( Peters et al., 2026 ) . Hoff and Bashir (2015) separate dispositional, situational and learned trust and note that learned trust updates dynamically with reliability, but only when people can compare the system’s performance with their own. Experiments bear this out. Stated and observed accuracy both shape trust, but observed accuracy dominates once users can see it ( Yin et al., 2019 ) ; trust can drift away from reliability when no feedback is available ( Rittenberg et al., 2024 ) ; and displaying an AI’s case-level confidence helps calibrate trust where explanations do not ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Computational models describe trust as moving towards recent experience, cumulative trust and a prior expectation bias; without outcome feedback, the experience term cannot register failure ( Hu et al., 2019 ) . For virtual and embedded AI, high initial trust typically drops after errors are experienced ( Glikson and Woolley, 2020 ) , and trust has affective as well as cognitive roots ( Gillath et al., 2021 ; Choung et al., 2023 ) . The recurring condition across this literature is visibility: trust calibrates to what users can observe. 2.2 Overreliance and automation bias with conversational AI When verification is costly, people lean on automated aids. Automation bias, the use of automated output as a substitute for vigilant information seeking, produces commission errors even when contradictory cues are available ( Skitka et al., 1999 ; Goddard et al., 2012 ) , and it shares an attentional mechanism with complacency that affects experts and novices alike ( Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ) . Labelling advice as algorithmic increases its weight regardless of its quality ( Logg et al., 2019 ) , and AI-labelled advice can override both contextual evidence and people’s own assessments, at real cost ( Klingbeil et al., 2024 ) . Appropriate reliance requires both relying on correct advice and overriding incorrect advice ( Schemmer et al., 2023 ) ; explanations can reduce overreliance when they lower the cost of verification ( Vasconcelos et al., 2023 ) but can also inflate reliance when they merely justify ( Dzindolet et al., 2003 ) . Sundar (2020) attributes part of this to a “machine heuristic”, the lay belief that machines are objective and accurate, which invites users to outsource vigilance. Large language models intensify the problem because they are fluent by default and rarely express uncertainty; users rely on their confident outputs whether or not those outputs are correct ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and overreliance on overconfident models appears across languages ( Rathi et al., 2025 ) . Users overestimate the accuracy of model answers from default explanations, and longer explanations raise confidence without improving discrimination ( Steyvers et al., 2025 ) . Model-generated explanations speed up fact-checking but mislead when the model is convincingly wrong ( Si et al., 2024 ) ; users overlooked the errors in ChatGPT answers to programming questions 39% of the time even though 52% of those answers were incorrect ( Kabir et al., 2024 ) ; and LLM-based search is fast but invites overreliance when the model errs ( Spatharioti et al., 2025 ) . First-person hedging reduces overreliance only in part ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , sources and visible inconsistencies help more than explanations ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , and combining visual and verbal uncertainty cues can sharpen subjective discrimination while worsening behavioural reliance ( Ojewale et al., 2026 ) . In conversational settings, dialogue cues increase trust even when an assistant spreads health misinformation, and only acted-upon, independent verification lowers it ( Liao and Sundar, 2026 ) . AI assistance can also make people perform better while making them worse at judging their own performance ( Fernandes et al., 2026 ) , and human confidence in themselves, rather than in the AI, often governs whether advice is adopted ( Chong et al., 2022 ) . Most of this work, however, studies single decisions with a fixed error rate. Less is known about learning from a conversational source whose reliability varies, where the learner has no independent knowledge and the only readily available check is the source itself. 2.3 Misinformation, fluency and epistemic vigilance Research on misinformation explains why confidently stated falsehoods persist. Once encoded, misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after it is retracted, and corrections work best when they supply an alternative account ( Lewandowsky et al., 2012 ) . Repetition increases perceived truth ( Hasher et al., 1977 ) , and prior knowledge offers surprisingly little protection against this illusory-truth effect ( Fazio et al., 2015 ) . Belief in misinformation is driven less by a lack of intelligence than by ordinary cognitive shortcuts, including reliance on fluency and familiarity ( Ecker et al., 2022 ) . People do possess mechanisms of epistemic vigilance that monitor the competence and benevolence of sources and the coherence of what they say ( Sperber et al., 2010 ) , and much human knowledge legitimately rests on trusting testimony we cannot check ( Hardwig, 1991 ) . These mechanisms evolved for human informants, however, and fluent machine text offers few of the signals they rely on; people form stronger and less revisable beliefs from sources that sound confident and knowledgeable ( Kidd and Birhane, 2023 ) . Access to external information can also inflate people’s sense of what they themselves know ( Fisher et al., 2015 ; Sparrow et al., 2011 ) , and offloading cognition to tools depends on metacognitive judgements that can be miscalibrated ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ) . Measuring such metacognition requires separating sensitivity (does confidence discriminate right from wrong?) from bias (is confidence too high overall?) ( Fleming and Lau, 2014 ) . 2.4 Sycophancy: the model adapts to the user Sycophancy refers to the tendency of language models to tailor responses to what users appear to want rather than to what is true. It was first documented as models repeating back users’ stated views, increasingly so at larger scales ( Perez et al., 2023 ) , and has been traced to human preference data that reward agreement and convincingly written responses over correct ones ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Models agree with users on subjective questions and follow plausible hints even on factual ones ( Ranaldi and Pucci, 2023 ) . A family of benchmarks now quantifies the behaviour. SycEval classifies answer changes under rebuttal as progressive (incorrect to correct) or regressive (correct to incorrect) and finds sycophancy in 58% of cases, with citation-based rebuttals producing the most regressive flips ( Fanous et al., 2025 ) . SYCON Bench measures how many turns a model holds its stance under sustained pressure and how often it flips ( Hong et al., 2025 ) . Adversarial scientific QA dialogues show that resistance to misleading cues depends more on alignment and reasoning than on scale ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . ELEPHANT broadens the construct to social sycophancy, the excessive preservation of the user’s face through validation, indirectness and acceptance of the user’s framing, and subtracts a human baseline to score it ( Cheng et al., 2026b ) . A psychometric Social Sycophancy Scale distinguishes uncritical agreement, obsequiousness and excitement as perceived by readers ( Rehani et al., 2026 ) . An expert survey shows that researchers share concern about sycophancy but not its boundaries ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Reinforcement learning from human feedback can also make models better at convincing human evaluators that wrong answers are right, raising evaluators’ false-positive rates ( Wen et al., 2025 ) , and training models to be warm can increase sycophancy and reduce accuracy ( Ibrahim et al., 2026 ) . The persuasive power of LLMs in conversation is itself well documented ( Salvi et al., 2025 ) . 2.5 Human consequences of sycophancy A smaller body of work traces what sycophancy does to people. In a between-subjects study, a custom GPT that never contradicted users lowered demonstrated trust, and the decline in self-reported trust was significant mainly when participants could verify answers ( Carro, 2024 ) . Sycophantic chatbots increase attitude extremity and certainty while being perceived as unbiased, an effect driven by one-sided facts rather than by validation ( Rathje et al., 2025 ) . Sycophancy decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence while users continue to prefer and trust sycophantic models ( Cheng et al., 2026a ) . Flattery combined with agreement lowers perceived authenticity, whereas agreement delivered in a neutral tone raises trust ( Sun and Wang, 2026 ) . Sycophantic assistants leave novices’ misconceptions uncorrected in problem-solving tasks without the novices noticing ( Bo et al., 2026 ) . Table 1 places our study relative to this work. Almost all of it asks whether the model adapts to the user, and measures the model. We hold the model’s behaviour fixed—confident, non-flattering and unyielding to pushback—and measure whether the user adapts to the model. Table 1: Where this study sits. Most sycophancy research varies or measures the model’s adaptation to the user; we hold a confident, non-adaptive model fixed and measure the human’s adaptation to it. The MATCH model distinguishes a system’s actual trustworthiness from the cues that signal it and warns that some prominent cues, such as the chatbot medium and a polished design look, are irrelevant to trustworthiness yet shape it ( Liao and Sundar, 2022 ) . Proposed remedies include cognitive forcing functions that make users commit before seeing AI output ( Buçinca et al., 2021 ) , adaptive cues delivered when over-trust is detected ( Okamura and Yamada, 2020 ) , seamful designs that expose a system’s limits rather than hide them ( Ehsan et al., 2024 ) , deliberate micro-frictions that interrupt automatic behaviour ( Cox et al., 2016 ) , and verification affordances that users act on

The architecture aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and defines coordinated requirements across compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling, and mechanical design. Factory integration moves complex assembly and testing into a controlled environment while site teams prepare foundations, power, and external connectivity in parallel. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens. NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform , and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support. A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation. This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD . NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. NVIDIA DSX POD adds a standardized path for large-scale deployments where schedule predictability, repeatability, and reduced onsite work are priorities. Architecture aligned with NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform NVIDIA DSX is the broad design framework for co-designed AI infrastructure. It brings compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, facility controls, and software together at the data center level. Customers and partners can implement that framework in different physical forms. NVIDIA DSX POD is a specific realization of that broader design: a standardized AI factory architecture composed of factory-built container types and defined interfaces between them. The architecture is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and its rack-scale systems. The reference design describes a complete AI factory rather than a compute enclosure in isolation. It accounts for compute, service and management functions, scale-out networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, and other supporting infrastructure. Technical requirements for factory-integrated deployment The central purpose of the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is to make the full deployment process repeatable. That requires coordinated requirements across the following areas: compute integration, networking and storage, cabling and controls, power delivery, liquid cooling, and mechanical design and transportation. Compute integration The NVIDIA DSX POD compute container is designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack scale infrastructure. The design defines how compute and supporting racks fit within the enclosure and how partners address structural support, weight distribution, equipment restraint, service clearances, airflow and liquid-cooling access, rack-level power, and network connectivity. Factory integration also changes the validation boundary. Instead of treating each rack as an independent shipment that will be assembled into a cluster onsite, partners validate the installed compute environment as a deployment unit. The validation plan can cover rack inventory, firmware and configuration baselines, power-on checks, fabric connectivity, sensor operation, cooling integrity, and system-level functional tests before the container leaves the factory. Networking and storage AI workloads depend on predictable movement of model data, training data, checkpoint data, and inference context across the AI factory. The reference design therefore treats networking and storage as part of the system architecture rather than as site-specific additions made after compute arrives. The design defines the connectivity required within a compute container, between containers, and from the modular system to the customer’s external network. It accounts for scale-out fabrics, service and management networks, fiber entry points, trunk cabling, cable routing, labeling, bend radius, service access, and validation of factory-installed link before shipment. Storage requirements follow the same principle. The architecture defines the required capacity, performance, connectivity, management, and service characteristics while allowing the final equipment implementation to reflect the deployment scale and partner solution. This enables storage and networking to arrive as coordinated parts of the AI factory instead of independent systems that must be reconciled late in site integration. Cabling and controls NVIDIA DSX POD reduces the onsite work of cabling in a rack-scale deployment, moving rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring, and sensor integration into the factory wherever practical. The reference design clearly defines cable paths, separation requirements, termination points, labeling conventions, test procedures, and serviceability requirements to help partners easily install and test these connections under controlled conditions to reduce the number of field terminations required after delivery. Power delivery DSX POD makes power delivery seamless with a standard input 800 VDC power design that begins with the electrical input to the core containers and continues through protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls, and telemetry. The reference design defines the power characteristics and interfaces required by the installed AI infrastructure. Partners then engineer the upstream generation, conversion, and regional electrical solution for the customer site. This separation is important because utility conditions, codes, equipment availability, and grid architectures differ across regions. A common interface at the container boundary enables repeatable core designs while preserving flexibility in how ecosystem partners deliver power to each deployment. NVIDIA software can complement the physical design by helping operators manage workloads within available power limits. Policy-driven power control, workload orchestration, and high-fidelity telemetry can help an AI factory convert a fixed power envelope into more productive computing. Liquid cooling Vera Rubin rack-scale systems require coordinated liquid-cooling infrastructure. Within the container, the design covers the plumbing that connects racks to the container cooling interface, including routing, manifolds, isolation, instrumentation, leak detection, pressure integrity, and service access. Partners can assemble, flush, pressure-test, and validate the internal cooling loop at the factory. At the site, they connect the container to prepared water and heat-rejection infrastructure, commission the complete loop, and verify performance under operating conditions. NVIDIA DSX POD changes where integration occurs. It does not eliminate the supporting facility infrastructure. Mechanical design and transportation Shipping high-value rack-scale systems already installed in an enclosure requires a design that treats logistics as an engineering requirement. The container structure, equipment restraints, weight distribution, center of gravity, lifting and handling points, access paths, and transport conditions must work together. The reference design also connects transportation requirements to factory quality gates. Partners inspect the integrated unit before shipment, document its configuration and test status, secure it for transport, and repeat defined checks after arrival. This process helps establish that the system delivered to the site matches the system validated at the factory. Parallelizing factory integration and site preparation The factory-built model changes the deployment sequence. Site teams can prepare land, foundations, power, and external connectivity while partners manufacture and integrate the containers in parallel. At the factory, partners install the rack-scale systems, complete internal cabling and plumbing, integrate controls, load approved configuration baselines, and run functional tests. At the deployment site, construction teams prepare the physical and utility interfaces that the containers require. After delivery, the work focuses on placement, inter-container connections, and hookup to external power, cooling, and networking. Teams then confirm transport integrity, validate the site connections, and complete system commissioning. This model does not remove onsite work. It reduces the amount of complex, repeatable integration performed in the field and moves it into an environment designed for consistent tooling, quality controls, and parallel production. Scaling with standardized deployment units A standardized container architecture gives operators a repeatable unit for planning and expansion. After preparing the supporting site infrastructure, an operator can add compute and supporting capacity using the same defined interfaces and validation process. Standardization also creates a consistent foundation for software optimization. When the underlying compute, network, power, cooling, and telemetry architecture is known software and operational practices for that environment can be tuned easily. Partners can still adapt each implementation to local codes, site conditions, customer requirements, and regional supply chains. This balance is central to NVIDIA DSX POD. The reference design supplies reusable NVIDIA engineering and validation. The ecosystem supplies manufacturing capacity, site expertise, regional engineering, customization, deployment, service, and support. A partner-led delivery model NVIDIA provides the validated AI infrastructure design foundation and works with the ecosystem to prove that rack-scale systems can be integrated, tested, transported, and deployed as repeatable factory-built units. OEMs and ODMs integrate the computing systems. Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and infrastructure specialists adapt power and cooling to the site. Modular solution providers manufacture the enclosures and integrate the subsystems. Site partners prepare the location, complete installation, and support commissioning. Together, these partners turn the reference design into a customer-specific AI factory. The model expands the modular data center market rather than replacing existing offerings. Partners can continue to deliver different levels of integration, from modular infrastructure that customers populate onsite to fully factory-integrated deployments. NVIDIA DSX POD gives the ecosystem a validated path for the latter while preserving room for differentiation in implementation and service. Learn more about NVIDIA DSX POD The value of an AI factory begins when the infrastructure starts producing tokens. By moving repeatable integration and validation into the factory, NVIDIA DSX POD is designed to reduce schedule exposure late in the build, simplify onsite work, and make deployment more predictable. The reference design brings NVIDIA Vera Rubin compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, controls, and validation into one coordinated architecture. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the engineering foundation. Partners build, customize, deliver, and support the resulting solutions. Learn more about how the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design can help turn available land, power, and prepared site infrastructure into productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. items.content: Developer Tools & Techniques How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage Oct 22, 2026 By Andrew Hoyle Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA KvikIO provides high-level Python and C++ interfaces that sit above the cuFile C API to enable accelerated file I/O into GPU memory. The library and cuFile make independent path-selection decisions: KvikIO chooses whether to invoke cuFile, while cuFile determines whether the transfer uses the accelerated nvidia-fs kernel module or a CPU-staged compatibility path. Runtime settings such as KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD control KvikIO's behavior, and cufile.json settings such as execution.parallel_io and execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb shape how cuFile decomposes and schedules requests. Per-process cuFile statistics collected with CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and inspected via gds_stats reveal whether operations traveled the nvidia-fs accelerated path (nvfs counters) or the compatibility path (posix counters). KvikIO is part of the NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries for data science and has been used to accelerate I/O in cuDF, cuCIM digital pathology workflows, cuPhoton scientific-image analysis, and GPU-accelerated Presto analytics workloads. Next Steps Run the KvikIO Python example on a GDS-enabled system to observe the accelerated data path. Permission to create, read, and write files at the storage endpoint, along with access to GDS tools such as gdscheck and gds_stats . For complete installation and platform requirements, refer to the NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage documentation . Tutorial system This tutorial was tested with the following configuration: An x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18. A local NVMe device formatted with ext4 . A PIX connection between the selected GPU and NVMe device, meaning the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge. IOMMU and ACS disabled to preserve PCIe peer-to-peer transfers. AUTO instructs KvikIO to try cuFile and fall back to its POSIX backend if cuFile is unavailable. Reads smaller than the threshold use the KvikIO POSIX path directly. These settings can also be controlled through KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD . For the complete list, refer to the KvikIO runtime settings . A terminal session checking the KvikIO version, cuFile version, compatibility mode, and GDS threshold, then running a GDS diagnostic KvikIO settings can also be changed in Python. The following command writes a 1 GiB file with random data using direct I/O and flushes it to storage: $ dd if=/dev/urandom \ of=/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin \ bs=1M count=1024 \ oflag=direct conv=fsync \ status=progress The following program allocates a 1 GiB CuPy array in GPU memory and supplies it to KvikIO as the destination buffer: from pathlib import Path import cupy as cp import kvikio file_path = Path( "/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin" ) # Allocate a GPU buffer large enough to hold the file. gpu_buffer = cp.empty( file_path.stat().st_size, dtype=cp.uint8, ) # Read the file into the GPU buffer. with kvikio.CuFile(file_path, "r") as file: bytes_read = file.read(gpu_buffer) # Validate that 1 GiB was read. assert bytes_read == gpu_buffer.nbytes The context manager opens the file and completes the read into GPU memory. Although the return value confirms that the complete file was read, it does not identify the underlying data path. These statistics can be enabled by setting CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and then inspected with gds_stats while the process remains active. For this KvikIO example, the environment variable keeps the setting scoped to a single run, although it can also be configured in cufile.json . $ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py Running Python interactively keeps the process alive after the read, allowing gds_stats to inspect its accumulated counters. Figure 3 demonstrates this workflow. In the per-GPU output, nvfs counts operations representing the path taken through the nvidia-fs kernel module, while posix counts operations handled by the cuFile compatibility path. Figure 3. Table 1. cuFile execution settings that shape how KvikIO requests are processed A 1 GiB read, step by step The configuration used here has four cuFile worker threads, max_request_parallelism set to four, and min_io_threshold_size_kb set to 8192 (8 MiB). The nvidia-fs path in this configuration uses slabs no larger than 16 MiB, so each 256 MiB piece is processed through smaller transfers. The 8 MiB scheduling target does not set their transfer size. When the 8 MiB split target matters In this configuration, execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb is set to 8192 (8 MiB). Together, these examples show the broader role of KvikIO as an application-facing I/O layer over the storage acceleration GDS provides. Get started with NVIDIA KvikIO This tutorial has demonstrated how to read data into GPU memory and use level-three GDS cuFile statistics to distinguish the accelerated nvidia-fs path from CPU-staged compatibility paths. KvikIO selects whether to call cuFile, while cuFile determines the final transfer path and execution strategy. Understanding these layers enables applications to understand the path the I/O is taking and tune the settings that matter for their workload. Ready to get started? Run the KvikIO Python example featured in this post on your GDS-enabled system. For more examples, explore the C++ and Python KvikIO code in the MagnumIO GDS samples directory . Use gds_stats to check whether reads appear under nvfs or posix , then apply the same verification to your own KvikIO workloads. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 22, 2026 Back to Top
